# Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code

CCS: Software and its engineering Software creation and
managementCCS: Computing methodologies Natural language
processingCCS: Software and its engineering Software verification and
validationCCS: General and reference Surveys and overviews

Prashank Kadam email: <prashank@cerby.com> Affiliation: Cerby Inc., USA

###### Abstract.

Large language models pass most functional-correctness benchmarks, but
passing tests says little about whether their code is readable,
efficient or secure. Many techniques claim to improve these qualities,
yet their evidence is scattered, usually covers one quality dimension
and is rarely compared at an equal compute budget. We contribute a
systematic review and a controlled re-evaluation. A systematic
literature review of 628 primary studies (July 2021 to October 2026),
with disclosed, author-reviewed LLM assistance, organizes the techniques
by stage, signal source and quality target. Most studies measure only
the dimension they target, gains often come with unchanged or unreported
correctness, single automated quality signals are gamed, and compute,
variance and contamination are rarely reported. A controlled
re-evaluation runs ten techniques on four models at matched budgets on
correctness, maintainability, efficiency and security benchmarks,
extends it to thirteen current models and repository-level tasks, and
compares 66 highlighted techniques head to head on Gemma 4 31B. At one
call, quality prompting raises analyzer issue counts and leaves
complexity and judge scores almost unchanged. At matched budgets,
best-of-$`n`$ sampling with an analyzer-weighted ranker matches or beats
prompting, planning, self-refinement, a reviewer agent and retrieval on
measures the ranker does not optimize, while an analyzer feedback loop
and fine-tuning beat it only on analyzer issue counts. Large correctness
losses on HumanEval+, a likely contaminated benchmark near its ceiling,
do not appear on contests held after the models’ training cutoffs. In
the head-to-head, 1 of 66 techniques beats best-of-$`n`$ on its primary
target beyond the 95% interval, a rate consistent with chance. Gains
should be reported against a budget-matched sampling baseline and on
measures independent of the technique’s own signal.

###### Keywords: 

large language models, code generation, code quality, maintainability,
efficiency, security, systematic literature review

## 1. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) now write a large share of new code, and
the benchmarks used to judge them are running out of headroom. On
SWE-bench Verified, the most cited measure of repository-level coding,
the leading system reached 97.00% as of September 1, 2026 ([Vals AI,
2026](#as1_bib.bib520)). OpenAI stopped evaluating on it on February 23,
2026, stating that it “is increasingly contaminated” and recommending
SWE-bench Pro instead ([OpenAI, 2026m](#as1_bib.bib399)). Function-level
suites such as HumanEval and MBPP saturated earlier
(§[5](#S5 "5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
When nearly every model passes, the tests no longer tell us which code
is better.

##### Code quality is not functional correctness.

A program can pass every test and still be hard to read, slow, or
exploitable, and evidence of a large gap predates current models. When
[Pearce et al. (2022)](#as1_bib.bib407) prompted GitHub Copilot with
scenarios tied to high-risk weaknesses, about 40% of the 1,689 generated
programs were vulnerable. In BaxBench, exploits succeeded on around half
of each model’s correct back-end programs ([Vero et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib521)). [Liu et al. (2024d)](#as1_bib.bib270) found
code-style and maintainability issues in 1,930 of 4,066 ChatGPT
solutions, and on EffiBench GPT-4’s code ran on average 3.12 times as
long as the human-written canonical solutions ([Huang et al.,
2024b](#as1_bib.bib182)). Agent code was 2.3x more verbose and 2.0x more
eroded than code in 473 open-source Python repositories ([Orlanski
et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib401)). These context studies
(Section [2](#S2 "2. Background: The Quality of LLM-Generated Code ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
support our thesis: _code quality is not the same as functional
correctness_, and a technique that raises pass@1 while degrading
maintainability, efficiency or security has produced a finding, not a
success.

##### Many techniques, scattered evidence.

A fast-growing literature improves LLM code beyond correctness through
quality-oriented prompting, analyzer feedback loops, self-refinement,
multi-agent pipelines, retrieval, constrained decoding and training-time
alignment. The evidence, spread across software-engineering,
machine-learning and security venues, is hard to use for three reasons.
First, most studies measure only the dimension they target, so a
security technique’s effect on readability, or a readability technique’s
on correctness, is rarely known. Second, iterative techniques spend
several times their baselines’ compute, and gains often shrink once
compute is matched ([Olausson et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib368)). Third,
base models change faster than the studies: a technique evaluated on
GPT-3.5 in 2023 says little about its value for a 2026 reasoning model.

##### Existing reviews.

[Sun et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib498) survey 109 studies of
non-functional quality through the ISO/IEC 25010 lens and add one
patching experiment with three LLMs. [Tony et al.
(2025)](#as1_bib.bib518) review prompting techniques for secure code and
evaluate a subset on GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, for security only. Others
focus on one dimension (maintainability ([Matias et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib279)), technical debt ([Ehsani et al.,
2026b](#as1_bib.bib126)), code optimization ([Gong et al.,
2025b](#as1_bib.bib143)), secure code generation ([Patir et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib404))) or survey code generation without quality
outcomes ([Jiang et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib222));
Section [3](#S3 "3. Related Surveys and Positioning ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
compares them. None maps techniques across all three non-functional
dimensions with their effects on correctness and non-targeted
dimensions, or re-tests them head to head on the same models at matched
compute.

##### This article.

This article has two parts. The first, a systematic literature review
(SLR), follows Kitchenham-style guidelines and is reported per
SEGRESS ([Kitchenham et al., 2023](#bib.bib93)) and PRISMA 2020 ([Page
et al., 2021](#bib.bib133)). We searched OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and
arXiv from July 2021 to October 2026, calibrated the search string
against a quasi-gold standard ([Zhang et al., 2011](#bib.bib209)),
screened 6942 records with LLM assistance disclosed under
GUEST ([Kitchenham et al., 2026](#bib.bib94)), and included 628 primary
studies; the author reviewed every LLM screening, eligibility and
extraction decision
(§[4](#S4 "4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
The second, a controlled re-evaluation
(§[16](#S16 "16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
re-runs ten techniques, one or more per family, and a single-shot
baseline on a fixed grid of one closed frontier and three open-weight
models, on fixed correctness, maintainability, efficiency and security
benchmarks at matched budgets; an extended grid of thirteen current
closed and open-weight models adds the repository- and agent-level
benchmarks that dominate 2026 model releases (DeepSWE, Terminal-Bench,
FrontierCode, SlopCodeBench, GSO, SWE-fficiency, SusVibes).

The review answers five research questions:

RQ1 (taxonomy).:  
What techniques have been proposed to improve the non-functional quality
of LLM-generated code, and how can they be organized?

RQ2 (targets and measurement).:  
Which quality dimensions does each technique target, and how is each
measured?

RQ3 (effects and trade-offs).:  
What effects are reported on the target, on correctness, and on
non-targeted dimensions?

RQ4 (evidence quality).:  
How rigorous and reproducible is the evidence (baselines, compute
reporting, contamination handling, human validation, artifacts)?

RQ5 (gaps).:  
Which combinations of technique, dimension and setting are unstudied or
under-studied?

The re-evaluation adds four empirical questions (ERQ1–ERQ4,
§[16](#S16 "16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")):
matched-budget effects on the target, correctness and other dimensions;
their dependence on model strength and architecture; and how the
highlighted techniques compare in one setting.

1.  (1)

##### Main findings of the review.

Against the extracted evidence: (i) only 70 of 628 extracted studies
measured any quality dimension beyond their target
(Table [11](#S17.T11 "Table 11 ‣ RQ1 and RQ2: what is targeted, and how it is measured. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"));
(ii) among technique rows reporting a target gain, correctness was
unchanged, mixed or lower in about a quarter and unreported in nearly
three in ten
(Table [12](#S17.T12 "Table 12 ‣ RQ3: effects on correctness and on non-targeted dimensions. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
and analyzer-driven loops held correctness mainly with a test or fitness
gate
(§[9](#S9 "9. Tool-Feedback Loops ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"));
(iii) optimizing a single automated quality signal invites gaming, from
fixes that satisfy the analyzer but not reviewers to
reinforcement-learning policies that emit trivial code
(§[9](#S9 "9. Tool-Feedback Loops ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"),
§[14](#S14 "14. Training-Time Alignment for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"));
and (iv) few studies match compute, report variance or handle
contamination
(Table [13](#S17.T13 "Table 13 ‣ RQ4: evidence quality and compute fairness. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Section [17](#S17 "17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
discusses them and
§[19](#S19 "19. Research Agenda ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
derives a research agenda.

##### Main findings of the re-evaluation.

The matched-budget re-evaluation confirms the review’s pattern
(§[16.1](#S16.SS1 "16.1. Results of the main re-evaluation ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")):
(i) at equal budgets of four, eight or sixteen calls, best-of-$`n`$
sampling with an analyzer-weighted ranker matches or beats quality
prompting, planning, self-refinement, a reviewer agent and retrieval in
13 to 16 of 16 cells on the measures it does not optimize (complexity,
two judges, CWEval and BaxBench;
Table [9](#S16.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
and the analyzer’s own counts agree, so much of their reported gain over
a single shot is a budget effect, and at a single call quality
instructions and planning raise maintainability issues on every model;
(ii) the analyzer loop and the training-time techniques beat
best-of-$`n`$ beyond the 95% interval only on the issue counts their
analyzers compute, while a judge rates the analyzer loop’s code lower on
every model; (iii) on the two models with the highest single-shot
correctness, almost every technique lowers HumanEval+ pass@1 below the
single shot, the analyzer loop by up to $`9.94`$ points despite its
public-test gate, and on both Gemma models best-of-$`n`$ itself loses
hidden-test correctness as it draws more samples; (iv) weaker models
gain more in absolute terms; (v) on LiveCodeBench Pro contests held
after every cutoff, no technique changes correctness beyond the 95%
interval, so much of the HumanEval+ loss is specific to HumanEval+,
which is likely contaminated and near its ceiling for the strongest
models; and (vi) across thirteen current models, maintainability and
security rise with capability while efficiency does not, and at
repository level frontier agents write working but insecure code on
about four in ten SusVibes tasks. In the head-to-head of the highlighted
techniques
(§[16.3](#S16.SS3 "16.3. E12: Head-to-head of the highlighted techniques ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
1 of 66 beats best-of-$`n`$ on its primary target beyond the 95%
interval and 22 fall below it, although 51 improve their target over a
single shot by point estimate; security techniques lower detector hits
far more often than they raise the share of functional and secure code;
and in about half the cases efficiency techniques speed up execution
time without improving instruction counts.

## 2. Background: The Quality of LLM-Generated Code

This section fixes our quality vocabulary and summarizes the _context
studies_: empirical work that measures the non-functional quality of
LLM-generated code without proposing a technique to improve it. These
studies are not part of the review corpus
(§[4](#S4 "4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
but establish the problem the reviewed techniques address. Several
include a small mitigation experiment, treated as context here and
screened as a candidate technique study in
§[4](#S4 "4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code").

### 2.1. Quality Model

We anchor quality in ISO/IEC 25010, whose 2023 edition defines a product
quality model that “is composed of nine characteristics” with further
subcharacteristics ([ISO/IEC, 2023](#bib.bib80)); we use four of them at
source-code level. _Functional suitability_ becomes correctness (COR),
measured with tests; it is a control variable, not a target, because a
technique that improves another dimension by breaking functionality has
not improved quality. _Maintainability_, through its analysability and
modifiability subcharacteristics, becomes readability and
maintainability (R/M): naming, structure, complexity, code smells,
idiomatic style and documentation. _Performance efficiency_ becomes EFF:
runtime and memory relative to a reference solution. _Security_ becomes
SEC: vulnerabilities, mapped to the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE).
Other characteristics (e.g., compatibility and reliability) are rarely
measurable on single-function or single-repository tasks and are out of
scope. We never collapse the four dimensions into one score;
§[5](#S5 "5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
describes each measure.

### 2.2. Security

The earliest context studies concern security. [Pearce et al.
(2022)](#as1_bib.bib407) prompted GitHub Copilot with scenarios built
around high-risk CWEs and found a large share of the completions
vulnerable. [Asare et al. (2023)](#as1_bib.bib41) replayed scenarios in
which human developers had introduced C/C++ vulnerabilities; Copilot
reproduced the vulnerable code more often than the fix, though less
consistently than a human developer would. [Khoury et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib90) report that ChatGPT is aware of potential
vulnerabilities yet often generates code not robust to attack. In a user
study by [Perry et al. (2023)](#as1_bib.bib414), participants with an AI
assistant wrote significantly less secure code and were more likely to
believe it was secure. Code in the wild confirms the controlled results:
[Fu et al. (2025)](#as1_bib.bib130) found security weaknesses spanning
43 CWE categories in Copilot, CodeWhisperer and Codeium snippets in
GitHub projects.

Recent benchmarks that measure security jointly with functionality
expose the gap. BaxBench ([Vero et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib521)) executes
end-to-end exploits against generated backend applications and succeeds
on around half of the _correct_ programs. Agentic benchmarks built from
real repositories show the same for coding agents: SusVibes ([Zhao
et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib602)) finds most functionally correct agent
solutions insecure, even with vulnerability hints in the request, and
SecureVibeBench ([Chen et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib69)) finds that even
the best agent produces few solutions that are both correct and secure
(Supplementary Table  (Supplementary Material, §)).

### 2.3. Readability, Maintainability and Code Smells

For R/M, [Liu et al. (2024d)](#as1_bib.bib270) ran static analyzers on
ChatGPT solutions to Java and Python tasks and found code-style and
maintainability issues in close to half. Compared with canonical
solutions, closed- and open-source LLMs “tend to produce code that is
shorter yet more complicated” ([Dou et al., 2026](#bib.bib43)).
[Yetiştiren et al. (2023)](#bib.bib204) measured code smells and
technical debt for Copilot, CodeWhisperer and ChatGPT on HumanEval. At
project level, a difference-in-differences study of GitHub projects that
adopted Cursor found “a statistically significant, large, but transient
increase in project-level development velocity, along with a substantial
and persistent increase in static analysis warnings and code complexity”
([He et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib169)). [Paul et al.
(2025)](#as1_bib.bib405) compare Java code from Gemini Pro, ChatGPT,
Codex and Falcon with professionally written reference solutions and
find more smells in every model, with the gap growing with task
complexity. CodeSmellEval ([Velasco et al., 2025](#bib.bib186)) measures
a model’s propensity to produce specific smells, and its
follow-up ([Velasco et al., 2026](#bib.bib187)) relates that propensity
to decoding strategy, model size, architecture and prompt formulation.
[Abbassi et al. (2025)](#bib.bib1) derive a taxonomy of inefficiencies
in LLM-generated Python code spanning logic, performance, readability
and maintainability. At repository scale, [Liu et al.
(2026b)](#as1_bib.bib271) attribute static-analysis issues to
AI-authored commits across thousands of GitHub repositories and find
that code smells dominate and a substantial share of introduced issues
persists to the latest revision.

Industry telemetry points the same way, with weaker methodological
guarantees; we report it as grey literature, never as evidence for or
against a technique. GitClear’s analysis of changed lines reports a
rising share of copy-pasted code and a falling share of moved,
refactored code over the analyzed period ([GitClear,
2025](#as1_bib.bib138)). Sonar’s SonarQube analysis of Java assignments
reports that a newer model raised benchmark pass rates while increasing
bug severity ([Sonar, 2025](#as1_bib.bib484)); the accompanying
vendor-authored preprint finds “no direct correlation” between a model’s
pass@1 and the number of issues in its passing solutions ([Sabra et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib451)).

### 2.4. Performance Efficiency

Efficiency benchmarks report LLM code relative to a fast human reference
solution per task. EffiBench ([Huang et al., 2024b](#as1_bib.bib182))
evaluates 42 models on LeetCode problems and finds generated code
generally slower than the canonical solutions. Mercury ([Du et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib122)) introduces a runtime-percentile-weighted pass
score (Beyond) and reports a clear gap between pass rate and Beyond.
EffiBench-X ([Qing et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib422)) extends the
comparison to Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, Ruby and Go and finds that
models “consistently underperform human experts in efficiency”, with
larger gaps in Java, C++ and Go than in Python, Ruby and JavaScript.
EvalPerf ([Liu et al., 2024b](#as1_bib.bib265)) stresses solutions with
expensive inputs and finds that “the scaling law fails to account for
code efficiency”. [Niu et al. (2024)](#as1_bib.bib343) run a similar
evaluation on HumanEval, MBPP and LeetCode and also try efficiency
prompts, and NoFunEval ([Singhal et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib480)) shows
that code models “generally falter” on non-functional requirements,
including efficiency, security and maintainability.

### 2.5. Verbosity, Erosion and Length Bias

A recurring finding is that LLM code is longer than necessary and
degrades as it is extended. SlopCodeBench ([Orlanski et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib401)) has agents repeatedly extend their own solutions
and measures two forms of degradation, structural erosion and verbosity;
both rise in most trajectories, and explicit quality guidance lowers
their initial level “without affecting degradation rates”. Two training
mechanisms plausibly contribute to verbosity, though neither was studied
on code quality directly. In reinforcement learning from human feedback
(RLHF), [Singhal et al. (2023)](#as1_bib.bib481) find reward
improvements “to largely be driven by increasing response length” and
trace this to reward models; length bias also distorts LLM-judge
evaluators ([Dubois et al., 2024](#bib.bib46)), which matters for
LLM-as-judge readability scores
(§[5](#S5 "5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), [Liu et al.
(2025d)](#as1_bib.bib272) identify an optimization bias in GRPO that
“artificially increases response length (especially for incorrect
outputs)”. Reasoning models add a related cost: [Chen et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib27) describe _overthinking_, “where excessive
computational resources are allocated for simple problems with minimal
benefit”, and a survey of efficient reasoning catalogues remedies ([Sui
et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib497)). For code generation, [Xue et al.
(2026a)](#bib.bib197) study thinking models’ reasoning traces on
BigCodeBench and find that modest reductions in step count often
preserve success on standard tasks. To our knowledge, whether verbose
reasoning yields verbose _code_ is not yet measured directly.

### 2.6. Implications for This Review

Three observations shape the paper. First, correctness and the other
dimensions diverge: BaxBench, SusVibes and SecureVibeBench report large
fractions of correct programs that are insecure, and the Sonar data
(grey literature) suggest that a model upgrade can raise pass rates
while making defects more severe, so a correctness benchmark alone
cannot show whether a technique improves code. Second, the gaps exist on
every dimension we study and persist across model generations, from
Copilot in 2021 to agents in 2026, so technique-level remedies are worth
reviewing. Third, the studies use different instruments (static
analyzers, exploits, runtime ratios, smell detectors), so their numbers
are not comparable across rows of Supplementary Table ;
§[5](#S5 "5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
addresses this measurement problem, and
§[16](#S16 "16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
re-evaluates techniques under one protocol for this reason.

## 3. Related Surveys and Positioning

Supplementary Table  compares this review with existing secondary
studies, grouped by breadth.

##### General surveys of LLMs for code.

Broad reviews map the field, not its quality dimensions: [Hou et al.
(2024)](#as1_bib.bib175) review LLMs across software engineering tasks,
[Jiang et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib222) organize LLM code generation by
data, training, prompting, retrieval and evaluation and collate reported
HumanEval, MBPP and BigCodeBench results, and [Dong et al.
(2025a)](#as1_bib.bib120) survey LLM-based code generation agents,
including single- and multi-agent architectures. They cover many
techniques we review but judge them by functional correctness. A
tertiary study of 30 secondary studies finds accuracy “strong on
benchmarks but weakly supported for real-world generalization” and calls
for “holistic, standardized evaluation” ([Chochlov et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib77)).

##### Dimension-specific reviews.

For SEC, [Tony et al. (2025)](#as1_bib.bib518) review prompting
techniques and test a subset on secure code generation, [Basic and
Giaretta (2024)](#as1_bib.bib54) review LLM-introduced vulnerabilities
and how prompting affects their detection and repair, and the SoK of
[Patir et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib404) systematizes prompting,
fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and agentic workflows for secure
code and measures a gap between models’ knowledge of secure-coding
principles and their code. For R/M, [Matias et al.
(2026)](#as1_bib.bib279) review how LLMs affect maintainability and
evolvability, the multivocal review of [Ehsani et al.
(2026b)](#as1_bib.bib126) on technical debt in LLM-assisted development
notes that “no standardized benchmarks or LLM-specific metrics yet
exist”, and [Alomari et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib19) review LLMs for
refactoring and smell detection and find LLM-refactored code “not
reliable”. For EFF, [Gong et al. (2025b)](#as1_bib.bib143) review
language-model-based code optimization, and [Ali et al.
(2026)](#as1_bib.bib16) review the energy efficiency of LLM-generated
code and find the evidence “limited and highly heterogeneous”. [Yang
et al. (2024c)](#as1_bib.bib572) cover non-functional properties of code
models, but their efficiency dimension concerns the models, not the code
they generate. [Pan et al. (2024)](#bib.bib134) taxonomize
self-correction by training-time, generation-time and post-hoc stage,
and [Kamoi et al. (2024)](#as1_bib.bib228) conclude that it “works well
in tasks that can use reliable external feedback”, which motivates our
signal-source facet
(§[6](#S6 "6. A Faceted Taxonomy of Quality-Improving Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
[He et al. (2026b)](#as1_bib.bib172) cover nine quality dimensions but
organize them around training-data causes of defects rather than
improvement techniques.

##### Closest prior work.

Two studies share parts of our design. [Sun et al.
(2026)](#as1_bib.bib498) use ISO/IEC 25010, review the literature on
non-functional quality of generated code, run industry workshops and
patch real issues with three LLMs. They find that research “primarily
emphasizes security, performance efficiency, and maintainability” while
practitioners prioritize maintainability and readability, and that
prompt-based optimization of these characteristics is unstable. Their
experiment, however, only regenerates SWE-bench Lite patches with
SWE-agent under quality-oriented prompts and feedback: one task type, no
comparison of technique families and no matched compute budgets. [Tony
et al. (2025)](#as1_bib.bib518) combine a systematic review with
controlled experiments, the design we follow, but cover only security
and prompting, with GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.

##### Test-time compute and cost-controlled evaluation.

A separate line of work asks what extra inference compute buys for
correctness. Repeated sampling raises the share of problems solved by at
least one sample roughly log-linearly with the number of samples, but
selecting the right sample without a verifier plateaus ([Brown et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18)); allocating test-time compute adaptively per prompt
beats a best-of-$`N`$ baseline ([Snell et al., 2024](#bib.bib172)); and
several samples from a smaller code model can beat one sample from a
larger model at the same budget when unit tests are available to select
among them ([Hassid et al., 2024](#bib.bib60)). [Kapoor et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib87) argue that agents should be evaluated jointly on
cost and accuracy, and [Stroebl et al. (2024)](#as1_bib.bib495) show
that with an imperfect verifier, such as unit tests, resampling cannot
remove false positives that pass the verifier, so its accuracy is
bounded at any budget, and that these false positives may also adhere
poorly to coding conventions. Closest to our first question, the gains
of self-repair over resampling at an equal number of programs are often
modest and sometimes absent for code correctness ([Olausson et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib368)), and two 2026 preprints on small open models
report that Self-Refine and Reflexion lose to repeated sampling at equal
token cost on mathematics benchmarks ([Mirzaei, 2026](#bib.bib120)) and
that none of 26 post-hoc selection, verification and repair operators
improves held-out code correctness over best-of-$`N`$ at matched compute
([Iscan, 2026](#bib.bib77)). Our re-evaluation builds on these results
rather than preceding them: it asks the same matched-budget question for
maintainability, efficiency and security as well as correctness, and
measures it on instruments independent of each technique’s own signal,
where the analyzer-weighted best-of-$`n`$ ranker we use is itself an
imperfect verifier whose loss of hidden-test correctness as $`n`$ grows
(Supplementary Material, §) is what [Stroebl et al.
(2024)](#as1_bib.bib495) predict.

##### Gap.

To our knowledge, no study re-tests quality-improvement techniques
across R/M, EFF and SEC and several models under matched budgets, on
measures independent of each technique’s own signal, and no review maps
techniques across R/M, EFF and SEC together while recording their effect
on COR and on non-targeted dimensions, which dimension-specific reviews
cannot do by construction. This review addresses both:
§§[8](#S8 "8. Prompting for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")–[14](#S14 "14. Training-Time Alignment for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
synthesize reported effects on targeted and non-targeted dimensions, and
§[16](#S16 "16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
re-evaluates representative techniques under one protocol.

## 4. Review Methodology

We followed the software-engineering guidelines for systematic
literature reviews and report per SEGRESS ([Kitchenham et al.,
2023](#bib.bib93)) and the PRISMA 2020 flow ([Page et al.,
2021](#bib.bib133)). Research questions, search strings, criteria,
extraction schema and quality-assessment items (Supplementary Material,
§), together with all queries, raw exports, screening decisions, prompts
and extraction data, will be released.
§[4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6. Use of generative AI in this review ‣ 4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
discloses LLM assistance per GUEST ([Kitchenham et al.,
2026](#bib.bib94)).

### 4.1. Scope, sources and search

We ask which techniques improve the non-functional quality (readability
and maintainability, performance efficiency, security;
§[2](#S2 "2. Background: The Quality of LLM-Generated Code ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
of code that LLMs generate or edit, with correctness recorded as a
co-outcome. A _technique_ is any intervention on the input, decoding, a
post-generation loop or the model’s weights that changes the code an LLM
produces. The window runs from the release of Codex and HumanEval
(2021-07-07) ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib26)) to the search in October 2026.

Scripted searches covered three sources: OpenAlex (title and abstract),
Semantic Scholar (bulk title-and-abstract search) and arXiv (title or
abstract). The primary string is S1 = F1 $`\wedge`$ F2 $`\wedge`$ F3,
with a model facet F1 (e.g., “large language model\*”, LLM, GPT\*,
Copilot), a task facet F2 (e.g., “code generation”, “generated code”,
“program synthesis”) and a quality facet F3 (e.g., readab\*,
maintainab\*, “code smell\*”, “execution time”, “energy efficien\*”,
vulnerab\*, CWE). A supplementary string S2 = F1 $`\wedge`$ F2
$`\wedge`$ F4 replaces F3 with technique terms (e.g., “self-refin\*”,
“static analy\*”, rerank\*, DPO, “reinforcement learning”) to catch
papers that measure quality without naming it in the abstract;
Supplementary Material § lists the exact per-source strings.

### 4.2. Calibration and recall

Before inspecting any result we froze a quasi-gold standard
(QGS) ([Zhang et al., 2011](#bib.bib209)) of 32 seed technique studies
meeting the inclusion criteria. The first S1 retrieved 22 (recall 0.688;
target 0.85): missed studies described editing, repairing or optimizing
code without the phrase “code generation” or wrote “code LM” for “LLM”,
and the technique facet lacked prompting terms. One logged iteration
widened F1 and F2, added prompting terms to F4 and re-ran S1 and S2 on
Semantic Scholar and arXiv; OpenAlex was queried with the original S1
only
(§[20](#S20 "20. Threats to Validity ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
The union retrieved 14664 records, 6942 after deduplication by DOI,
arXiv ID and normalized title, with QGS recall 0.938 (30 of 32;
Self-Refine ([Madaan et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib276)), which names
neither a task nor a quality term, was left to snowballing).

Some added terms came from QGS misses, so post-iteration QGS recall is
optimistic; two independent checks complement it. A venue sweep found
274 papers from 2021 onward in 21 software-engineering, machine-learning
and security venues whose _titles_ match F1 and F2; of the 131 not in
our results, 16 passed title/abstract screening, against 55 relevant
papers the search found, a screening-stage venue-level recall estimate
of 0.775. OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar retrieved 10 of the 11 QGS papers
published by ACM or IEEE. Studies from these checks, snowballing and our
section-level searches enter the flow as “other methods”
(Fig. [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4.3. Selection ‣ 4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).

### 4.3. Selection

A study is included if it (IC1) proposes or evaluates a technique
applied to an LLM, (IC2) evaluates code an LLM generated or edited,
(IC3) reports at least one quantitative non-functional outcome for that
code (tool-based, execution-based, LLM-judged or human-rated), and (IC4)
is a full paper, peer-reviewed or a preprint of four or more pages. It
is excluded if it is not in English (EC1), is a secondary study (EC2),
targets non-code artifacts such as tests or comments (EC3), only
analyzes or repairs human-written code (EC4), measures quality only as
correctness or compilability (EC5), concerns model robustness or attacks
rather than code quality (EC6), uses pre-LLM models (EC7), or duplicates
another study (EC8). Excluded studies feed three side lists: _context_
studies measuring LLM code quality without an intervention
(§[2](#S2 "2. Background: The Quality of LLM-Generated Code ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
_adjacent_ studies of LLM refactoring or repair of human code, and
influential _correctness-only_ techniques, untested for quality and thus
candidates for our re-evaluation.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1. PRISMA 2020 flow diagram. Screening, full-text assessment and
extraction were LLM-assisted and author-reviewed.Flow diagram of the
review: records identified by database searches, other methods and
snowballing, then screened, sought for retrieval, assessed for
eligibility and included, with the number excluded at each step.

### 4.4. Screening, snowballing, extraction and appraisal

Claude Opus 5.5, as single screener, applied the criteria to titles and
abstracts through a frozen prompt (Supplementary Material, §) with a
recall-favouring rule: records judged _include_ or _uncertain_ go
forward, as do, unscreened, records it declined to classify. Of 6942
database records, 1242 went forward. One backward and one forward
snowballing iteration over the Semantic Scholar citation graph, seeded
with the title/abstract inclusions and screened the same way, added 4580
new records, of which 506 went forward to full text and were assessed
and extracted like the database reports; 210 were included
(Fig. [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4.3. Selection ‣ 4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).

Full texts came from arXiv, open-access copies and the ACL Anthology.
Only reports whose full text was retrieved were assessed: the 687 of the
1777 reports sought for which no full text could be retrieved were
excluded as not retrieved, so no report was assessed, extracted or
synthesized from its abstract alone. In two stages, a low-cost model
(Claude Haiku 5.5) removed only reports that unambiguously failed the
criteria, and Claude Opus 5.5 read every remaining report in full,
decided eligibility and filled the extraction schema (Supplementary
Material, §): bibliographic data, study type, technique, the three
facets, tools, iteration budget, targeted and measured dimensions,
metrics and their instrument type, benchmarks, languages, models,
baselines, the direction of effect on the target, on correctness and on
each other dimension with the headline numbers as printed, compute
reporting, contamination handling, human evaluation and artifacts. Every
row carries a confidence level; low-confidence rows are flagged for
human review. Each study was scored on ten quality-assessment (QA) items
(0, 0.5 or 1 each): reimplementable description, appropriate baseline,
validated metric, correctness reported, more than one model, variance
reported, compute reported, artifacts, contamination considered, and
threats discussed. QA weights confidence in the synthesis but excludes
nothing. A final consistency pass over the studies included from the
database and other-method searches found six duplicate records (EC8),
none with a retrievable full text, so
Fig. [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4.3. Selection ‣ 4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
counts them among the reports not retrieved, and removed six studies
whose only intervention was not evaluated as a way to improve code
quality: two quantization studies, three benchmark papers and a
mathematical problem-solving benchmark (IC1); the five that measure the
quality of LLM code moved to the context list. A second audit of each of
these studies against the criteria, reading each full text, removed five
further duplicates (the EC8 count of
Fig. [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4.3. Selection ‣ 4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
and three studies outside the criteria (no code evaluated, EC3; safety
rather than code quality, EC6; no quality outcome for the generated
code, IC3), moved two studies without an intervention to the context
list, and corrected one publication year; every change is logged in the
replication package.

Every number attributed to a specific paper was re-read in its primary
source: a script downloads the source text, checks that a verbatim
quotation containing the number occurs in it, and logs the number with
its location and setting. Effect directions in the synthesis tables come
from the author-reviewed, LLM-assisted extraction; numbers quoted in the
text and per-family tables do not rely on it.

### 4.5. Synthesis

Effects come from different benchmarks, metrics and models, so we do not
pool them in a meta-analysis. Following SWiM ([Campbell et al.,
2020](#bib.bib20)), we (i) classify each technique on the three facets
of
§[6](#S6 "6. A Faceted Taxonomy of Quality-Improving Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
and map families and signal sources against quality dimensions; (ii)
count directions of effect, tabulating effect on correctness against
effect on the target
(Table [12](#S17.T12 "Table 12 ‣ RQ3: effects on correctness and on non-targeted dimensions. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"));
(iii) report how often non-targeted dimensions were measured at all
(Table [11](#S17.T11 "Table 11 ‣ RQ1 and RQ2: what is targeted, and how it is measured. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"));
and (iv) summarize evidence quality by family
(Table [13](#S17.T13 "Table 13 ‣ RQ4: evidence quality and compute fairness. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Vote counts ignore effect and study size, so they describe the evidence
rather than rank techniques. Every included study was assessed and
extracted from its full text; 59% are preprints. Few included studies
predate 2023: of 647 records from 2021–2022, 9 passed screening (early
work mostly targets correctness or pre-LLM models) and 1 was included.
Re-counted on the peer-reviewed studies alone (Supplementary Material,
§), the synthesis is unchanged: the target improves in 74.8% of
technique rows (76.1% overall), correctness is unreported in 27.2%
(28.5%) and worsens in 7.8% (7.5%), a non-targeted dimension is measured
in 12% (11%), and the median QA score is 6.0 (6.0 overall).

### 4.6. Use of generative AI in this review

Per GUEST ([Kitchenham et al., 2026](#bib.bib94)), LLMs (i) screened
titles and abstracts (Claude Opus 5.5, frozen prompt, effort=low), (ii)
assessed full-text eligibility (Claude Haiku 5.5 for clear exclusions,
Claude Opus 5.5 for all other reports), (iii) extracted data and QA
scores (Claude Opus 5.5; for the snowballing reports the same model and
prompt ran as agents that read each full text from a file, with a check
that every line was read), and (iv) helped draft text, which authors
checked against the primary sources. All prompts, model identifiers,
dates and raw outputs are archived. The author reviewed the screening,
eligibility and extraction decisions and corrected those found wrong. To
measure the error rate of the LLM decisions, as [Baltes et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib12) recommend, a second coder, an engineer who is not an
author and was blind to the LLM’s decisions, recoded random samples of
322 title/abstract records, 186 full-text eligibility decisions and 139
technique rows from 124 included studies. Agreement with the LLM was
91.4% at title/abstract (Cohen’s $`\kappa=`$ 0.78) and 80.1% at full
text ($`\kappa=`$ 0.69); of the 53 sampled records the second coder
included, the LLM screener excluded 2 (a false-exclusion rate of 3.8%).
On the extraction sample, field-level agreement was 85.6% overall, 88.4%
for the three facets and 79.1% for the directions of effect.
Disagreements were resolved by discussion between the second coder and
the author. Because the vote counts rest on the directions,
Table [12](#S17.T12 "Table 12 ‣ RQ3: effects on correctness and on non-targeted dimensions. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
shows for every count the range it could take if directions were wrong
at the rate at which the second coder disagreed (20.9%): most technique
rows still report an improved target (55–82%), and 20–35% leave
correctness unreported. The author overturned none of the screener’s
title/abstract decisions (the reports sought are exactly those it marked
include or uncertain), reversed no full-text exclusion, overturned 11 of
the 644 inclusions on the criteria (1.7%; the six IC1 studies, three
studies outside the criteria and two moved to the context list,
described below) and removed five more as duplicates, and corrected 4 of
the 920 extracted technique rows (three missing targets, one year);
every correction is logged in the replication package. The
title/abstract screener ran at effort=low, the setting of its pilot on
30 records.

## 5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks

A technique improves code quality only relative to an instrument that
measures it. We review the instruments for each dimension of
§[2](#S2 "2. Background: The Quality of LLM-Generated Code ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"),
the benchmarks that package them (Supplementary Tables  and ,
Supplementary Material, §), and the threats that limit them. Two
observations recur: every non-functional metric is a proxy whose
validity has been questioned empirically, often by authors of later
benchmarks; and most quality numbers come from the kind of tool some
techniques use as feedback
(§[9](#S9 "9. Tool-Feedback Loops ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
entangling measurement and optimization.

### 5.1. Metrics per quality dimension

##### Correctness (COR).

Function-level benchmarks report pass@$`k`$, the probability that at
least one of $`k`$ samples passes the hidden tests, computed with the
unbiased estimator of [Chen et al. (2021)](#bib.bib26) from $`n\geq k`$
samples of which $`c`$ pass. Repository-level benchmarks report the
resolve rate, the share of instances whose patch makes the fail-to-pass
and regression tests pass ([Jimenez et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib224)).
Both are only as strong as the tests: EvalPlus extended the HumanEval
tests by 80x, lowering pass@$`k`$ by up to 19.3-28.9% and changing model
rankings ([Liu et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib263)). Since several quality
benchmarks condition on correctness, weak tests propagate into every
other dimension.

##### Readability and maintainability (R/M).

The oldest instruments are structural metrics: cyclomatic complexity
([McCabe, 1976](#bib.bib117)), Halstead’s operator and operand counts,
and the Maintainability Index (MI), a composite of lines of code,
cyclomatic complexity and Halstead volume ([Coleman et al.,
1994](#bib.bib33); [contributors, 2026c](#bib.bib36)). Cognitive
Complexity, introduced by SonarSource in 2017 ([SonarSource,
2026](#bib.bib174)), weights nesting and breaks in linear flow; a
meta-analysis of about 24,000 ratings of 427 snippets found it
correlates with comprehension time and subjective understandability but
gives mixed results for comprehension correctness ([Barón et al.,
2020](#bib.bib13)). Linters and smell detectors (Pylint, Ruff,
SonarQube, PMD) count rule violations ([contributors,
2026b](#bib.bib35); [Astral, 2026](#bib.bib9); [contributors,
2026a](#bib.bib34)). Recent results undercut these proxies for
LLM-generated code. In MaintainCoder, MI and cyclomatic complexity moved
in opposite directions, and multi-agent pipelines scored high MI yet
lost correctness after a requirement change ([Wang et al.,
2025c](#as1_bib.bib534)). Across 787,562 human and AI-written function
pairs, complexity metrics carried little signal once size was controlled
for ([Improta et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib194)). On C# tasks, correctness
and structural quality were nearly uncorrelated (Pearson $`r`$ = 0.075)
([Ghalandarian et al., 2026](#bib.bib51)). Learned readability models
([Buse and Weimer, 2010](#bib.bib19); [Scalabrino et al.,
2018](#bib.bib158)), trained on human-written code, showed only limited
correlation with developer ratings on AI-generated Java ([Sergeyuk
et al., 2024](#bib.bib160)).

LLM judges are proposed as a scalable substitute for human readability
assessment ([He et al., 2026b](#bib.bib64)); ICE-Score and CodeJudge
were validated against correctness and human preference ([Zhuo,
2024](#bib.bib225); [Tong and Zhang, 2024](#bib.bib182)). Validity
evidence is weaker for quality than for correctness: on CoReEval, LLM
readability scores correlated with human ratings at Pearson 0.25 in
Java, below the 0.31 of [Scalabrino et al.](#bib.bib158)’s static model,
and at 0.02 in Python ([Ouédraogo et al., 2025](#bib.bib132)). Judges
are also sensitive to presentation: general-purpose judges show
position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases ([Zheng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib217)), which motivated length-controlled scoring ([Dubois
et al., 2024](#bib.bib46)). For code, all judges tested by [Moon et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib122) shifted scores under superficial edits such as
renamed variables or added comments, even when asked to write tests
first; software-engineering judge decisions change with prompt cues on
unchanged code ([Zhao et al., 2026b](#bib.bib215)); order effects
persist in CodeJudgeBench ([Jiang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib82)); and
judges prefer longer code explanations where developers prefer shorter
ones ([Mittal et al., 2026](#bib.bib121)). Human evaluation remains the
reference but is expensive ([He et al., 2026b](#bib.bib64)); recent
developer studies show it surfaces production-readiness issues no
benchmark metric captures ([Szych and Schwerk, 2026](#bib.bib179)).

##### Efficiency (EFF).

Efficiency metrics differ in what they time and how they normalize.
EffiBench reports execution time, peak memory and total memory usage (a
time integral of memory), normalized by a canonical solution ([Huang
et al., 2024b](#as1_bib.bib182)). Mercury’s Beyond weights pass by
runtime percentile among human solutions ([Du et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib122)), and Venus uses percentiles to avoid
hardware-specific absolute numbers ([Du et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib123)).
ENAMEL’s eff@$`k`$ generalizes pass@$`k`$ to efficiency against expert
references, with an unbiased estimator for right-censored (timed-out)
runs ([Qiu et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib423)). EvalPerf’s Differential
Performance Score (DPS) ranks a solution against clusters of reference
solutions by CPU instruction count, not wall-clock time ([Liu et al.,
2024b](#as1_bib.bib265)), as does COFFE ([Peng et al.,
2025c](#as1_bib.bib411)); PIE measures speedup in the gem5 simulator
([Shypula et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib475)). The reason is noise: WEDGE
measured run-to-run variation of 12% for physical time against 0.03% for
instruction counts ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib200)), and PIE’s authors
note that hardware variability yields spurious improvements ([Shypula
et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib475)). Few studies measure energy; where they
do, rankings of human and LLM code flip across a server, a PC and a
Raspberry Pi ([Apsan et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib35)). Passing solutions
to one task can differ widely in memory behavior ([Rajput et al.,
2026](#bib.bib151)), so one sample per task understates variance.

##### Security (SEC).

Most security benchmarks rely on static application security testing
(SAST) ([Peng et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib409)): CodeQL, Bandit and
Semgrep ([GitHub, 2026](#bib.bib53); [PyCQA, 2026](#bib.bib143);
[Semgrep, 2026](#bib.bib159)), with findings mapped to CWE identifiers
([Pearce et al., 2022](#as1_bib.bib407); [Fu et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib130)). These tools disagree and miss vulnerabilities:
on the same generated code, Bandit flags 28% to 46% of programs and
CodeQL 9.1% to 17% ([Alrashedy et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib20)). CodeQL
detected 27 of 120 manually validated Java vulnerabilities ([Li et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib100)); a single C/C++ SAST warned on 52% of real
vulnerability-contributing commits, at least 76% of its warnings were
irrelevant, and 22% of commits went undetected ([Charoenwet et al.,
2024](#bib.bib22)); and across 15 SAST tools detection rates were low
([Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib224)). Studies therefore require tool
agreement ([Sajadi et al., 2025](#bib.bib156)) or replace SAST with
execution: exploit- and test-based oracles (BaxBench, CWEval, SeCodePLT)
run expert-written attacks or security unit tests against the program
([Vero et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib521); [Peng et al.,
2025a](#as1_bib.bib409); [Nie et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib342)). They pair
naturally with correctness: CWEval’s func-sec@$`k`$ applies the
pass@$`k`$ estimator to samples both functional and secure ([Peng
et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib409)), and BaxBench’s sec_pass@$`k`$ counts
programs that pass all tests and resist all exploits ([Vero et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib521)). The joint metric matters because a program that
does nothing is trivially secure: [Dai et al. (2026a)](#as1_bib.bib97)
found that secure-code techniques often trade functionality for
security, many degrading the base model’s joint performance by more than
50%.

### 5.2. Benchmarks

Supplementary Tables  and  list the most used benchmarks, which fall
into three generations. Correctness benchmarks (HumanEval+, MBPP+,
LiveCodeBench, BigCodeBench, SWE-bench) carry no quality oracle, so
quality is scored post hoc on their outputs. Function-level quality
benchmarks from 2022–2024 (RACE, NoFunEval, EffiBench, Mercury,
EvalPerf, ENAMEL, ECCO, the early security sets) attach one oracle to
short algorithmic or snippet tasks. Since 2025, benchmarks have moved to
repositories and agents: SWE-Perf, GSO and SWE-Pro for performance ([He
et al., 2026c](#as1_bib.bib173); [Shetty et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib469);
[Sarıkayak et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib455)); SecRepoBench,
SecureVibeBench, SusVibes and RealSec-bench for security ([Shen et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib467); [Chen et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib69); [Zhao
et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib602); [Wang et al., 2026g](#as1_bib.bib533));
and SlopCodeBench, MaintainBench and CQBench for maintainability
([Orlanski et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib401); [Wang et al.,
2025c](#as1_bib.bib534); [Improta et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib194)).
Repository-level results are uniformly low: the best agent passes 14.8%
of SlopCodeBench checkpoints, with structural erosion rising in 77% of
trajectories ([Orlanski et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib401)); leading agents
succeed on fewer than 5% of GSO tasks ([Shetty et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib469)); and on SusVibes 57% of one agent’s solutions
are functionally correct but only 11.8% are secure ([Zhao et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib602)). PerfCodeBench extends the efficiency gap to
systems code with parallelism and GPU tasks ([Jing et al.,
2026](#bib.bib85)), and SWE-fficiency to 498 optimization tasks in nine
data-science and HPC repositories, where agents reach on average “less
than 0.23x the expert speedup” ([Ma et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib274)). On
the newest security benchmark, built from 150 real vulnerabilities, the
strongest of six frontier agents writes functional and secure code for
only 25.1% of 450 tasks ([Wu et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib542)).

Two further lines broaden what “quality” means for agents. Refactoring
and long-horizon maintenance benchmarks score behaviour-preserving
structural change in real repositories: SWE-Refactor (1,099 Java
refactorings, where a Codex agent succeeds on 39.4% of compound ones)
([Xu et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib563)), SmellBench (294 injected smells;
best smell-elimination score 50.34) ([Lin et al.,
2026b](#as1_bib.bib260)), CodeTaste ([Thillen et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib514)), SWE-Bench ProMax ([Shi et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib472)), SWE-CI, which infers maintainability from
correctness changes across a repository’s commit history ([Chen et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib68)), SWE-EVO ([Le et al., 2025](#bib.bib97)), the
refactoring track of SWE Atlas ([Raghavendra et al.,
2026](#bib.bib149)), and SWE-NFI, where at most 70.0% of valid agent
outputs preserve functionality while making non-functional improvements
([Xue et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib564)). Instruction-following benchmarks
attach checkable quality constraints to ordinary tasks: SWE-IF’s 30
verifiable instructions ([Zhong et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib609)), CIFE’s
1,000 tasks with constraints in 13 categories, with strict adherence of
39-66% ([Gunnu et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib163)), and CodeAlignBench
([Mehralian et al., 2025](#bib.bib118)). Like RACE and NoFunEval, they
measure compliance rather than default quality
(§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3. Critiques ‣ 5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
The coding benchmarks most reported at the leading 2026 model launches
are Terminal-Bench ([Merrill et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib284)) and DeepSWE
([Huang et al., 2026d](#as1_bib.bib187)), which writes 113 long-horizon
tasks from scratch in 91 repositories and grades them with hand-written
verifiers that an independent judge disputes in 1.4% of runs against
32.4% for SWE-Bench Pro’s inherited tests; FrontierCode adds a
code-quality rubric to functional blockers and publishes the composite
score and the plain correct rate ([Cognition, 2026](#as1_bib.bib81)).
For correctness, live benchmarks add tasks to stay ahead of training
data: LiveCodeBench Pro (Codeforces, ICPC and IOI problems, best model
53% pass@1 on medium and 0% on hard problems without tools) ([Zheng
et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib607); [LiveCodeBench Pro authors,
2025](#bib.bib112)), SWE-rebench ([Badertdinov et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib44)) and SWE-bench-Live ([Zhang et al.,
2025b](#as1_bib.bib597)); Multi-SWE-bench extends issue resolution to
seven languages ([Zan et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib590)).

### 5.3. Critiques

##### Saturation.

As of September 2026, the top vals.ai score on the 500-task SWE-bench
Verified was 97.00%, with the third model at 96.20%, and vals.ai has
archived it as saturated ([Vals AI, 2026](#as1_bib.bib520)). On February
23, 2026, OpenAI stopped reporting it as “increasingly contaminated” and
recommended SWE-bench Pro instead: in an audited subset of tasks that
models often failed, at least 59.4% had flawed tests that reject correct
submissions, and all frontier models tested could reproduce the gold
patch or verbatim problem details for some tasks ([OpenAI,
2026m](#as1_bib.bib399)). SWE-bench Pro is already under strain: an
audit found reward hacking through leaked gold solutions and hidden
evaluation information, with models scoring “substantially worse” once
these were removed ([Zheng et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib606)). HumanEval+,
MBPP+, LiveCodeBench v6 and SWE-bench Verified now serve only as legacy
anchors to earlier work.

##### Contamination.

Popular code benchmarks overlap substantially with open pre-training
corpora, and models score higher on the overlap ([Riddell et al.,
2024](#bib.bib153)); leakage also enters through synthetic training data
and model selection on test sets ([Matton et al., 2024](#bib.bib116)).
LiveCodeBench was built for this: DeepSeek and GPT-4-O dropped on
LeetCode problems released after their cutoffs ([Jain et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib217)). Its protection lasts only while releases
continue: the latest, v6, holds 1055 problems from May 2023 to April
2025 ([LiveCodeBench authors, 2025](#bib.bib111)), leaving no clean
split for models with later cutoffs. LiveCodeBench Pro was refreshed
quarterly until its last public set, for July to September 2025
([LiveCodeBench Pro authors, 2025](#bib.bib112)), so a clean split for
2026 models requires applying its protocol to contests held after their
cutoffs; SWE-rebench and SWE-bench-Live still add tasks ([Badertdinov
et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib44); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#as1_bib.bib597)).
Most efficiency benchmarks reuse LeetCode, HumanEval or MBPP problems,
which EffiBench-X names as a contamination risk, filtering to problems
released after October 2023 ([Qing et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib422)).
SWE-bench Pro uses copyleft and private codebases to resist training
exposure ([Deng et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib117)). Only the benchmarks
marked _date_, _held-out_ or _new_ in Supplementary Tables  and  offer
any protection for models with 2026 cutoffs.

##### Quality measured only when requested.

RACE states each non-functional requirement in the prompt and scores
whether the model follows it ([Zheng et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib604));
NoFunEval likewise names the requirement in the edit instruction
([Singhal et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib480)). They thus measure instruction
following on quality, not a model’s default quality, which is what a
technique must change. CWEval deliberately avoids security hints in
prompts ([Peng et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib409)), and RealSec-bench found
that generic security guidance in the prompt often broke compilation
without preventing vulnerabilities ([Wang et al.,
2026g](#as1_bib.bib533)).

##### Similarity to a reference.

Because latency and resource use are hard to measure across target
platforms, NoFunEval scores those edits with DiffBLEU, the similarity of
the model’s diff to a reference diff, and weights CodeQL success by
DiffBLEU for maintainability and security edits ([Singhal et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib480)). A correct but different improvement scores low.
Token-matching metrics correlate weakly with human judgment ([Zhuo,
2024](#bib.bib225)) and are unreliable indicators of functional
correctness ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib26)).

##### Weak tests and weak oracles.

Insufficient tests mis-rank models on correctness ([Liu et al.,
2023](#as1_bib.bib263)), and on efficiency too: re-running 1,538 tasks
of EffiBench, ENAMEL, EvalPerf and Mercury 30 times, [Le et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib96) found that only 6.11% of the benchmark-provided
performant solutions were significantly faster than the canonical ones
under the provided tests. For security, CWEval reports that its own
analyzer still flags only 562/1916 of CyberSecEval’s vulnerable samples,
and that SecurityEval’s CodeQL checks have frequent false negatives and
positives ([Peng et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib409)), while CyberSecEval’s
authors report 96% precision and 79% recall for their detector ([Bhatt
et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib56)). The first figure is a later re-run on
extracted snippets and the second a manual check by the benchmark’s
authors; neither is an independent audit.

##### Timing noise.

EffiBench, Mercury and many technique papers rely on physical execution
time ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib200)), despite the 12% run-to-run
variation noted above and EvalPerf’s warning that light computation
makes timing flaky ([Liu et al., 2024b](#as1_bib.bib265)). Small
reported speedups on these benchmarks are within noise unless
repetitions and dispersion are reported. Repository-level efficiency
benchmarks are not immune: replaying the official reference patches on
four machine types, [Chen et al. (2026d)](#bib.bib30) found they met the
benchmarks’ own validity rules in every replay for only 39/102 GSO
tasks, 11/140 SWE-Perf tasks and 411/498 SWE-fficiency tasks.

### 5.4. Implications for evaluating techniques

No instrument is valid for all four dimensions and each has documented
failure modes, so comparisons need layered measurement. Static analysis
(complexity, smells, lint and SAST findings) is cheap and reproducible
but weakly valid and tool-dependent, so it should be reported per tool
and CWE. Execution profiling should use instruction counts or repeated,
pinned timing relative to a reference, with exploit or security tests
where they exist. An LLM judge can cover readability aspects that
metrics miss, but only if calibrated against humans and controlled for
length and presentation. Human review of a sample should validate the
other three layers, not merely add a score. Since several techniques
optimize against the analyzers benchmarks use, each dimension needs at
least one held-out instrument. Report quality scores both
unconditionally and conditional on correctness, since a degenerate
program can look secure or simple.
Section [16](#S16 "16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
applies this four-layer stack to correctness benchmarks with
post-2026-cutoff tasks where possible.

## 6. A Faceted Taxonomy of Quality-Improving Techniques

A flat list of families (prompting, feedback loops, self-refinement,
multi-agent pipelines, retrieval, decoding, training) mixes axes: one
static analyzer can drive both a “feedback loop” and a
“reinforcement-learning” method, and a “multi-agent” pipeline is often a
feedback loop with another LLM as critic. We therefore classify
techniques on three orthogonal facets, keeping the families only as
familiar labels.

##### Stage

(when it acts): _pre-generation_ (prompt or context: instructions,
plans, exemplars, retrieved documents), _in-decoding_ (constraining or
reranking the token or sample distribution), _post-generation loop_ (the
model itself, another model, a tool or an agent team inspects and
revises code) and _training-time_ (weights change through data curation,
supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization or reinforcement
learning).

##### Signal source

(what drives the improvement): _none_ (only the instruction), _self_
(the model’s own critique), _other LLM_ (reviewer, judge or agent),
_static analyzer_ (linters, SAST tools), _compiler_, _test execution_,
_profiler_ (runtime or memory measurements), _retrieved knowledge_
(documents, exemplars, repository context), _human_, _learned verifier_
(trained classifier or reranker) and _reward model_. Techniques often
combine sources, and combinations matter: in
§[9](#S9 "9. Tool-Feedback Loops ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"),
analyzer feedback preserved correctness mainly when gated by test
execution.

##### Quality target

: readability/maintainability (R/M), efficiency (EFF) and security
(SEC), with correctness (COR) as a control.

|                 |                      |                                                      |                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------- | -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Family          | Stage                | Typical signal sources                               | Section                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Prompting       | pre-generation       | none; self (planning, chain of thought)              | §[8](#S8 "8. Prompting for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")                         |
| Tool feedback   | post-generation loop | static analyzer, compiler, tests, profiler           | §[9](#S9 "9. Tool-Feedback Loops ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")                           |
| Self-refinement | post-generation loop | self; tests (self-debugging)                         | §[10](#S10 "10. Self-Refinement ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")                            |
| Multi-agent     | post-generation loop | other LLM; tools invoked by agents                   | §[11](#S11 "11. Multi-Agent and Agentic Pipelines ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")          |
| Retrieval       | pre-generation       | retrieved knowledge                                  | §[12](#S12 "12. Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code") |
| Decoding        | in-decoding          | grammar or type constraints, learned verifier, tests | §[13](#S13 "13. Decoding-Time Control and Reranking ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")        |
