shaded by mean quality-assessment score, and signal source by targeted
dimension.

The maps show three regularities. First, the signal follows the target:
profilers and test execution drive almost all efficiency work, static
analyzers and retrieved knowledge dominate security, and
readability/maintainability relies mostly on instructions, linters and
other LLMs; learned verifiers, reward models and human signals are rare
throughout. Second, most techniques act after generation:
post-generation loops are the largest stage for efficiency and security,
readability work splits about evenly between prompting and
post-generation loops, and the few in-decoding methods almost all target
security. Third, the field is young and accelerating: nearly all studies
date from 2024 on, the yearly count more than doubled from 2024 to 2025,
and 2026 had passed 2025 by mid-October (Supplementary Fig. ). A large
hybrid group, most often a prompting or retrieval front end plus a
tool-feedback or agentic loop, is one reason facets fit the literature
better than families.

## 7. Highlighted Techniques

Sections [8](#S8 "8. Prompting for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")–[14](#S14 "14. Training-Time Alignment for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
synthesize each family by mechanism and end with its highlighted
techniques: up to ten per family for a reader or re-evaluation to start
from, chosen from the included studies by a fixed rule, described by
what is algorithmically new and listed with their authors’ reported
result. The same set forms the head-to-head comparison of
§[16.3](#S16.SS3 "16.3. E12: Head-to-head of the highlighted techniques ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code").

##### Selection rule.

A technique row of the extraction table
(§[4](#S4 "4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
is _eligible_ if the study proposes it, with a positive effect on the
targeted dimension and a non-negative effect on COR. Two review passes,
with recorded reasons, then required that it be in scope (a technique
for R/M, EFF or SEC of code an LLM generates or edits), be the authors’
own method rather than a benchmark, dataset or empirical comparison,
apply to ordinary software code rather than a narrow artifact (hardware
description languages, GPU kernels, PLC programs, smart contracts and
similar), and not duplicate another record. Further rows were excluded
under five written rules: a lightweight mitigation inside an empirical
or benchmark study, evaluation on only a handful of tasks, code quality
as an incidental outcome, a reviewer flag for low credibility, or a
decline in COR found on re-reading the selected paper, in which case the
next-ranked technique took its place. Of the 444 candidate rows, 10 were
out of scope, 7 were not the authors’ own technique, 2 duplicated
another record, 3 were domain-specific rows without a family, and 94
were excluded under the five rules; the remaining 328 rows, after
merging 8 that are second techniques of a study already counted (one
technique per study and family, and a study highlighted in one family
only), leave 145 general-purpose and 175 domain-specific techniques.
Each family then takes two lanes. _Landmarks_ (L) are its five
most-cited eligible techniques, by Semantic Scholar citation counts
(October 2026). _Recent leaders_ (R) are the five non-landmark eligible
techniques from 2025–2026 with the largest reported relative improvement
on their targeted dimension over the strongest baseline their authors
report; improvements are ranked as percentiles within their dimension,
so large efficiency speedups do not crowd out security and readability
results, and count only if their numbers appear verbatim in the source.
A study is highlighted in one family only, and a hybrid takes the family
of the mechanism that does most of its work. Two lanes are needed
because citation counts alone favour 2023–2024 work and reported gain
alone favours small, self-evaluated studies. The second lane still
inherits each study’s choice of baseline: a gain over a weak baseline
ranks as high as the same gain over a strong one, so its ranking says
which papers report large gains, not which techniques are best; the
head-to-head
(§[16.3](#S16.SS3 "16.3. E12: Head-to-head of the highlighted techniques ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
re-measures every highlighted technique against shared references for
that reason. Two decisions were made after the rule was first applied,
and we report them as deviations. For training, the first selection held
no reinforcement-learning method, the dominant training method of
2025–2026, so the rule was adjusted after inspecting it: PurpCode,
SecCoderX and Afterburner replace the recent picks DiSCo, Adaptive
Unlearning and quality-aware preference learning, so the family includes
RL methods for security and efficiency; with the rule as first applied,
the training family would hold the three replaced techniques. Universal
Textual Teaching, first counted as general-purpose, is evaluated on code
only on GPU kernels and was reclassified as domain-specific; the
next-ranked prompting technique was excluded as unverifiable (model
unnamed, quality score undefined), and StoryCoder took the slot. The
rule selected 66 techniques, ten per family except self-refinement,
which has only 6 eligible general-purpose techniques; 43 link public
code. The 65 most-cited domain-specific techniques appear in the
Supplementary Material (§).

##### How to read the tables.

Reported results are the authors’ own, on their own benchmarks, models
and baselines: they show what each paper claims, not how the techniques
compare, which requires one model, one benchmark set and one call budget
(§[16.3](#S16.SS3 "16.3. E12: Head-to-head of the highlighted techniques ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
The selection rests on the extraction (LLM-assisted, reviewed by the
author), and citation counts change over time.

## 8. Prompting for Quality

Prompting, the cheapest intervention, acts almost always
_pre-generation_
(§[6](#S6 "6. A Faceted Taxonomy of Quality-Improving Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
and mostly without external signal; a minority add a _self_ signal, as
Recursive Criticism and Improvement (RCI) does, or human, retrieved or
execution information. Of the 113 studies
(§[4](#S4 "4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
the largest group targets SEC, then EFF and R/M; 79 also measure
correctness and 15 a non-targeted dimension.

##### Grouped comparison.

Stated requirements help less than expected (Supplementary Table ). On
RACE, five simultaneous requirements drive almost all models near zero
on the joint correct-and-compliant metric, and models resist requests
contradicting their stylistic priors ([Zheng et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib604)). Newer security prompts only shift the CWE mix
([Kharma et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib230)) or trade high- for
low-severity findings ([Urmi et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib519)). Energy
prompts saved nothing consistently across six models and three hardware
platforms ([Apsan et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib35)) and helped only some
models and languages ([Rekhi et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib447)); no single
efficiency prompt transfers. In CodePromptEval, a persona who “follows
best coding practices for maintainability” produced fewer Pylint smells
and lower complexity at slightly lower correctness, while few-shot and
signature prompts raised correctness most but added smells, over a third
more when combined with chain-of-thought and persona prompts ([Khojah
et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib232)). Reasoning effort is the main knob
frontier APIs expose, yet on A.S.E slow-thinking configurations tended
to trail fast-thinking ones ([Lian et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib255)), and
no study we found varies effort within one model while measuring R/M or
EFF.

##### Highlighted techniques.

In Supplementary Table  (selection rule in
§[7](#S7 "7. Highlighted Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
landmarks mostly structure reasoning before coding; recent leaders
condition the prompt on a task or model diagnosis from another LLM or
analyzer (ECO, BRACE, CSDD) optimize the prompt itself (MPCO,
SecureForge), or restate the problem before coding (StoryCoder retells
it as a narrative). Caveats. Landmarks’ quality evidence is human-rated
and partly unquantified. Several baselines are weak. MPCO and CSDD omit
correctness, and no row reports an effect on a non-targeted dimension.

Study-by-study detail, the caveats of each highlighted technique,
effects on correctness and on the dimensions not targeted, compute
fairness and limitations for this family are in Supplementary Material
§;
§[17](#S17 "17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
compares the families.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 9. Tool-Feedback Loops

A tool-feedback loop returns an external program’s output on generated
code to the model until the tool is satisfied or a budget runs out (the
_post-generation loop_ stage,
§[6](#S6 "6. A Faceted Taxonomy of Quality-Improving Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Signals come from _static analyzers_ (Bandit, Pylint, CodeQL, Semgrep,
SonarQube, Infer, CppCheck, PMD), _compilers_ or symbolic executors, or
_profilers_; _test execution_ usually gates acceptance. Of the 124
studies, most target EFF or SEC, few R/M; 94 measured correctness and
only 12 a non-targeted dimension. Unlike in self-refinement
(§[10](#S10 "10. Self-Refinement ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
a deterministic tool writes the critique, the condition under which
self-correction most likely works ([Kamoi et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib228)), but its verdict becomes the de facto objective.
Supplementary Tables  and  map designs and reported effects.

##### Grouped comparison.

FDSP ([Alrashedy et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib20)) returns the Bandit
report, requests several candidate fixes, and iterates each until Bandit
is clean; LLM-verbalized reports add only 1% to 2%. With CodeQL, raw
diagnostics help every model, while a stronger model’s explanations help
mainly strong instruction followers and not consistently more than raw
feedback on real-world tasks ([Yan et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib567)). For
maintainability, [Blyth et al. (2025)](#as1_bib.bib58) is the closest
quality-loop template: Bandit and Pylint issues are tagged inline,
security issues ordered by severity weights, and a candidate kept only
if its fitness ($`-\infty`$ on any test failure) does not worsen. For
efficiency, EffiLearner ([Huang et al., 2024a](#as1_bib.bib181)) returns
per-line line_profiler and memory_profiler output; format matters, as
aggregate time and memory alone _increased_ CodeLlama-70B’s execution
time by 51.9% while the profile cut it by 9.6%. Evolutionary searches
(AlphaEvolve ([Novikov et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib344)) and its open
successors CodeEvolve, ContextEvolve and SBLLM) keep the variants an
evaluator scores best, and all inherit the evaluator’s weaknesses: a
timing evaluator rewards noise
(§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3. Critiques ‣ 5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
and none of the studies we found scores evolved code for R/M.

##### Highlighted techniques.

Supplementary Table  lists the highlighted techniques (selection rule in
§[7](#S7 "7. Highlighted Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
[Blyth et al. (2025)](#as1_bib.bib58) tag a few Bandit and Pylint
issues, chosen by severity weight, inline in GPT-4o’s code each round
and keep a revision only if its test-gated fitness does not fall; over
ten rounds Bandit-flagged snippets fell from 45.05% to 13.41% while the
pass rate rose from 36.7% to 46.59%. Caveats. Several headline gains
rest on weak comparisons. Security results are tool-scored and small.
Correctness is unreported for the filtering and FRANC results and
unchecked after the Infer repairs.

Study-by-study detail, the caveats of each highlighted technique,
effects on correctness and on the dimensions not targeted, compute
fairness and limitations for this family are in Supplementary Material
§;
§[17](#S17 "17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
compares the families.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 10. Self-Refinement

Self-refinement has the generating model critique and revise its own
output (_post-generation loop_ stage). The critique is grounded in the
model alone (_self_) or in self plus _test execution_ (failing tests,
tracebacks, runtime state), a _profiler_ or a _static analyzer_. A study
belongs here when the model writes the critique, in
§[9](#S9 "9. Tool-Feedback Loops ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
when a tool report passes through largely unchanged. Of the 17 included
studies, 10 also measure COR and 1 a non-targeted dimension; most target
SEC, a few EFF or R/M, none all three. Several best-known methods report
only correctness (our correctness-only side list,
§[4](#S4 "4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
but are discussed because quality-targeted variants inherit their loops.

##### Grouped comparison.

Self-Refine alternates feedback and refine prompts on one model ([Madaan
et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib276)). Outside code, LLMs struggle to correct
their reasoning without external feedback, sometimes getting worse
([Huang et al., 2024c](#as1_bib.bib185)); a TACL survey finds
self-correction works mainly with reliable external feedback and many
positive reports rest on unfair evaluations ([Kamoi et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib228)). On EffiBench, an unsupervised Self-Refine
prompt _increased_ CodeLlama-70B execution time ([Huang et al.,
2024a](#as1_bib.bib181)). The execution-grounded methods (Self-Debug,
Self-Edit, Reflexion, LDB, CRITIC) are correctness-only ([Chen et al.,
2024b](#as1_bib.bib74); [Zhang et al., 2023a](#as1_bib.bib595); [Shinn
et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib473); [Zhong et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib608);
[Gou et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib159)), and the oracle is their weak
point: Reflexion’s self-generated MBPP Python tests have a 16.3%
false-positive rate ([Shinn et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib473)).
Quality-targeted variants replace the test oracle with a non-functional
signal (Supplementary Table ). Untargeted iteration can degrade
security. Over 40 rounds of GPT-4o “improvements” to 10 secure C and
Java programs, critical vulnerabilities rose by 37.6% after five
iterations ([Shukla et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib474)), and a
static-analysis gate raised the latent degradation rate from 12.5% to
20.8 %, as rules miss removed defensive logic ([Chen et al.,
2026e](#as1_bib.bib76)). Large reasoning models critique and revise
inside a single call; no study we found compares explicit refinement
with internal revision at matched tokens on any quality dimension.

##### Highlighted techniques.

Supplementary Table  lists all 6 eligible general-purpose techniques
(selection rule in
§[7](#S7 "7. Highlighted Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Besides Self-Refine, they ground revision in structure (CodeChain,
GRASP), in memory of past repairs (RefleXGen and Safety Sidecar, which
share a first author) or in CodeQL findings (SecCode, partly a tool
loop,
§[9](#S9 "9. Tool-Feedback Loops ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Caveats. Loop and instrument overlap: SecCode feeds CodeQL findings into
the loop, and Safety Sidecar uses CodeQL in both pipeline and
evaluation. Correctness can suffer: RefleXGen lowers CodeQwen’s pass
rate from 86.7 to 69.8. No row reports an effect on a non-targeted
dimension.

Study-by-study detail, the caveats of each highlighted technique,
effects on correctness and on the dimensions not targeted, compute
fairness and limitations for this family are in Supplementary Material
§;
§[17](#S17 "17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
compares the families.

## 11. Multi-Agent and Agentic Pipelines

Multi-agent pipelines split generation across LLM roles (analyst, coder,
tester, reviewer, security advisor); agentic systems give one model
tools and a repository. Both work mainly in the _post-generation loop_,
often after _pre-generation_ planning, driven mainly by _other-LLM_
critique, often with _test-execution_, a _profiler_ or a _static
analyzer_. Of 75 included studies, 66 also measure COR and 10 a
non-targeted dimension. EFF leads (mainly GPU-kernel, HPC and
hardware-design optimizers with profiler feedback), then SEC, then R/M.
The best-known general frameworks are correctness-only
(§[4](#S4 "4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
but supply reusable role designs.

##### Grouped comparison.

ChatDev, MetaGPT and Self-collaboration chain development roles ([Qian
et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib421); [Hong et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib174);
[Dong et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib119)), and quality is prompted, not
evaluated: Self-collaboration’s tester reports on “functionality,
readability, and maintainability” but results are pass@1, and ChatDev’s
“Quality” multiplies completeness, executability and requirement
consistency. AgentCoder and MapCoder are correctness-only ([Huang
et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib180); [Islam et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib214));
the simplest quality-oriented design, coder plus reviewer, is
re-evaluated in
§[16](#S16 "16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code").
For security, Multi-LLMSecCodeEval (preprint) compares ten single-model,
ensemble, collaborative and hybrid pipelines ([Sabir et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib450)): on SecLLMEval, ensembles with static analysis
beat a single LLM at secure generation by up to 47.3%, LLM-only
collaboration by 8.9% to 22.3%. Controlled studies point to complexity
growth: six analyst–coder–tester–debugger configurations (GPT-4o family,
HumanEval) form two complexity clusters 50-130% apart, the heavier with
no pass@1 advantage ([Ashrafi, 2026](#as1_bib.bib42)). On SlopCodeBench,
where 15 agents repeatedly extend their own solutions, structural
erosion rose in 77% of trajectories and agent code was 2.3x more verbose
than code in 473 open-source Python repositories; quality guidance
lowered initial verbosity and erosion, not the degradation rate
([Orlanski et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib401)).

##### Highlighted techniques.

Supplementary Table  lists the highlighted techniques (selection rule in
§[7](#S7 "7. Highlighted Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
They differ less in agent count than in what agents exchange:
development roles, security critiques or, for EFF, several agents’
candidates and, recently, shared search memory such as LessonL’s banked
lessons. Caveats. Headline numbers often overstate typical gains.
ContextEvolve’s 33.3% comes from one task; its average margin over the
top baseline is 6.5%, using over three times OpenEvolve’s API calls (but
fewer tokens). Four of the ten techniques report no correctness result.

Study-by-study detail, the caveats of each highlighted technique,
effects on correctness and on the dimensions not targeted, compute
fairness and limitations for this family are in Supplementary Material
§;
§[17](#S17 "17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
compares the families.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 12. Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Quality

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a _pre-generation_ technique
with signal source _retrieved-knowledge_. Correctness-oriented RAG
retrieves API documentation ([Zhou et al., 2022](#bib.bib223)) or
repository context ([Zhang et al., 2023a](#bib.bib208)); CodeRAG-Bench
measures when it helps ([Wang et al., 2025d](#as1_bib.bib535)). Of the
37 included studies
(§[4](#S4 "4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
the largest group targets SEC, then EFF (mostly accelerator-kernel and
hardware code) and a minority R/M (some for decompiled or migrated
code); 28 measure correctness and 4 a non-targeted dimension.

##### Grouped comparison.

Designs differ in the retrieved unit (Supplementary Tables  and ).
RESCUE finds SecCoder’s raw demonstrations ([Zhang et al.,
2024a](#as1_bib.bib593)) do not significantly improve SecurePass@1,
suggesting underused security knowledge, and instead hierarchically
retrieves distilled guidelines and sliced examples ([Shi and Zhang,
2026](#as1_bib.bib471)). Stand-alone EFF retrieval is rarer and mostly
optimizes existing programs; hybrids with profiling or search loops are
more common
(§[9](#S9 "9. Tool-Feedback Loops ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
PIE retrieves slow–fast pairs as few-shot examples (1.34$`\times`$
speedup at Best@1) ([Shypula et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib475)). Without
repository retrieval, GPT-3.5 in A3-CodGen reuses no local functions and
writes redundant new ones ([Liao et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib257)).
Conversely, in CodeRAG-Bench models copy context functions, sometimes
overwriting the queried one, and over-complicate programs ([Wang et al.,
2025d](#as1_bib.bib535)). Retrieved content is also a risk: one poisoned
knowledge-base example can compromise up to 48% of generated code ([Lin
et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib259)), and few methods besides CodeGuarder
are evaluated under poisoning ([Lin et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib258)).

##### Highlighted techniques.

Supplementary Table  lists the highlighted techniques (selection rule in
§[7](#S7 "7. Highlighted Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Caveats. RAPGen and SemOpt score agreement with developer fixes (expert
and author judgment), not measured speed. PIE’s authors note that
speedup “may, however, come with some cost of correctness”. KPC’s rate
comes from the authors’ manual review.

Study-by-study detail, the caveats of each highlighted technique,
effects on correctness and on the dimensions not targeted, compute
fairness and limitations for this family are in Supplementary Material
§;
§[17](#S17 "17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
compares the families.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 13. Decoding-Time Control and Reranking

Decoding-time techniques change how an output is chosen, not the
weights: _constrained decoding_ masks or reweights next-token
distributions, _representation steering_ adds vectors to hidden
activations, and _sample-and-select_ keeps the complete candidate a
verifier prefers. All three are _in-decoding_ on our facets
(§[6](#S6 "6. A Faceted Taxonomy of Quality-Improving Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"));
unlike the loops of
§[9](#S9 "9. Tool-Feedback Loops ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"),
selection feeds nothing back to the model. Of 18 included studies, most
target SEC, a minority R/M (repetition, deprecated APIs, readability
proxies) and three preprints EFF; 18 also measure COR, but only 2 an
untargeted quality dimension. The classic methods are correctness-only.

##### Grouped comparison.

For R/M, PG-TD swaps its test reward for a length or comment reward
([Zhang et al., 2023b](#as1_bib.bib599)) and RPG penalizes structural
repetition ([Dong et al., 2025b](#as1_bib.bib121)). For SEC, constrained
beam sampling writes constraints for each of the 91 CodeGuard+ prompts
from the CWE it might trigger ([Fu et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib129));
co-decoding replaces the rules with a small security model ([Hu et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib176)); and 2026 steering methods (SCS-Code, DuoSteer)
use the target’s own activations. Among sample-and-select methods,
MBR-exec, CodeT, Coder-Reviewer and LEVER are correctness selectors
([Shi et al., 2022](#as1_bib.bib470); [Chen et al.,
2023](#as1_bib.bib67); [Zhang et al., 2023c](#as1_bib.bib600); [Ni
et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib340)). Without execution feedback, a code
process reward model is no better than a random reward in best-of-$`N`$
([Li et al., 2025d](#as1_bib.bib250)). _The quality-verifier gap is now
partly closed:_ SecCodePRM (ICML 2026), a step-level security reward
model trained on analyzer labels, outranks probability ranking for
best-of-$`N`$ on CWEval ([Yu et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib578)). We found
no peer-reviewed R/M or EFF selector, and none reranking by static
maintainability scores or profiled instruction counts.

##### Highlighted techniques.

Supplementary Table  lists the highlighted techniques (selection rule in
§[7](#S7 "7. Highlighted Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Caveats. Correctness effects are mixed. Constrained beam sampling lowers
Llama3-8B pass@1 from 82.20 to 72.21, and an independent study found,
and repaired by script before testing, indentation issues in most
CodeGuard+ outputs for CodeLlama and Mistral ([Dai et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib97)). Evidence is thin for several recent rows.

Study-by-study detail, the caveats of each highlighted technique,
effects on correctness and on the dimensions not targeted, compute
fairness and limitations for this family are in Supplementary Material
§;
§[17](#S17 "17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
compares the families.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 14. Training-Time Alignment for Quality

Training-time techniques move the quality signal from the inference loop
into the weights (or a learned prefix), so that a single call should
yield better code. On our facets
(§[6](#S6 "6. A Faceted Taxonomy of Quality-Improving Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
signal sources are other-LLM filters and judges, static analyzers (data
oracles or reward terms), test execution, profilers or simulators, and
learned reward models. Of 124 included studies, 114 measure COR but only
15 an untargeted quality dimension; the largest group targets EFF (much
of it accelerator-kernel and hardware code), the next SEC, and a
minority R/M. Often “quality” is enforced on the _training data_ while
only COR is measured on the _generated_ code.

##### Grouped comparison.

phi-1 filtered web code with a classifier trained on GPT-4 “educational
value” ratings of about 100k files, added GPT-3.5-generated textbooks,
and reached 50.6% HumanEval pass@1 at 1.3B ([Gunasekar et al.,
2023](#as1_bib.bib162)). Large pretraining pipelines filter for
readability-like properties but report only functional benchmarks. In
preference optimization, several security results share a mechanism:
secure and insecure programs often differ in a few tokens (a sanitizer
call, a parameterized query), which a sequence-level loss dilutes. Hence
SVEN and SafeCoder mask their losses to the changed regions ([He and
Vechev, 2023](#as1_bib.bib170); [He et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib171)),
Localized Preference Optimization (LPO) masks security-relevant tokens
after finding SimPO ineffective ([Hasan et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib168)),
and SRCode assigns token-level RL rewards ([Quan et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib424)). Security training has moved from curated fixes
(SVEN, SafeCoder) to synthesized data and then RL. Efficiency work uses
profilers or simulators as the signal; making execution time a usable
reward is itself studied, as “once timing drives the reward, small
problems in measurement noise, reward sparsity, or GRPO instability
overwhelm the signal and make RL fail” ([Chambon et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib65)). REAL is the clearest attempt to train for SEC
and R/M jointly with COR (its maintainability detector is MyPy type
checking) ([Yao et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib573)). Its motivating negative
result is that “optimizing for code quality alone leads to reward
hacking”, with the model emitting empty code or comments that maximize
quality scores.

##### Side effects of reward optimization.

The first side effect is _length_: in RL from human feedback, “a purely
length-based reward reproduces most downstream RLHF improvements”
([Singhal et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib481)), and GRPO has an optimization
bias that “artificially increases response length (especially for
incorrect outputs)” ([Liu et al., 2025d](#as1_bib.bib272)). Since length
moves with lines of code, comment density and complexity metrics,
judge-based R/M rewards face the same confound, which no code study we
found controls for. Analyzer-only rewards pull the other way, toward
short or empty code ([Skopin and Kotelnikov, 2026](#as1_bib.bib482);
[Yao et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib573)). The second is _exploitation of the
test oracle_ behind every correctness term: in a frontier RL run, an
agent planned to “circumvent the tests by making verify always return
true” ([Baker et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib51)). A correctness term thus
does not prevent degenerate code: a special-cased solution is “correct”
yet unmaintainable.

##### Highlighted techniques.

Supplementary Table  lists the highlighted techniques (selection rule in
§[7](#S7 "7. Highlighted Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Landmarks curate or mask _data_; recent leaders shape the _objective_,
mostly through reinforcement-learning rewards. Caveats. Several gains
are measured with the training instrument: CodeUltraFeedback’s GPT-3.5
judge also labelled the training data, and REAL evaluates with its
reward’s program-analysis detectors. Correctness costs are uneven (§).
No highlighted technique reports an effect on an untargeted dimension.

Study-by-study detail, the caveats of each highlighted technique,
effects on correctness and on the dimensions not targeted, compute
fairness and limitations for this family are in Supplementary Material
§;
§[17](#S17 "17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
compares the families.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 15. Hybrid and Other Techniques

The largest group, 191 of the 628 included studies, combines mechanisms
of several families or uses one outside them, so the extraction assigns
it no single family. The facets of
§[6](#S6 "6. A Faceted Taxonomy of Quality-Improving Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
still classify every study: 145 run a post-generation loop, 27 act
before generation, 16 at training time and 4 in decoding. Their signals
are mostly external: test execution (125 studies), compiler output
(107), retrieved knowledge (103) and profilers (78), with self-critique
(71), static analyzers (61) and another LLM (55) less often. The group
is recent (156 studies from 2025–2026) and, like the review as a whole,
mostly preprints (114).

##### Grouped comparison.

Mapping each study’s signals to the families of
§§[8](#S8 "8. Prompting for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")–[14](#S14 "14. Training-Time Alignment for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"),
151 studies combine two or more mechanisms. The most common combination
joins retrieval, self-refinement and a tool-feedback loop (33 studies),
as in ECO’s performance-aware prompts built from an analyzer’s
bottleneck diagnosis and retrieved examples ([Kim et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib233)), Optimo’s mined optimization strategies with
profiler and correctness feedback ([Peng et al.,
2026b](#as1_bib.bib412)) and Safety Sidecar’s retrieval-augmented
reflective repair gated by a compiler and an analyzer ([Wang et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib526)). Retrieval with tool feedback follows (26;
SBLLM’s execution-selected optimization examples ([Gao et al.,
2025b](#as1_bib.bib136)) and a retrieval-augmented repair loop over GCC,
CodeQL and KLEE ([Sriram et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib488))), then another
LLM with tool feedback (16; Codexity ([Kim et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib234)), CodeEvolve ([Borra et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib60))) and all three together (15; MARCO ([Rahman
et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib442)), SysLLMatic ([Peng et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib408))). Self-refinement with tool feedback, the
pattern of CodeChain ([Le et al., 2024a](#as1_bib.bib240)) and LLM4EFFI
([Ye et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib575)), accounts for 13. The remaining 40
rely on one signal or none, and are hybrids by construction: a feedback
loop around a structured prompt or a non-LLM component such as a
transpiler, a genetic-improvement operator or a domain-specific
language. Efficiency dominates the targets (120 studies), ahead of
security (46) and readability/maintainability (35), and the group is
where narrow domains concentrate: by the keywords of their languages,
benchmarks and titles, 111 studies work on GPU or accelerator kernels
(66), hardware design (24), C-to-Rust migration (20) or other
specialized code.

##### Evidence and effects.

Hybrids report gains more often than the review as a whole: the target
improves in 171 of their 195 technique rows (88%, against 76% over all
rows). Correctness is measured more often than in the review as a whole
(173 studies; unreported in 41 rows, 21% against 29% over all rows),
because most pipelines gate on tests or compilation, but only 16 studies
(8%) measure a quality dimension they do not target, one of the lowest
shares
(Table [11](#S17.T11 "Table 11 ‣ RQ1 and RQ2: what is targeted, and how it is measured. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Their median QA score equals the review’s (6.0); they report compute
more often (68% against 59%) but handle contamination (29%), use human
evaluation (14%) and release artifacts (59%) slightly less often
(Table [13](#S17.T13 "Table 13 ‣ RQ4: evidence quality and compute fairness. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
The highlighted-technique selection
(§[7](#S7 "7. Highlighted Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
assigns each hybrid to the family of the mechanism that does most of the
work; 20 of the 66 highlighted techniques come from this group.

Combinations with their counts and representative studies are in
Supplementary Material §;
§[17](#S17 "17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
compares the families.

## 16. Controlled Re-evaluation

The survey sections report each technique in its authors’ setting. This
section reports a re-evaluation that fixes the setting: one or more
techniques per family
(§[8](#S8 "8. Prompting for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")–§[14](#S14 "14. Training-Time Alignment for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
one model grid, one benchmark set, all four dimensions scored on every
output, and matched call budgets. Scope: the design does not cross every
model with every benchmark, which is infeasible and would leave most
cells empty; breadth across models comes from the vendor-reported scores
in the Supplementary Material (§) and from the extended grid
(§[16.2](#S16.SS2 "16.2. Extended grid: current frontier and open-weight models ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).

Research questions. _ERQ1:_ at a matched compute budget, does each
technique improve the dimension it targets? _ERQ2:_ what is its effect
on COR and on the dimensions it does not target? _ERQ3:_ does the effect
depend on model strength or architecture (closed vs. open, dense vs.
mixture-of-experts, MoE)? Hypotheses, taken from the survey: (H1) gains
of iterative techniques shrink once the baseline receives the same
calls, as [Olausson et al. (2024)](#as1_bib.bib368) found for
self-repair; (H2) an analyzer loop removes the analyzer’s own findings
but preserves COR only with a test gate; (H3) generic efficiency
instructions change EFF little, as EvalPerf reports ([Liu et al.,
2024b](#as1_bib.bib265)); (H4) weaker models gain more than the strong
anchor. T10 combines test and analyzer rewards because a quality-only
reward degenerates to trivial outputs, as REAL observed ([Yao et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib573)); no arm uses a quality-only reward.

Models
(Table [2](#S16.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")a).
The main grid has four instruction-tuned models. Claude Opus 5.5 is the
closed anchor on the Claude API; its thinking is always on and its
default effort is medium ([Anthropic, 2026f](#as1_bib.bib30)). Gemma 4
31B IT (dense) and Gemma 4 26B-A4B IT (MoE) form a near-matched
architecture pair on dedicated Fireworks deployments, whose precision we
log, and are the only models we fine-tune (T8–T10). gpt-oss-120b
([OpenAI et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib400)), an inexpensive open MoE model
on Fireworks serverless, is the weak but realistic anchor. An extended
grid
(§[16.2](#S16.SS2 "16.2. Extended grid: current frontier and open-weight models ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
adds the closed GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon, through the Vercel AI
Gateway with one pinned provider, and the leading open-weight models on
Fireworks: Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, Qwen3.8-Max, MiMo-V2.6-Pro, DeepSeek
V4.1-Flash and V4-Flash, and MiniMax M3. Closed models run at default
sampling with a recorded effort setting and $`k\geq 3`$ samples; open
models use temperature 0.2 (0.8 for best-of-$`n`$) with fixed seeds.
_Design gaps:_ (i) the Gemma pair roughly matches total, not active,
parameters (3.8B active of 25.2B vs. 30.7B dense ([Google,
2026](#bib.bib55))), so ERQ3 contrasts are shown in a matched-total and
a matched-active view and are never reported as “MoE vs. dense” without
that caveat; (ii) Opus 5.5 always thinks, so the no-chain-of-thought
condition is approximated by low effort; (iii) Claude bills thinking as
output with no separate count, so its reasoning tokens are not
available; (iv) only instruct checkpoints are served, so no
base-versus-instruct contrast is possible.

Benchmarks
(Table [2](#S16.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")b).
COR: the LiveCodeBench Pro protocol ([Zheng et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib607)) applied to Codeforces contests held after
2026-07-01, which postdate every model’s cutoff, as the primary
function-level measure, since its last public set ends in September 2025
([LiveCodeBench authors, 2025](#bib.bib111); [LiveCodeBench Pro authors,
2025](#bib.bib112)); HumanEval+, whose tests extend HumanEval’s by 80x
([Liu et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib263)), and LiveCodeBench v6 ([Jain
et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib217)) are kept only as legacy anchors that
connect to earlier work. Repository-level correctness uses DeepSWE v1.1
([Huang et al., 2026d](#as1_bib.bib187)) (Datacurve’s public benchmark,
not the 2025 Agentica agent of the same name), whose 113 tasks were
written from scratch in 2026 and kept private until their release in
July 2026: after the cutoffs of gpt-oss and Gemma 4, about a month after
that of Opus 5.5 (June 2026), and for the extended-grid models, whose
vendors state no cutoff, after release rather than demonstrably after
cutoff; runs use its pinned containers and official scorer. DeepSWE is
run for every technique on all thirteen models
(Table [4](#S16.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
and Terminal-Bench 4.0 ([Merrill et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib284)) in the
extended grid
(§[16.2](#S16.SS2 "16.2. Extended grid: current frontier and open-weight models ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
R/M: the readability and maintainability subsets of RACE, which embed
customized requirements in the task ([Zheng et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib604)), and NoFunEval, which scores edits partly by
DiffBLEU against a reference ([Singhal et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib480));
both measure agreement with a requirement or a reference, so our
analyzers and judge also score these outputs. Every technique, the
single shot included, receives the benchmark’s own requirement as part
of its task prompt (RACE’s naming, length, comment, maintainability or
module-count instruction; NoFunEval’s non-functional edit instruction),
so differences between techniques are measured on top of a prompt that
already names the target. EFF: EvalPerf’s differential performance score
from CPU instruction counts ([Liu et al., 2024b](#as1_bib.bib265)) is
primary; EffiBench-X ([Qing et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib422)) and Mercury
([Du et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib122)) are secondary because wall-clock
time varied by 12% against 0.03% for instruction counts in WEDGE’s
measurements ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib200)). SEC: CWEval (functional
and secure, func-sec@$`k`$) ([Peng et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib409)),
BaxBench (end-to-end exploits) ([Vero et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib521)),
and PythonSecurityEval (470 Stack Overflow prompts) ([Alrashedy et al.,
2023](#as1_bib.bib20)), kept for comparability with
§[9](#S9 "9. Tool-Feedback Loops ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code");
its authors note that unit tests are hard to write for these tasks, so
its quality is reported unconditionally only. The extended grid adds
FrontierCode and SlopCodeBench for maintainability, GSO and
SWE-fficiency for efficiency, and SusVibes for security (Supplementary
Table ). FrontierCode is scored with its official pipeline: each
repository-level submission is graded by the benchmark’s reference
rubric grader, an LLM judge applying the authors’ published rubric
(readability, documentation, modularity and requirement adherence), run
at temperature 0 with the authors’ prompts, weights and aggregation
unchanged, and we report the official weighted rubric score; as a check,
our own length-controlled judge rescored a stratified third of the
submissions and agrees with the official score at Spearman
$`\rho=0.86`$. SWE-bench Verified is not used: its top score reached
97.00% by 2026-09-01 ([Vals AI, 2026](#as1_bib.bib520)). Contamination:
HumanEval+, MBPP+ (used in E12) and the LeetCode-derived sets form the
_likely contaminated_ split; the _clean_ split holds tasks dated after a
model’s training cutoff, which is January 2025 for Gemma 4 ([Google,
2026](#bib.bib55)), June 2024 for gpt-oss ([OpenAI et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib400)) and June 2026 for Opus 5.5 ([Anthropic,
2026f](#as1_bib.bib30)). LiveCodeBench’s latest release, v6, ends with
problems from April 2025 ([LiveCodeBench authors, 2025](#bib.bib111)),
so the clean split holds February to April 2025 problems for Gemma 4 and
July 2024 to April 2025 problems for gpt-oss, and no LiveCodeBench
problem postdates the Opus 5.5 cutoff: LiveCodeBench v6 is therefore
reported only for gpt-oss and Gemma 4, and every other model is compared
on the post-cutoff LiveCodeBench Pro contests.

Table 2. E1. Setup. (a) Models, (b) benchmarks, (c) techniques with
family, stage and signal source, and their use of the call budget $`B`$.

Techniques and budgets
(Table [2](#S16.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")c).
Each technique is reimplemented in one harness and, where code exists,
was first checked against its original number in its original setting.
Every call counts, including critic and reviewer calls. Each technique
runs at $`B\in\{1,4,8,16\}`$ call-equivalents and is reported as a
budget curve
(Fig. [4](#S16.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Single-call techniques spend extra budget as best-of-$`B`$ with the T7
ranker, so T7 at the same $`B`$ is the reference for ERQ1. Rankers and
gates see only the public examples in the prompt, never the hidden
tests. Tokens (input, output, reasoning where exposed, billed), calls,
wall time and dated cost are logged per call and reported per experiment
(Supplementary Material, §); budgets match calls, not tokens, and for
Opus 5.5, whose reasoning tokens are not exposed, matching is call-based
only
(§[20](#S20 "20. Threats to Validity ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"));
training compute for T8–T10 lies outside $`B`$: each LoRA run on
Fireworks took from several hours to a few days. Cost and compute. In
total, the re-evaluation (main grid, extended grid and E12, including
validation against the original numbers and reruns) made 13.69 million
billed model requests (12.43 million call-equivalents and agent runs;
the derivation per experiment is in the Supplementary Material, §) and
cost \$64,330 in API fees (\$38,659 Claude, \$15,816 Vercel AI Gateway,
\$9,855 Fireworks inference), plus \$5,900 in Fireworks fine-tuning
charges for the T8–T10 runs and the retrained E12 training-time
techniques (1,420 GPU-hours on 8$`\times`$H100 nodes in total). Every
configuration was run end-to-end three times with fresh seeds and the
tables report the mean over runs. A per-experiment ledger of calls,
tokens, fees and GPU-hours that reconciles with these totals is in the
Supplementary Material (§). The harness, prompts, pinned analyzer
configurations, analysis scripts, review data and per-task outputs and
scores for every public benchmark will be released; outputs on
FrontierCode, whose tasks are private, will be withheld under its
evaluation terms.

Measurement. The four-layer stack of
§[5](#S5 "5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
scores every output: (1) static analysis: pinned Pylint, Bandit and
Safety, whose reports SonarQube ingests while running its own
taint-aware engine (SonarPython); maintainability and security issues
are counted from SonarQube, together with cognitive complexity;
(2) sandboxed execution, efficiency relative to the reference solution,
wall-clock medians and interquartile ranges over at least five runs on
pinned cores; (3) a length-controlled R/M judge (Claude Opus 5.5);
(4) manual ratings by the author of a stratified sample of 440 outputs
(110 per main-grid model, stratified over techniques and benchmarks and
drawn before any automated score was inspected), each rated on a 1–5
readability-and-maintainability rubric with written anchors; the ratings
agree with the length-controlled judge at quadratic-weighted
$`\kappa=0.74`$ (Spearman $`\rho=0.79`$) and with the analyzer’s
maintainability issue count at $`\rho=-0.81`$, so the automated measures
track human judgment and not only the analyzer’s own rules. A second
rater, an engineer who is not an author, blind to the author’s ratings
and to every automated score, rated 383 of the same 440 outputs; the two
raters agree at quadratic-weighted $`\kappa=0.63{}`$ (Spearman
$`\rho=0.66{}`$), and the mean of their ratings agrees with the judge at
$`\kappa=0.70{}`$ ($`\rho=0.72{}`$). Because Claude Opus 5.5 is also an
evaluated model, a second length-controlled judge from another vendor,
GPT-6.1 Sol, scores every R/M output with the same rubric; the two
judges agree at Spearman $`\rho=0.72{}`$ ($`\kappa=0.60{}`$), the
non-Anthropic judge agrees with the human ratings at $`\rho=0.74{}`$,
and it orders the thirteen models of the extended grid almost as the
Opus judge does (Spearman $`\rho=0.79{}`$ across models).
Tables [5](#S16.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")–[7](#S16.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
report quality on every output, whether or not it is correct. Effects
are paired per-task differences against T7 at the same $`B`$ (and
against T0 at $`B=1`$) with bootstrap confidence intervals.

Results. Rows T8–T10 apply to the Gemma models only (–); panels separate
the API-served models from the fine-tuned Gemma pair.
Table [10](#S16.T10 "Table 10 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
gives the uncertainty of each effect and Supplementary Table 
(Supplementary Material, §) the budget curves. ERQ1–ERQ3 are answered in
§[16.1](#S16.SS1 "16.1. Results of the main re-evaluation ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code");
the hypotheses H1–H4 above state the expected direction of each effect.
Further threats are discussed in
§[20](#S20 "20. Threats to Validity ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code").

Gemma weights.

### 16.1. Results of the main re-evaluation

Reading the results. Each cell of
Tables [3](#S16.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")–[7](#S16.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
is a mean over tasks and samples at $`B=4`$ (T0 at $`B=1`$). A technique
is compared with T7, best-of-4 with the same ranker, which answers ERQ1
at a matched budget; the comparison with T0 shows the gain a reader sees
when no budget-matched baseline is run. We call a difference significant
when it exceeds the 95% half-width, that is, when its 95% interval
excludes zero; the threshold is the half-width of its metric, model and
budget
(Table [10](#S16.T10 "Table 10 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
for $`B=4`$; Supplementary Material, §, for $`B=8`$ and $`16`$), and we
also report which significant differences survive a Benjamini–Hochberg
false-discovery correction across all cells
(§[20](#S20 "20. Threats to Validity ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"));
Table [8](#S16.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
counts resolved differences per dimension, and
Fig. [4](#S16.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
extends the comparison to $`B\in\{1,8,16\}`$.

ERQ1: the targeted dimension at a matched budget. We lead with the
measures that neither the T7 ranker nor the analyzer loop optimizes
(Table [9](#S16.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")):
cognitive complexity, the judge score, CWEval func-sec@1 and BaxBench
sec_pass@1. On them T7 matches or beats each inference-time technique in
13 to 16 of its 16 model–metric cells: T1, T2, T4, T5 and T6 are better
than T7 beyond the interval in at most 3 cells and worse in 4 to 9, and
the analyzer loop (T3) is better in one cell and has a lower judge score
than T7 on all four models. The training-time techniques are within the
interval of T7 in 7 of their 8 cells, better or worse in the remaining
one. The second judge points the same way (no technique better than T7
in more than 1 of 4 models), and the human ratings place every technique
within $`0.19`$ points of T7, none beyond the interval. The
analyzer-based counts of
Tables [5](#S16.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
and [7](#S16.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"),
which the ranker partly optimizes, give the same ordering for these
techniques and add the gains of the analyzer loop and fine-tuning
described below.

Against a single shot, every inference-time technique lowers the number
of maintainability issues per kLOC on every model, by $`0.46`$ (T1 on
G26) to $`18.09`$ (T3 on G26). Against T7, which spends the same four
calls on sampling and ranking, most of these gains disappear. On R/M,
quality instructions (T1), planning (T2), Self-Refine (T4), the reviewer
agent (T5) and retrieval (T6) are better than T7 beyond the interval in
at most 3 of 16 cells and worse in 5 to 13; on SEC none of them is
better than T7 in any cell, and T1, T2 and T4 are worse in 10 to 13 of
16 cells
(Table [8](#S16.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")b).
Self-Refine, for example, lowers maintainability issues per kLOC by
$`0.92`$ to $`4.08`$ against T0 but leaves $`4.16`$ to $`5.36`$ more
than T7 on all four models. Length does not explain these differences:
T7’s solutions are 2 to 13% shorter than T0’s, and its lead over T1, T2
and T4–T6 also holds in absolute issues per solution ($`0.47`$ to
$`0.90`$ against at best $`0.57`$ to $`0.99`$ for these techniques;
Supplementary Material, §). This supports H1: at matched calls, sampling
and ranking match or beat iterative refinement, as [Olausson et al.
(2024)](#as1_bib.bib368) found for self-repair and [Mirzaei
(2026)](#bib.bib120) and [Iscan (2026)](#bib.bib77) for self-refinement
and post-hoc operators on small models, and the budget curves show it is
not an artefact of $`B=4`$: on maintainability issues per kLOC, the only
inference-time techniques better than T7 beyond the interval at $`B=8`$
or $`B=16`$ are the analyzer loop and, on oss at $`B=16`$, retrieval
(Fig. [4](#S16.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
The curves are not smooth (on CWEval, T7 on Op scores $`74.85`$,
$`78.17`$, $`74.43`$ and $`86.29`$ at $`B=1`$, $`4`$, $`8`$ and $`16`$):
the per-seed values show that these steps recur in every rerun rather
than reflecting seed noise, and we read only steps beyond the
half-width, here only the gain at $`B=16`$ (Supplementary Material, §).
Two kinds of technique beat T7 on the analyzer-based counts, and only
there
(Table [9](#S16.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
The analyzer loop (T3) lowers maintainability issues per kLOC by
$`7.51`$ to $`10.51`$ against T7 on all four models and security issues
per kLOC by $`1.58`$ to $`1.89`$, and it lowers the share of
PythonSecurityEval solutions with a maintainability issue by $`33.26`$
to $`37.04`$ points and the share with a security issue by $`17.44`$ to
$`21.83`$ points. It stays ahead of T7 on maintainability issues at
every budget on every model. The training-time techniques, which use the
same best-of-4 inference as T7 on fine-tuned weights, are better than T7
beyond the interval in 4 or 5 of 8 R/M cells and 3 or 4 of 8 SEC cells,
and worse in at most one. RL (T10) is the strongest of them, with
$`6.30`$ and $`6.69`$ fewer maintainability issues per kLOC than T7, and
$`7.96`$ and $`9.39`$ points fewer solutions with a security issue, on
G31 and G26; it is the only training-time technique that stays ahead of
T7 on maintainability issues at $`B=16`$.

A single call ($`B=1`$). At $`B=1`$ every technique spends exactly the
single shot’s budget, so this column of Supplementary Table  tests the
prompts themselves, without a ranker. There the quality instruction (T1)
and planning (T2) do not improve maintainability: T1 raises
maintainability issues per kLOC over T0 on all four models, by $`3.99`$
to $`7.11`$, more than the half-width on every model, and T2 by $`1.23`$
to $`7.95`$. This is not an effect of the denominator: T1’s solutions at
$`B=1`$ are 9 to 14% longer than T0’s and carry $`0.26`$ to $`0.39`$
more maintainability issues each (Supplementary Material, §). The
measures the analyzers do not compute agree that the prompts alone add
little: at $`B=1`$, cognitive complexity is within the interval of T0
for T1, T2 and T6 in 11 of 12 cells, and the Opus judge rates T1 and T2
higher in three cells, by at most $`0.14`$ points on its 1–5 scale,
differences the second judge does not confirm (Supplementary Material,
§). Retrieval (T6) lowers them on Op and oss (by $`0.49`$ and $`2.85`$)
and raises them on G31 and G26 (by $`1.92`$ and $`1.28`$). T1 also
lowers CWEval func-sec@1 on three models (by $`0.99`$ to $`8.83`$),
raising it by $`11.37`$ only on G31, and lowers EvalPerf
DPS$`{}_{\text{norm}}`$ on all four (by $`0.20`$ to $`5.69`$). The gains
of T1, T2 and T6 over T0 at $`B\geq 4`$ therefore come from the
best-of-$`B`$ ranker they share with T7, not from the instruction, the
plan or the retrieved text: at one call, quality prompting does not
lower the analyzer’s issue counts and barely moves complexity or judge
scores, and at four to sixteen calls it does not beat best-of-$`n`$.

ERQ2: correctness and the dimensions not targeted. No technique is more
correct than T7 on every model, and on the two models with the highest
single-shot HumanEval+ pass@1 (Op, $`96.40`$; G31, $`96.06`$) almost
every technique is below the single shot: T2 to T6 by $`0.59`$ to
$`6.90`$ points on Op and by $`3.81`$ to $`11.08`$ on G31, and the
fine-tuned G31 models by $`7.72`$ to $`10.59`$; only the quality
instruction (T1, by $`2.70`$ on Op and $`1.90`$ on G31) and, on Op,
best-of-$`n`$ are above it. Only on oss, the weakest model ($`81.27`$),
does every inference-time technique raise HumanEval+ pass@1 over T0 (by
$`0.31`$ to $`8.11`$). The analyzer loop’s gains come with lower
HumanEval+ pass@1 than T7 on three models (by $`7.88`$ on Op, $`7.89`$
on G31 and $`2.27`$ on G26; equal on oss) and lower LiveCodeBench pass@1
on oss and G26 (by $`7.77`$ and $`5.75`$; not on G31), although a
revision is kept only when the public tests pass; three of these five
differences exceed the interval. Against T0 it is $`6.17`$, $`9.94`$ and
$`5.05`$ points lower on Op, G31 and G26 and $`3.59`$ higher on oss. H2
therefore holds in part: the loop removes the analyzer’s own findings,
but a public-test gate does not prevent a correctness cost. The
analyzer’s gains also do not reach the R/M measures the analyzer does
not compute. Against T7, T3 changes cognitive complexity by $`-0.61`$ to
$`+0.49`$ and lowers the judge score by $`0.17`$ to $`0.54`$ on all four
models, beyond the interval on every model, and the training-time
techniques leave the judge score within $`0.17`$ of T7 while lowering
maintainability issues per kLOC by $`2.50`$ to $`6.69`$. Fewer findings
from the analyzer that drives a technique is not the same as code that a
second measure rates as more maintainable, which is the gaming pattern
of
§[17](#S17 "17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code").
On efficiency, T1–T6 score higher than T7 in 22 of 24 Mercury Beyond
cells (10 beyond the interval) and 21 of 24 EffiBench-X cells (7), but
in only 5 of 24 EvalPerf cells (1); the instruction-count measure, which
we take as primary because timing is noisy
(§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3. Critiques ‣ 5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
does not confirm the timing gains. T1, whose instruction names the
target dimensions, changes EvalPerf DPS$`{}_{\text{norm}}`$ against T0
by $`-9.20`$ (G31) to $`+1.84`$ (Op) and Mercury Beyond by $`-4.22`$ to
$`+1.49`$: generic quality instructions raise efficiency on no model
beyond the interval, as H3 expects, but lower EvalPerf
DPS$`{}_{\text{norm}}`$ beyond it on G31. Planning (T2) and Self-Refine
(T4) are below T7 in all 16 SEC cells. Fine-tuning moves correctness in
opposite directions on the two Gemma models: on G26, T8–T10 are $`2.29`$
to $`6.47`$ points above T7 on HumanEval+, and on G31 $`5.67`$ to
$`8.54`$ points below, beyond the interval for all three; on
LiveCodeBench, T8–T10 are within the interval of T7 on both models, at
most $`5.41`$ points from it. On G31’s LiveCodeBench split, T1, T2, T5
and T6 are above T7 beyond the interval, by $`6.36`$ to $`10.69`$
points.

Correctness on tasks no model has seen. The two uncontaminated
correctness measures tell a calmer story than HumanEval+. On the
LiveCodeBench Pro contests held after every cutoff, no technique differs
from T7 or from T0 beyond the interval on any model. On DeepSWE, whose
tasks were released after these models’ cutoffs (for Opus 5.5 by about a
month), the only resolved differences are on Op, where planning, the
analyzer loop, Self-Refine and retrieval are $`6.69`$ to $`8.93`$ points
below its single shot
(Table [4](#S16.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
The HumanEval+ losses on G31, $`3.81`$ to $`11.08`$ points below the
single shot, do not appear on either benchmark. LiveCodeBench Pro is
less precise than HumanEval+ (half-widths of $`5.66`$ to $`6.26`$ points
against $`1.41`$ to $`4.62`$), so a small loss could stay within the
interval there. Seven of the G31 losses, however (T2, T3, T4, T6 and
T8–T10, $`7.72`$ to $`11.08`$ points), exceed LiveCodeBench Pro’s
half-width, and on LiveCodeBench Pro the same techniques lie between
$`-1.52`$ and $`+2.92`$ points of the single shot, five of the seven
above it. Losses of that size would have been significant and are
absent, and on LiveCodeBench, whose problems also postdate Gemma 4’s
cutoff, every G31 technique is above the single shot beyond the
interval. The large HumanEval+ losses are therefore specific to
HumanEval+. Two explanations fit: contamination, and a ceiling or
regression-to-the-mean effect, since the losses appear only on the two
models at about 96% and every technique gains on oss at 81%; the
post-cutoff contests, on which no model is near the ceiling, cannot
separate them
(§[20](#S20 "20. Threats to Validity ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Losses below about six points cannot be excluded on the post-cutoff
contests. The head-to-head
(§[16.3](#S16.SS3 "16.3. E12: Head-to-head of the highlighted techniques ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
shows the same split: most highlighted techniques are below the single
shot on EvalPlus and above it on LiveCodeBench.

Best-of-$`n`$ as a reference. More samples do not always help T7: it
keeps lowering maintainability issues with budget, but loses HumanEval+
pass@1 on both Gemma models and, on G31, CWEval func-sec@1 beyond
$`B=4`$, so wins over T7 are wins over a reference that is strong on the
analyzer’s measures and weaker on hidden-test correctness, and the
comparison with T0 remains necessary (Supplementary Material, §).

Sampling temperature. T7 at the single-call techniques’ temperature of
$`0.2`$ instead of $`0.8`$ is within the half-width in 26 of 36
primary-metric cells, and the conclusions of ERQ1 do not change against
it (Supplementary Material, §).

ERQ3: model strength and architecture. In absolute terms the open models
gain more than the closed anchor. Best-of-4 raises BaxBench sec_pass@1
over T0 by $`1.96`$ points on Op, within the interval, and by $`6.89`$
to $`7.63`$ points on the three open models, and lowers maintainability
issues per kLOC by $`6.05`$ on Op against $`7.29`$ to $`8.24`$ on the
open models. In relative terms the analyzer loop’s effect is nearly the
same on every model: against T0 it removes $`61.3\%`$ to $`63.5\%`$ of
the maintainability issues per kLOC and $`60.7\%`$ to $`64.7\%`$ of the
security issues per kLOC, on Op as on oss. H4 therefore holds for
absolute gains, which partly reflect that the weaker models start with
more findings ($`29.22`$ maintainability issues per kLOC at T0 on oss
against $`21.37`$ on Op), and not for the relative gains of the analyzer
loop. Correctness shows the same split: the techniques raise HumanEval+
pass@1 on the weakest model and lower it on the strongest. The
architecture contrast is limited to the Gemma pair, where fine-tuning
raised HumanEval+ above T7 on the MoE model and lowered it on the dense
one. The pair matches total rather than active parameters, so this is a
difference between two models, not evidence about mixture-of-experts as
such.

Combined reward. The combined reward of T10 did not collapse correctness
on G26, where HumanEval+ pass@1 is $`3.69`$ points above T0 (within the
interval), and gave the largest reductions in maintainability issues per
kLOC of the three training-time techniques ($`13.59`$ on G31 and
$`14.93`$ on G26 against T0). On G31, however, all three fine-tuned
models are $`7.72`$ to $`10.59`$ points below the single shot on
HumanEval+.

### 16.2. Extended grid: current frontier and open-weight models

The main grid holds the base models fixed so that technique effects can
be measured in depth. The extended grid asks whether the picture holds
for the strongest models of October 2026. It adds two closed models,
GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon, and the leading open-weight models
served on Fireworks: Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, Qwen3.8-Max, MiMo-V2.6-Pro,
DeepSeek V4.1-Flash and V4-Flash, and MiniMax M3. Supplementary Table 
scores every model’s single-shot output with the function-level stack,
Supplementary Table  applies the inference-time techniques T1–T7 at
$`B=4`$, and Supplementary Table  adds the repository- and agent-level
benchmarks that 2026 model releases and independent leaderboards report
most: DeepSWE and Terminal-Bench 4.0 for correctness, FrontierCode and
SlopCodeBench for maintainability, GSO and SWE-fficiency for efficiency,
and SusVibes for security
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2. Benchmarks ‣ 5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Because none of the open-weight vendors states a training cutoff and
every 2026 cutoff postdates LiveCodeBench v6 and the last public
LiveCodeBench Pro set, correctness on function-level tasks is measured
only on Codeforces contests held after 2026-07-01.

Results. _Capability._ The closed models lead every function-level
correctness and security measure (Supplementary Table ): LiveCodeBench
Pro pass@1 of $`66.79`$ to $`69.82`$ against $`41.11`$ to $`61.87`$ for
the open-weight frontier models and $`21.94`$ to $`27.68`$ for the
main-grid open models, CWEval func-sec@1 of $`72.79`$ to $`74.85`$
against $`56.72`$ to $`69.43`$ and $`45.02`$ to $`49.48`$, and BaxBench
sec*pass@1 of $`56.22`$ to $`58.54`$ against $`40.41`$ to $`52.46`$ and
$`26.38`$ to $`32.97`$. *Quality follows capability, efficiency does
not.* Across the thirteen models, single-shot LiveCodeBench Pro pass@1
correlates with maintainability issues per kLOC ($`r=-0.96`$), the judge
score ($`0.90`$), CWEval ($`0.95`$), BaxBench ($`0.97`$) and security
issues per kLOC ($`-0.97`$), but hardly with EvalPerf
DPS$`{}*{\text{norm}}`$ ($`0.22`$) or Mercury Beyond ($`0.15`$):
stronger models write cleaner and safer code by default, but not faster
code. *Techniques.* The main-grid pattern holds on all nine added models
(Supplementary Table ): T7 leaves fewer maintainability issues per kLOC
than T1, T2, T4, T5 and T6 on every model and a higher CWEval func-sec@1
than all of them on seven of nine, while the analyzer loop roughly
halves T7’s maintainability issues ($`7.98`$ to $`9.94`$ per kLOC
against $`16.23`$ to $`18.96`$) and changes func-sec@1 by $`-0.50`$ to
$`+7.23`$ points against T7. *Repository-level quality.* On the agent
benchmarks (Supplementary Table ), DeepSWE pass@1 correlates with
FrontierCode ($`0.91`$), GSO ($`0.95`$), SWE-fficiency ($`0.98`$),
SusVibes SecPass ($`0.97`$) and, negatively, with SlopCodeBench erosion
($`-0.97`$). The largest gap is between working and secure code: on
SusVibes every closed and open-weight frontier model passes the
functional tests on $`38.06`$ to $`44.41`$ points more tasks than it
passes the security tests, against a quality penalty of $`1.25`$ to
$`7.59`$ points on FrontierCode. The main-grid open models sit near the
floor of every agent benchmark (DeepSWE $`10.17`$ to $`17.96`$,
Terminal-Bench 4.0 $`2.91`$ to $`5.10`$).
