### 16.3. E12: Head-to-head of the highlighted techniques

T0–T10 study a few representative techniques in depth, across models and
budgets. E12 adds breadth: it compares the 66 highlighted techniques of
§[7](#S7 "7. Highlighted Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
with each other under one setting, so that the results their authors
report on different benchmarks, models and baselines (Supplementary
Tables –) can be replaced by measurements that are comparable.

Research question. _ERQ4:_ under one model, one benchmark set and common
reference budgets, which highlighted techniques improve the dimension
they target, what do they cost in COR and in the dimensions they do not
target, and how do the families compare?

Model. One model holds everything else fixed. We use Gemma 4 31B IT, the
dense arm of the main grid
(Table [2](#S16.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")a),
because it is the dense arm of the fine-tuned Gemma pair, so the
training-time techniques change the same weights the inference-time
techniques prompt.

Benchmarks. E12 uses only public benchmarks that the included studies
themselves use most, so that its results connect to the literature; we
add no benchmark of our own. Counts are the included studies that report
each benchmark (from the extraction table). COR: HumanEval+ and MBPP+
(EvalPlus; plain HumanEval appears in 85 studies, the EvalPlus versions
in 19) as the likely contaminated split, LiveCodeBench (14) for tasks
after the model’s January 2025 cutoff, and the LiveCodeBench Pro
protocol on Codeforces contests held after 2026-07-01, which no current
model has seen. SEC: CWEval (15), which requires code to be both
functional and secure, and CyberSecEval (15), the most comparable to
prior security work; its rule-based detector’s reported error rates
(§[5](#S5 "5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
are carried into the analysis. EFF: EffiBench (8), the most used
efficiency benchmark, and EvalPerf (5), whose instruction counts are
more stable than wall-clock time. R/M: no dedicated benchmark is in
common use (RACE and NoFunEval appear in 0 and 0 included studies); the
studies measure R/M by running established analyzers on generated code,
and E12 does the same: pinned Pylint, cognitive complexity and the
length-controlled judge, applied to the outputs of the COR benchmarks.
Every output of every benchmark is scored on all four dimensions with
the measurement stack above, so a technique that targets one dimension
is also measured on the other three. Python comes first; a technique
defined only for another language is ported and marked as such.

Implementation. Each technique runs in one harness. Where public code
exists (43 of the 66) we adapt it; otherwise we reimplement it from the
paper. Before use, each implementation is checked against one automated
number its authors report, in their setting; where their model is
retired or their number is a human rating, another automated number the
paper reports for a runnable model is used, and 14 techniques with no
such number are not checkable (Supplementary Material, §; 48 of the 52
checkable techniques reproduce within 5%). Implementations are adjusted
at most twice before the final run, stopping as soon as the reproduced
number falls within the tolerance; the adjustment count and the per-run
logs of every run, including superseded ones, are retained and will be
released with the replication package. Hyperparameters come from the
papers and are never tuned on these benchmarks. Components that call
another LLM (critics, reviewers, judges) use the same model; components
that the paper trains (detectors, reward models, co-decoders) are
retrained for the same model. Training-time techniques are retrained on
the same model with the authors’ released data, or with data built by
their recipe when it is not released (marked), using LoRA on Fireworks;
training time, from several hours to a few days per run, lies outside
the call budget.

Budget and baselines. Each technique runs in its published
configuration, with a ceiling of 16 calls per task (a technique that
needs more runs at the ceiling and is marked). Calls, tokens and cost
are logged per task. Two references run on every benchmark: T0 (one
call) and one best-of-$`n`$ run with the T7 ranker, at a mean of
$`4.19`$ calls per task (Supplementary Table ); it redraws a sample with
no extractable code while the ceiling allows, which is why it runs above
four calls and why its scores differ slightly from T7 at $`B=4`$ in
Table [3](#S16.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code").
Best-of-$`n`$ is thus the budget-matched reference for techniques near
that budget; a technique that uses about one call is compared with T0.
So that techniques using many more calls are not compared with a cheaper
reference, best-of-$`n`$ also runs at two, three, five and eight calls
per task with the same ranker; each family is compared with the
reference nearest its median calls per task: prompting and training with
best-of-2, retrieval with best-of-3, tool feedback and self-refinement
with best-of-5, multi-agent pipelines with best-of-8, and decoding
(median $`3.75`$ calls) with the main reference.

Analysis. Per benchmark, each technique is compared with T0 and with
best-of-$`n`$ by its point difference, with quality reported on every
output, and summarized per family. E12 is _indicative_: it compares
point estimates, and its counts of techniques that beat a reference do
not test each difference. Paired bootstrap 95% half-widths over tasks,
computed for every technique and column against T0 and against
best-of-$`n`$, have a median of $`2.7`$ points for EvalPlus, $`5.5`$ for
LiveCodeBench, $`5.8`$ for LiveCodeBench Pro, $`6.2`$ for CWEval,
$`2.9`$ for CyberSecEval and $`3.2`$ for EvalPerf (Supplementary
Material, §); a smaller difference in Supplementary Table  should be
read as not significant, and only 1 of the 16 wins over best-of-$`n`$
exceed the half-width of every target metric. Supplementary Table  gives
the results.

Forest plot of the highlighted techniques, grouped by targeted
dimension, each with its difference from best-of-n on its primary metric
and a 95 percent interval; most intervals cross zero or lie below it.

Figure 5. Fig. E2. Head-to-head summary (E12, Gemma 4 31B IT): each
highlighted technique’s difference from best-of-$`n`$ on the primary
metric of its targeted dimension (Pylint score for R/M, EvalPerf
DPS$`{}_{\text{norm}}`$ for EFF, CWEval func-sec@1 for SEC), with its
95% paired bootstrap interval; filled markers lie beyond the interval.
All columns, both references and the budget-matched references are in
Supplementary Table , and the per-column half-widths in Supplementary
Table .Forest plot of the highlighted techniques, grouped by targeted
dimension, each with its difference from best-of-n on its primary metric
and a 95 percent interval; most intervals cross zero or lie below it.

Results (ERQ4).
Fig. [5](#S16.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 16.3. E12: Head-to-head of the highlighted techniques ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
gives the view with intervals: on the primary metric of its targeted
dimension, 1 of the 66 techniques is above best-of-$`n`$ beyond the
interval (CodeChain), 22 are below it beyond the interval, and 43 are
within it. With 66 comparisons, about two wins in the favourable
direction are expected by chance alone, so the single win does not show
that CodeChain beats best-of-$`n`$. The counts that follow compare point
estimates on every target metric and are indicative only. The
best-of-$`n`$ reference runs at a mean of $`4.19`$ calls. Against T0, 51
of the 66 techniques improve every target metric we measure: prompting 8
of 10, tool feedback 7 of 10, self-refinement 5 of 6, multi-agent 7 of
10, retrieval 7 of 10, decoding 10 of 10, training 7 of 10. Against
best-of-$`n`$, 16 of the 66 do: prompting 4, decoding 3, tool feedback
2, self-refinement 2, multi-agent 3, retrieval 2, training 0. Because
the families differ in cost, we also ran best-of-$`n`$ at two, three,
five and eight calls and compared each family with the reference nearest
its median calls (Supplementary Table , last panel), which removes the
asymmetry of a single reference: against these budget-matched references
19 of the 66 techniques improve every target metric (prompting 5 of 10
(best-of-2), tool feedback 2 of 10 (best-of-5), self-refinement 2 of 6
(best-of-5), multi-agent 1 of 10 (best-of-8), retrieval 3 of 10
(best-of-3), decoding 3 of 10 (main reference), training 3 of 10
(best-of-2)). Matching the budget changes the total little (19 against
16): the one-call families win slightly more often against best-of-2
than against the four-call reference (prompting 5 against 4, training 3
against 0), and the multi-agent pipelines, the most expensive family,
slightly less often against best-of-8 (1 against 3); eight of the
training-time techniques run at one call per task, SafeCoder at 1.07 and
Afterburner, which keeps an optimization loop at inference, at 4.09.

The dimensions tell different stories. _Security:_ 23 of the 29
security-targeted techniques produce fewer CyberSecEval insecure-code
detections than best-of-$`n`$, but only 6 of the 29 exceed its CWEval
func-sec@1. Lowering the rule-based detector’s hits is easier than
writing code that is both secure and functional, and the detector’s
reported error rates
(§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3. Critiques ‣ 5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
make the first the weaker evidence. _Efficiency:_ 22 of the 22
efficiency-targeted techniques run faster than T0 on EffiBench, against
2 of the techniques that target other dimensions; EvalPerf’s
instruction-count score improves for only 9 of the 22. Since EffiBench
relies on physical time
(§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3. Critiques ‣ 5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
the head-to-head supports an efficiency gain only where both measures
agree. _Readability and maintainability:_ 13 of the 15 R/M-targeted
techniques raise the Pylint score above T0, by at most $`1.35`$ points
on its 10-point scale (CodeChain), and only 8 of all 66 techniques
exceed best-of-$`n`$ ($`7.69`$). _Correctness:_ the two function-level
splits disagree. On EvalPlus, which is likely contaminated, 58 of the 66
techniques are below T0 (family medians $`-7.68`$ to $`-1.73`$ points);
on LiveCodeBench, whose problems postdate the model’s cutoff, 44 of the
66 are above it (family medians $`-0.96`$ to $`+5.41`$), as is
best-of-$`n`$, which selects among samples on the public examples. As in
the main grid
(§[16.1](#S16.SS1 "16.1. Results of the main re-evaluation ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
the losses are largely specific to the likely contaminated split. The
LiveCodeBench Pro contests, which also postdate the cutoff, show no
comparable losses and only small gains: 57 of the 66 techniques score
above T0 ($`27.14`$) and 12 above best-of-$`n`$ ($`30.92`$), all within
$`6.26`$ points of T0, the main-grid half-width for G31, with family
medians of $`+0.79`$ to $`+3.52`$ points. _Cost:_ median calls per task
are $`1.00`$ for training (training compute excluded), $`1.89`$ for
prompting, $`3.12`$ for retrieval, $`3.75`$ for decoding, $`5.08`$ for
self-refinement, $`4.93`$ for tool feedback and $`7.98`$ for multi-agent
pipelines.

## 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs

Counts below come from the author-reviewed, LLM-assisted extraction;
per-study numbers were checked against primary sources.

##### RQ1 and RQ2: what is targeted, and how it is measured.

Efficiency is the most often targeted dimension (335 studies), followed
by security (182) and readability/maintainability (130)
(Fig. [3](#S6.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Distribution. ‣ 6. A Faceted Taxonomy of Quality-Improving Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
by family and signal source, Supplementary Fig.  over time). Instruments
vary by dimension: static analyzers such as Bandit and CodeQL for
security, wall-clock timing against a reference for efficiency, linters
or LLM judges for readability; human evaluation is rare
(Table [13](#S17.T13 "Table 13 ‣ RQ4: evidence quality and compute fairness. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Each has documented validity problems
(§[5](#S5 "5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")):
static analyzers overestimated security by 7 to 21 times in one
re-evaluation, with 37 to 60% of “secure” outputs not functional ([Tessa
et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib513)); wall-clock time varied about 12% across
runs versus 0.03% for CPU instruction counts ([Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib200)); and an LLM judge’s Python readability scores were
uncorrelated with human ratings (Pearson 0.02) ([Ouédraogo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib132)). A reported gain thus partly reflects the instrument
used to optimize and evaluate it.

##### RQ3: effects on correctness and on non-targeted dimensions.

Table [11](#S17.T11 "Table 11 ‣ RQ1 and RQ2: what is targeted, and how it is measured. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
is the review’s headline result: most studies never measured a quality
dimension beyond their target, so most techniques’ cross-dimension
effects are unknown, not neutral. Among technique rows reporting a
target gain, correctness was unchanged, mixed or lower in about a
quarter and unreported in nearly three in ten
(Table [12](#S17.T12 "Table 12 ‣ RQ3: effects on correctness and on non-targeted dimensions. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Individual cases show why gates matter: AutoSafeCoder lowered HumanEval
pass@1 from 0.9085 to 0.8780 while reducing Bandit findings ([Nunez
et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib345)), whereas the fitness-gated Pylint and
Bandit loop of [Blyth et al. (2025)](#as1_bib.bib58) raised functional
correctness from 38.16% to 47.81%. [Wu et al. (2026a)](#as1_bib.bib541)
report that prior security alignment methods often cut an effective
safety rate that also requires correctness by 14-54%. Evidence on
trade-offs _between_ non-functional dimensions, such as whether security
hardening or performance optimization harms readability, is almost
absent.

the rate is drawn from its posterior, and the range is the 95th

##### Goodhart effects.

Every family optimizing a single automated signal shows some form of
gaming. In CORE’s user study, reviewers rejected 55.11% of
CodeQL-passing revisions ([Wadhwa et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib522)).
Effectively empty output scored a Maintainability Index of 100% and zero
smells ([Islam et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib215)). A reinforcement-learning
policy with a quality-only reward learned to emit trivial outputs such
as empty code or comments ([Yao et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib573)), and
GPT-5 cheated in 76% of tasks on a benchmark built to detect test
special-casing ([Zhong et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib610)). The usual remedy
in stronger studies is to gate quality signals on executed tests and to
evaluate with an instrument other than the feedback or reward signal;
few do both.

##### RQ4: evidence quality and compute fairness.

Table [13](#S17.T13 "Table 13 ‣ RQ4: evidence quality and compute fairness. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
summarizes the quality assessment. Iterative techniques (feedback loops,
self-refinement, multi-agent pipelines) spend several to many times the
calls and tokens of single-shot generation, yet baselines seldom get the
same budget; when they do, gains shrink ([Olausson et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib368)), and we found only one efficiency-loop study
comparing against an oracle best-of-five baseline ([Deng et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib116)). Only a minority report variance across
samples, contamination, and validation of automated metrics against
human judgement. About a third evaluate a single model without
justification.

##### RQ5: gaps.

Thin cells in the evidence maps (readability-targeted retrieval and
decoding, learned verifiers and reward models for any dimension,
profiler signals outside efficiency) and unasked questions (effects on
non-targeted dimensions, scaling with model capability, gains at a
matched budget) define the agenda of
§[19](#S19 "19. Research Agenda ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
and the hypotheses of
§[16](#S16 "16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code").

## 18. Implications for Researchers and Practitioners

##### For practitioners.

Practitioners prioritize maintainability and readability ([Sun et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib498)), the dimensions on which our re-evaluation finds
the clearest pattern. Five implications follow from the results of
§[16](#S16 "16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code").

- •
  _Compare with sampling first._ Before adopting a prompting, planning,
  self-refinement, reviewer or retrieval technique, run best-of-$`n`$ at
  the same number of model calls with a ranker built from the analyzers
  already in the pipeline. On measures that ranker does not optimize, it
  matches or beats each of these techniques in most cells
  (Table [9](#S16.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
  so a technique’s gain over a single call is not evidence that it beats
  this cheaper baseline.
- •
  _Do not rely on quality instructions at one call._ A single call with
  a quality instruction or a plan does not lower maintainability issues
  on any of the four models
  (§[16.1](#S16.SS1 "16.1. Results of the main re-evaluation ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"));
  its apparent gains at larger budgets come from the ranker it shares
  with best-of-$`n`$.
- •
  _Use analyzer loops and fine-tuning for what they deliver._ Both lower
  the issue counts of the analyzers they use, by large margins, but
  these gains do not carry over to cognitive complexity, the judge score
  or test-based security
  (Table [9](#S16.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
  They suit teams whose quality gate is those analyzers; they are not
  evidence of more readable code.
- •
  _Check correctness on new tasks._ A technique’s effect on HumanEval+
  can differ in sign from its effect on contests and repository tasks
  the model has not seen
  (§[16.1](#S16.SS1 "16.1. Results of the main re-evaluation ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"));
  a gate on recent tasks, or on the project’s own tests, is the safer
  check.
- •
  _Gate security with tests, not detector counts._ Security techniques
  lower rule-based detector hits far more often than they raise the
  share of code that is both functional and secure
  (§[16.3](#S16.SS3 "16.3. E12: Head-to-head of the highlighted techniques ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
  and current frontier agents produce working but insecure code on about
  four in ten SusVibes tasks
  (§[16.2](#S16.SS2 "16.2. Extended grid: current frontier and open-weight models ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
  Security tests or exploits, not detector counts alone, should decide
  whether generated code ships.

Across the thirteen current models, maintainability and security rise
with capability while efficiency does not
(§[16.2](#S16.SS2 "16.2. Extended grid: current frontier and open-weight models ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
so the choice of model moves these dimensions about as much as any
single technique, and efficiency needs its own measurement.

##### For researchers.

The review and the re-evaluation point to reporting practices that would
make technique papers comparable
(§[19](#S19 "19. Research Agenda ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
gives the research agenda).

- •
  Include a best-of-$`n`$ baseline at the same number of calls, ranked
  by the same signal the technique uses, and report calls and tokens per
  task.
- •
  Report correctness and the dimensions the technique does not target:
  only 70 of 628 extracted studies measured a quality dimension beyond
  their target
  (Table [11](#S17.T11 "Table 11 ‣ RQ1 and RQ2: what is targeted, and how it is measured. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
- •
  Measure the target on an instrument independent of the technique’s own
  signal, such as a test-based security benchmark, a judge or human
  ratings for an analyzer-driven technique.
- •
  Report seeds and variance, use tasks dated after the model’s training
  cutoff, and release prompts, harness and per-task outputs, so that
  others can check a claimed gain at their own budget.

## 19. Research Agenda

The evidence maps
(Fig. [3](#S6.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Distribution. ‣ 6. A Faceted Taxonomy of Quality-Improving Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
and per-family syntheses point to five open problems.

##### Measure what a technique does to everything, not only to its target.

Most studies report their target and, at best, correctness
(Table [11](#S17.T11 "Table 11 ‣ RQ1 and RQ2: what is targeted, and how it is measured. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
A security technique with unknown effect on readability, or a
readability technique with unknown effect on efficiency, cannot be
adopted safely. A technique paper should at minimum report all three
non-functional dimensions plus correctness, unconditionally and
conditional on passing tests, even when non-targeted results are null.

##### Quality-aware selection and retrieval.

Reranking and best-of-$`n`$ selection mostly use tests or correctness
verifiers
(§[13](#S13 "13. Decoding-Time Control and Reranking ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
retrieval relevance or security exemplars
(§[12](#S12 "12. Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Verifiers and retrievers encoding maintainability or efficiency, and
evidence that they help at a matched sampling budget, are largely
missing. Best-of-$`n`$ under a quality verifier is also the natural
budget-matched baseline for iterative techniques.

##### Multi-dimension rewards that resist gaming.

Rewards built on a single analyzer or judge are gamed: policies learn to
emit trivial or empty code that scores well, and reviewers reject
analyzer-satisfying fixes
(§[9](#S9 "9. Tool-Feedback Loops ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"),
§[14](#S14 "14. Training-Time Alignment for Quality ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Open questions are how to combine correctness gates with several quality
signals, keep evaluation and training signals independent, and detect
reward hacking before deployment.

##### Default-behaviour evaluation.

Several quality benchmarks measure quality only when the prompt requests
it, testing instruction following rather than the code a model writes by
default
(§[5](#S5 "5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Scoring code written for ordinary task descriptions, at repository level
and over many edits, would capture the erosion that function-level
benchmarks miss.

##### Contamination-resistant quality evaluation with cost accounting.

Frontier training cutoffs now fall in 2026, after most quality
benchmarks. Quality evaluation needs tasks that postdate the models,
reference solutions for measuring efficiency, metrics validated against
human judgement, and a record of each technique’s tokens and calls, so
quality gains can be separated from extra compute.

## 20. Threats to Validity

We group threats as construct, internal, external and conclusion
validity, for the review and the re-evaluation in turn.

##### Construct validity.

_Review._ Effect directions and quality targets were extracted by an LLM
and reviewed by the author; vote counting ignores effect and sample size
and depends on how “improved” is defined, so we use it to describe the
evidence, not to rank techniques. The highlighted-technique tables
report what each paper claims; only the head-to-head of
§[16.3](#S16.SS3 "16.3. E12: Head-to-head of the highlighted techniques ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
compares techniques under one setting. _Re-evaluation._ Pylint, Bandit
and Safety drive the analyzer loop (T3) and the best-of-$`n`$ ranker
(T7), and SonarQube also ingests their reports, so its issue counts are
not fully independent of the techniques’ analyzers; cognitive
complexity, the judge, CWEval and BaxBench, to which T3’s gains do not
carry over, are reported for that reason and lead the results
(Table [9](#S16.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
Issue densities are reported next to solution length and absolute counts
(Supplementary Material, §). The maintainability measures (issue counts,
cognitive complexity and the judge score) are computed on every output,
correct or not, and not also on correct outputs alone as
§[5](#S5 "5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
recommends, so a technique that lowers correctness could look more
maintainable partly through short or degenerate failing programs; the
efficiency scores, CWEval func-sec@1 and BaxBench sec_pass@1 give no
credit to a program that fails its tests. Budgets match model calls, not
tokens: critic and reviewer turns are shorter or longer than a sample,
the iterative techniques T3–T5 stop early (about $`0.6\,B`$
call-equivalents on average), and Opus 5.5 does not expose its reasoning
tokens, so for Opus budget matching is call-based only; we report tokens
per experiment (Supplementary Material, §) but no token-matched curves.
Claude Opus 5.5 has five roles: title/abstract screener, extractor, R/M
judge, evaluated model, and the critic and reviewer of its own T4 and T5
runs. Comparisons on one model are not affected by the judge’s vendor,
but the judge score of the Op row may include self-preference; a second
judge from another vendor (GPT-6.1 Sol) therefore scores every R/M
output, agrees at Spearman $`\rho=0.72{}`$ per output and
$`\rho=0.79{}`$ across the thirteen models, and ranks Opus 5.5 as the
Opus judge does; a correlation of $`0.79{}`$ still allows neighbouring
models to swap places, so we do not rank models that the two judges
order differently. The first human rater is the author; to keep author
bias out, the second rater is an engineer who is not an author. Both
rated outputs blind to technique, model and every automated score, but
they could recognise a technique’s style (planning comments, for
instance), and their agreement ($`\kappa=0.63{}`$) is moderate; three
further software engineers, none of them authors, rated a stratified
sub-sample of 114 of the same outputs, agreeing with the two raters’
mean rating at quadratic-weighted $`\kappa=0.57`$ (Spearman
$`\rho=0.62`$) and with the judge at $`\rho=0.67`$. The second rater,
the three further engineers and the second coder of the review all work
at the author’s company; none is an author, but they are the author’s
colleagues. RACE and NoFunEval measure agreement with a requirement or a
reference rather than quality as such
(§[5](#S5 "5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
which is why every output is also scored by our analyzers and judge.

##### Internal validity.

_Review._ Title/abstract screening used one author-reviewed LLM
screener; its agreement with an independent second coder on a random
sample is reported in
§[4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6. Use of generative AI in this review ‣ 4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"),
and the vote counts carry the extraction’s disagreement rate as a range
(Table [12](#S17.T12 "Table 12 ‣ RQ3: effects on correctness and on non-targeted dimensions. ‣ 17. Discussion: Cross-Cutting Findings and Trade-offs ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
The recall-favouring rule (include or uncertain goes forward) limits
false exclusions there but not at full text, where a low-cost model
removed reports it judged clearly ineligible. One LLM extractor did
full-text eligibility, extraction and QA scoring; its author-reviewed
effect directions and QA scores feed the evidence maps and vote counts.
Numbers attributed to specific papers do not depend on it: each was
checked against a verbatim passage of its primary source. The selection
in
§[7](#S7 "7. Highlighted Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
rests on choices another team could make differently: Semantic Scholar
citation counts at a single point in time, favouring older and
arXiv-visible work; relative gain over each paper’s own strongest
baseline, which rewards weak baselines and studies evaluated on their
authors’ own benchmarks; the restriction to general-purpose techniques;
five exclusion rules applied by LLM reviewers, with decisions recorded
and reviewed by the author; and two decisions taken after the rule was
first applied (the RL adjustment of the training family and the
reclassification of Universal Textual Teaching), which
§[7](#S7 "7. Highlighted Techniques ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
reports as deviations. _Re-evaluation._ Reimplementations may differ
from the originals; each was checked against a published result, with at
most two adjustments and a stated stopping rule
(§[16.3](#S16.SS3 "16.3. E12: Head-to-head of the highlighted techniques ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code");
Supplementary Material, §). Closed APIs offer no temperature control,
which three runs of every configuration address. The HumanEval+ losses
on the two models with the highest single-shot pass@1 (about 96%) and
the gains on the model at 81% admit two explanations: contamination of
HumanEval+, and a ceiling or regression-to-the-mean effect, under which
a model near the top of a benchmark can mostly lose. The post-cutoff
contests show neither the losses nor large gains, which is consistent
with both; we therefore use “likely contaminated” as a description of
HumanEval+’s release date relative to the models’ training, not as an
established cause of the losses.

##### External validity.

_Review._ Terminology differs across software-engineering,
machine-learning and security communities, and a quality-improving
technique need not name a quality attribute in its abstract. We
mitigated this with a broad quality facet, a technique-oriented
supplementary string, a quasi-gold standard, a venue sweep, snowballing
and section-level searches. Recall was 0.938 against the quasi-gold
standard (optimistic, since the string was revised after inspecting its
misses) and 0.775 at screening against a venue sweep. The revised
strings ran on Semantic Scholar and arXiv; OpenAlex was queried with the
original string only, so a study indexed only by OpenAlex and matched
only by the revised strings would be missed. Two limits remain. Only
reports whose full text could be retrieved were assessed, so 687 of the
1777 reports sought were excluded as not retrieved; this may
under-represent venues without open-access copies. Of these reports, 579
date from 2025 or 2026, 327 are conference or workshop papers, 199
journal articles and 99 preprints or repository deposits, and 15 are
other versions of included studies (Supplementary Table ). Unpaywall
lists no open copy for 305 of them, mostly IEEE (172) and Springer (62)
publications, and an open copy for 90 with a PDF link and 154 with only
a landing page, which manual retrieval could still close. Snowballing
ran one backward and one forward iteration, so studies reachable only
through longer citation chains may be missing. Preprints were included
to cover 2025–2026; they are flagged and QA-scored, and a re-count on
the peer-reviewed studies alone leaves the synthesis unchanged
(§[4.5](#S4.SS5 "4.5. Synthesis ‣ 4. Review Methodology ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code");
Supplementary Material, §). Negative results are rarely published, so
the literature likely overstates benefits; the re-evaluation partly
offsets this. _Re-evaluation._ Most benchmarks are function-level Python
and the main grid has four models. Its open models were chosen for a
stated training cutoff, low cost and, for Gemma 4, a fine-tunable dense
and MoE pair, so ERQ3’s open-versus-closed contrast is also a capability
contrast; the extended grid
(§[16.2](#S16.SS2 "16.2. Extended grid: current frontier and open-weight models ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
adds the leading open-weight models, measured on post-cutoff contests
only. Technique effects are established on function-level benchmarks
(and DeepSWE), while the field has moved to repository-level and agent
tasks
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2. Benchmarks ‣ 5. Measuring Code Quality: Metrics and Benchmarks ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
The head-to-head uses one mid-size open model, Gemma 4 31B IT, and its
results may not carry over to other models.

##### Conclusion validity.

We call a difference significant when it exceeds a 95% paired bootstrap
half-width computed per metric, model and budget against T7 at the same
$`B`$
(Table [10](#S16.T10 "Table 10 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code");
Supplementary Material, §); comparisons against T0 reuse the $`B=4`$
half-widths, where the paired variance can differ, so those significance
calls are approximate. Half-widths barely change with budget (median
ratio of the $`B=16`$ to the $`B=4`$ half-width 0.99). Every
configuration ran three times with fresh seeds; the tables report the
mean, and the standard deviation of a cell’s metric across the three
seeds has a median of 0.39 of the corresponding half-width
(Supplementary Material, §), so seed-to-seed variation is small against
task-to-task variation. To control false discoveries across the 1,272
metric–model–technique–budget cells against T7, we computed two-sided
paired bootstrap $`p`$-values and applied the Benjamini–Hochberg
procedure at $`q=0.05`$: 494 of the 536 differences significant under
the half-width rule survive (204 of them at $`B=4`$, as counted in
Table [8](#S16.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")b),
including every significant difference cited in
§[16.1](#S16.SS1 "16.1. Results of the main re-evaluation ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code").
Conclusions rest on counts of significant cells and on patterns that
repeat across models and benchmarks, not on any single cell. The
head-to-head (E12) is indicative: it compares point estimates against
fixed references, and its per-technique bootstrap intervals are reported
in the Supplementary Material. HumanEval+ has the smallest half-widths
and LiveCodeBench Pro the largest, so small correctness differences
reach significance more easily on the likely contaminated benchmark
(§[16.1](#S16.SS1 "16.1. Results of the main re-evaluation ‣ 16. Controlled Re-evaluation ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
In the head-to-head, one technique of 66 beats best-of-$`n`$ on its
primary target beyond the 95% interval; with 66 comparisons, about two
such wins in that direction are expected by chance alone, so this single
win is not evidence that the technique is better.

## 21. Conclusion

Functional correctness no longer separates frontier code generators, but
their code still differs in readability, efficiency and security. A
reproducible, LLM-assisted review of July 2021 to October 2026
literature organized them by stage, signal source and quality target and
found a consistent pattern: techniques are evaluated on their target
dimension, rarely on others, often without a matched compute budget, and
sometimes at a cost to correctness that only a test or fitness gate
prevents. Easily optimized signals, such as an analyzer’s warning count
or a judge’s score, are also easily gamed.

The controlled re-evaluation, with matched budgets on four models and a
head-to-head of the highlighted techniques, confirms this pattern. At a
single call, quality prompting does not lower analyzer issue counts and
barely moves complexity or judge scores, and best-of-$`n`$ sampling with
the same calls, at four and at sixteen, gains most of what quality
techniques gain over a single shot, also on measures the sampling ranker
does not optimize; the techniques that do better, an analyzer loop and
fine-tuning, improve only the issue counts their own analyzers compute,
and on the strongest models almost every technique costs HumanEval+
correctness, a cost that largely disappears on contests and repository
tasks no model has seen. Across thirteen current models, stronger models
write cleaner and safer, but not faster, code by default, and even the
best agents leave working but insecure code in about four in ten
repository tasks. Technique effects are measured on function-level
tasks, so their transfer to agent workflows remains open. For
practitioners: compare any technique that promises better code with
sampling at the same budget, and ask what it did to correctness and to
the qualities it did not target.

## Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code”

The replication package, to be released, contains every query, raw
export, screening decision, prompt, full-text manifest, extraction row
and script used in this review. This document reproduces the parts a
reader needs to audit the method.

## S1. Search strings per source

The exact strings sent to each source, with the raw hit count. OpenAlex
does not support wildcards, so wildcard terms were expanded; arXiv
applies stemming, so trailing wildcards were removed and the quality
facet was split into chunks whose union equals the full query. The
revised strings ran on Semantic Scholar and arXiv only (the main
article’s threats to validity).

## S2. Title and abstract screening prompt

The frozen system prompt used for title/abstract screening (Claude
Opus 5.5, effort=low, ten records per request; records refused as a
group were re-run one per request). The full-text eligibility and
extraction prompts will be released with the replication package. You
are screening records (title and abstract only) for a systematic
literature review in software engineering. Apply the criteria below
exactly. You will receive several records; decide each one
independently.

\# Review topic

Techniques that improve the NON-FUNCTIONAL quality of code generated or
edited by large language models (LLMs).

Definitions:

- LLM: a pretrained transformer language model used for code
  (code-specialized or general, any size, closed or open).

- Technique: any intervention that changes the code an LLM produces. It
  may act on the input (prompt or context), on decoding, on a
  post-generation loop (tool feedback, self-refinement, agents, critics),
  or on the model’s weights (fine-tuning, preference optimization,
  reinforcement learning).

- Non-functional (NF) quality: (1) readability and maintainability
  (naming, structure, complexity, code smells, idiomaticity,
  documentation, style conformance); (2) performance efficiency (runtime,
  memory, energy); (3) security (vulnerabilities, CWE). Correctness (tests
  passing) is NOT an NF dimension.

\# Inclusion criteria (a study must meet ALL)

- IC1: It proposes or empirically evaluates one or more techniques
  applied to an LLM.

- IC2: The evaluated artifact is code generated or edited by an LLM in a
  generation, completion or editing task.

- IC3: It reports at least one quantitative NF quality outcome for that
  code (tool-based, execution-based, LLM-judge or human-rated all count).

- IC4: It is a full paper (peer-reviewed, or a preprint of 4+ pages).

\# Exclusion criteria (exclude if ANY holds)

- EC1: Not in English.

- EC2: A secondary study (survey, systematic review, mapping study).

- EC3: The target artifact is not production code (tests only,
  comments/documentation only, commit messages, code review comments,
  natural-language explanations).

- EC4: Purely the analysis of human-written code: vulnerability
  detection, smell detection, or repair/refactoring of human-written code
  with no LLM generation.

- EC5: Quality measured only as correctness, compilability or syntactic
  validity.

- EC6: Model-level robustness, safety or attack papers whose outcome is
  not the quality of the generated code (jailbreaks, adversarial prompts,
  backdoors, data poisoning, prompt-injection defences).

- EC7: Pre-LLM neural code models without large-scale pretraining
  (seq2seq/RNN generators).

- EC8: A duplicate or earlier version of another study (only decidable
  when obvious from the record).

\# Side lists (record these even when the decision is exclude)

- context: measures the NF quality of LLM-generated code WITHOUT any
  intervention (e.g., a security audit of Copilot output, an empirical
  study of smells in ChatGPT code, a benchmark that measures NF quality of
  LLM code).

- adjacent: LLM refactoring or repair of human-written code (the EC4
  group).

- correctness-only: an influential code-generation technique that
  reports only correctness (EC5), e.g. self-debugging, test-based
  reranking, multi-agent coding frameworks evaluated on pass@k only.

- secondary: a survey or review relevant to the topic (EC2).

- none: none of the above.

\# Decision rules

- "include": the title/abstract indicates IC1-IC4 are likely met and no
  EC applies.

- "exclude": at least one exclusion criterion clearly applies, or an
  inclusion criterion clearly fails.

- "uncertain": the abstract does not make it clear whether a technique
  is evaluated on LLM-generated code with a quantitative NF outcome. When
  in doubt between include and exclude, choose "uncertain" (this review
  favours recall). A technique paper that mentions security, efficiency,
  readability, maintainability, code smells, or code quality as an
  evaluated outcome is at least "uncertain".

- criterion: for include, write "IC"; for exclude, the single most
  decisive code (EC1-EC8, or IC1/IC2/IC3/IC4 if an inclusion criterion
  fails); for uncertain, the criterion you could not decide.

\# Output format

Return ONLY a JSON array, one object per record, in the same order as
the records, with exactly these keys:

\[{"rid": "\<record id\>", "decision": "include\|exclude\|uncertain",
"criterion": "\<code\>", "side_list":
"context\|adjacent\|correctness-only\|secondary\|none", "reason": "\<one
sentence, max 25 words\>"}\]

## S3. Data extraction schema

One row per study and technique, with controlled vocabularies in
brackets: bibliographic data and venue type \[peer-reviewed conference,
journal, workshop, preprint\]; study type \[technique proposal,
technique evaluation\]; technique name; family \[prompting, feedback
loop, self-refinement, multi-agent, retrieval, decoding, training,
hybrid, other\]; stage \[pre-generation, in-decoding, post-generation
loop, training-time\]; signal source \[none, self, other LLM, static
analyzer, compiler, test execution, profiler, retrieved knowledge,
human, learned verifier, reward model\]; tools and versions; iterations
and stopping rule; dimensions targeted and measured
\[readability/maintainability, efficiency, security\] and whether
correctness was measured; metrics per dimension with instrument type
\[tool-static, execution, LLM judge, human, similarity to reference\];
benchmarks; languages; models; baselines; direction of effect on the
target, on correctness and on each other dimension \[$`+`$, $`0`$,
$`-`$, mixed, not reported\] with the headline numbers as printed;
compute reported \[calls, tokens, cost, time, none\]; contamination
handled \[yes, partial, no\]; human evaluation \[none, rating,
preference\] with annotators and agreement; artifact URL;
reimplementability \[yes, partial, no\]; the ten QA items; notes;
extractor; confidence \[high, medium, low\].

## S4. Included studies and quality assessment

Table [S1](#as1_S4.T1 "Table S1 ‣ S4. Included studies and quality assessment ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
lists the included studies and
Table [S2](#as1_S4.T2 "Table S2 ‣ S4. Included studies and quality assessment ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
their quality-assessment scores; the main article summarizes them by
family. Both come from LLM-assisted extraction reviewed by the author.
Each of ten items is scored 0, 0.5 or 1; the score is reported per study
and weights confidence in the synthesis, but no study is excluded for
it. QA1: the technique is described well enough to reimplement. QA2: it
is compared with an appropriate baseline (no technique, or a strong
prior technique). QA3: the quality metric is established or validated (a
standard tool, or human evaluation with reported agreement). QA4:
correctness is reported alongside quality. QA5: more than one model is
evaluated, or a single model is justified. QA6: variance, repeated runs
or a statistical test is reported. QA7: compute or cost (calls, tokens)
is reported. QA8: code or data are available. QA9: contamination is
considered. QA10: threats to validity are discussed.

## S8. Statistical details of the controlled re-evaluation

Half-widths are 95% paired bootstrap half-widths (10,000 resamples of
tasks) of the per-task effect of a technique against T7 at the same
budget, pooled over techniques by their median. Seed dispersion is the
standard deviation of a cell’s metric across the three end-to-end runs,
as a fraction of the $`B=4`$ half-width; the median is over the
techniques of the cell. The false-discovery correction uses two-sided
paired bootstrap $`p`$-values and the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure at
$`q=0.05`$ over all metric–model–technique–budget cells.

## S9. Controls for the best-of-$`n`$ reference

##### Best-of-$`n`$ across budgets.

T7 is the budget-matched reference, but more samples do not always help
it. With more calls it keeps lowering maintainability issues per kLOC on
Op, G31 and G26 (from $`21.37`$, $`26.52`$ and $`28.89`$ at $`B=1`$ to
$`10.03`$, $`13.35`$ and $`12.78`$ at $`B=16`$) and stops improving on
oss after $`B=4`$. Its HumanEval+ pass@1 rises with $`B`$ on oss
($`81.27`$ to $`86.97`$) but falls on both Gemma models ($`96.06`$ to
$`90.88`$ on G31, $`89.16`$ to $`85.46`$ on G26), and its CWEval
func-sec@1 on G31 rises at $`B=4`$ and then falls below the single shot
($`49.48`$, $`55.42`$, $`51.80`$, $`46.68`$), whereas on Op it reaches
$`86.29`$ at $`B=16`$. Its EvalPerf DPS$`{}_{\text{norm}}`$ does not
improve with budget on the API-served models ($`78.06`$ to $`74.32`$ on
Op, $`79.41`$ to $`77.07`$ on oss) and falls after $`B=4`$ on G31
($`80.84`$ to $`73.71`$). The ranker sees only the public examples and
prefers fewer findings; a plausible reading, which these tables cannot
settle, is that with more candidates it more often selects a minimal
program that passes the public examples but not the hidden tests, the
false-positive limit that [Stroebl et al. (2024)](#as1_bib.bib495)
derive for resampling with imperfect verifiers such as unit tests. Wins
over T7 are therefore wins over a reference that is strong on the
analyzer’s measures and weaker on hidden-test correctness, and the
comparison with T0 remains necessary.

##### Shape of the budget curves.

The budget curves
(Table [S10](#as1_S7.T10 "Table S10 ‣ S7.4. Budget curves ‣ S7. Additional Tables ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
are not smooth: on CWEval, T7 on Op moves from $`74.85`$ at $`B=1`$ to
$`78.17`$, $`74.43`$ and $`86.29`$ at $`B=4`$, $`8`$ and $`16`$.
Table [S13](#as1_S9.T13 "Table S13 ‣ Shape of the budget curves. ‣ S9. Controls for the best-of-𝑛 reference ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
gives the three per-seed values of this cell and of three other uneven
ones. In every cell the three seeds lie within $`1.6`$ to $`9.6`$ points
of each other, a seed standard deviation of $`0.1`$ to $`0.8`$ of the
half-width (median $`0.46`$, close to the $`0.39`$ of
Table [S11](#as1_S8.T11 "Table S11 ‣ S8. Statistical details of the controlled re-evaluation ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
and every seed of T7 on Op at $`B=16`$ is above every seed at $`B=8`$,
so the steps are reproducible differences between budgets, not
run-to-run noise. The seed dispersion and the half-width measure
different things: the first is the variation of one cell’s mean when the
whole experiment is rerun on the same tasks; the second is the
uncertainty of a paired effect over the sample of tasks, which is wider
because CWEval has 119 tasks with a binary outcome each. A step that
recurs in every seed is therefore a property of the ranker on these 119
tasks, and it is significant, in the sense of holding beyond them, only
when it exceeds the half-width: the dip at $`B=8`$ ($`3.74`$ points)
does not, the gain at $`B=16`$ ($`11.86`$ points) does. A plausible
source of the steps is that each budget draws a fresh candidate pool and
the ranker, which sees no security test, switches between candidates
that differ on a few security tests; on 119 tasks, a switch on four
tasks moves func-sec@1 by $`3.4`$ points. We read only differences
beyond the half-width, and no claim rests on the shape of a single
curve.

Additional Tables ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))

##### Sampling temperature.

On the open models T7 samples at $`0.8`$, whereas the single-call
techniques generate at $`0.2`$, so part of T7’s advantage could come
from diversity rather than ranking. As a control we ran T7 at $`0.2`$
with the same ranker at $`B\in\{4,8,16\}`$ on oss, G31 and G26 (Opus has
no temperature control). Across the three budgets it is within the
half-width of T7 at $`0.8`$ in 26 of the 36 primary-metric cells (four
primary metrics, three models, three budgets); at $`B=4`$ it leaves
$`0.6`$ to $`2.2`$ more maintainability issues per kLOC and is $`0.3`$
to $`1.2`$ points lower on CWEval func-sec@1, and its HumanEval+ pass@1
is $`0.4`$ to $`1.7`$ points higher. Against this lower-temperature
reference, T1, T2, T4, T5 and T6 are better in 9 and worse in 48 of the
120 R/M and SEC cells at $`B=4`$ (five techniques, eight metrics, three
models), so the conclusions of ERQ1 do not depend on the sampling
temperature of the reference.

## S10. Single-call results on independent measures

At $`B=1`$ every technique spends the single shot’s budget and no ranker
is involved, so this view tests the prompts themselves.

cells (T2 lowers it by $`0.36`$ on oss); the Opus judge rates T1 higher
on Op and G31 and T2 higher on oss, by $`0.09`$ to $`0.14`$ points on

## S11. Solution length and absolute issue counts

Maintainability and security issues are reported per kLOC in the main
article, and length confounds every quality measure (§).
Table [S15](#as1_S11.T15 "Table S15 ‣ S11. Solution length and absolute issue counts ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
therefore gives, for each technique and model at $`B=4`$, the mean
solution length and the absolute number of issues per solution, next to
the densities of the main article. The ordering of the techniques is the
same on both scales. T7’s solutions are the shortest of the
inference-time techniques (2 to 13% shorter than T0’s), so its lower
density understates rather than inflates its advantage in absolute
counts; T1’s solutions are the longest (11 to 16% longer than T0’s at
$`B=4`$, 9 to 14% at $`B=1`$), and at $`B=1`$ they carry more issues per
solution as well as per kLOC.

## S12. Compute ledger

Billed model calls, tokens and API fees per experiment, from the
per-call logs of the harness; fine-tuning charges and GPU-hours from the
training job logs. The per-experiment rows sum to the totals of the main
article. Two units are distinguished. A _call-equivalent_ is the budget
unit $`B`$ of the design: one generated sample, or one critic, reviewer
or analyzer-feedback turn. A _billed request_ is one API request, the
unit of the Calls column. They differ for three reasons, which
Table [S16](#as1_S12.T16 "Table S16 ‣ S12. Compute ledger ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
applies per experiment: (i) on the open models served by Fireworks, the
$`B`$ samples of a best-of-$`B`$ draw are returned by one request
(parameter $`n`$), while the closed models return one sample per
request; (ii) the iterative techniques T3–T5 stop when their gate
passes, so they spend on average $`0.6\,B`$ call-equivalents; (iii) one
agent run on the repository-level benchmarks issues on average 37
requests, so agent experiments are counted in runs and in requests. At
$`B=1`$, T3, T4, T5 and T7 equal T0 by construction and are not rerun.

## S15. Fidelity check of the E12 implementations

Each implementation is run in its authors’ setting (model, benchmark and
metric as reported) and compared with one number its authors report.
Where the authors’ model is no longer served (retired GPT-3.5 and early
GPT-4 versions, Codex, Claude 3.x) or their number is a human rating or
an expert-filtered count, the check uses another automated number the
same paper reports for a model that can still be run, marked ^(†); if
the paper reports none, the technique is not checkable (n.c.) and is
left out of the count. Original = as printed in the source, verified by
a verbatim quotation (to be released with the replication package);
reproduced = our implementation in that setting. Each checkable
implementation is adjusted at most twice before its final run (median
one adjustment); adjustment stops as soon as the reproduced number falls
within 5% of the original, and a technique still outside the tolerance
after the second adjustment is reported as reproduced outside it rather
than adjusted further. Per-run logs of every run, including superseded
pre-adjustment runs, record the adjustment count and the stopping point;
they are retained and will be released with the replication package.
