## S17. Per-family detail: studies, highlighted techniques, effects, compute fairness and limitations

For each technique family: the study-by-study grouped comparison and the
caveats of each highlighted technique, which the family sections of the
main article summarize, followed by effects on correctness and on
non-targeted dimensions, compute fairness, and limitations (§ of the
main article compares the families).

### S17.1. Prompting

##### Explicit non-functional requirements.

Stated requirements help less than expected
(Table [S27](#as1_S18.T27 "Table S27 ‣ Prompting ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
On RACE, five simultaneous requirements drive almost all models near
zero on the joint correct-and-compliant metric, and models resist
requests contradicting their stylistic priors ([Zheng et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib604)). ISO/IEC 25010-grounded requirements lowered
unreadability density for all four requirements and reduced wording
sensitivity ([Pereira and Garcia, 2026](#as1_bib.bib413)). Adding
“secure” to a GPT-4 prompt cut weakness density by 42.85% (not
significant); the best zero-shot variant was CWE-specific for GPT-3 and
generic “comprehensive” for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 ([Tony et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib518)). Newer security prompts only shift the CWE mix
([Kharma et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib230)) or trade high- for
low-severity findings ([Urmi et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib519)). Energy
prompts saved nothing consistently across six models and three hardware
platforms ([Apsan et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib35)) and helped only some
models and languages ([Rekhi et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib447)); no single
efficiency prompt transfers.

##### Personas, exemplars and style specifications.

In CodePromptEval, a persona who “follows best coding practices for
maintainability” produced fewer Pylint smells and lower complexity at
slightly lower correctness, while few-shot and signature prompts raised
correctness most but added smells, over a third more when combined with
chain-of-thought and persona prompts ([Khojah et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib232)). In ECCO, both effects of few-shot examples are
model-dependent ([Waghjale et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib523)); retrieved
exemplars are in §. Personality-guided generation improves pass rates in
23 out of 28 model–dataset combinations but measures no non-functional
dimension ([Guo et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib164)).
Instruction-plus-example system prompts controlled verbosity most stably
over a two-turn revision; example-only prompts lost effect once code was
extended ([Bohr, 2025](#as1_bib.bib59)). Signatures, constraints and
style descriptions are the prompt elements most tied to readability,
though prompt design’s overall role is bounded ([Ye et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib574)).

##### Reasoning scaffolds.

SCoT and self-planning
(Table [S28](#as1_S18.T28 "Table S28 ‣ Prompting ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
target correctness (relative pass@1 gains up to 13.79% and 25.4%) but
also report human-judged quality gains ([Li et al.,
2025b](#as1_bib.bib248); [Jiang et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib223)).
LLM4EFFI carries plan-first to efficiency ([Ye et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib575)). “Think step by step” was dominated by simpler
zero-shot security prompts ([Tony et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib518)), and
WA-0CoT increased code size and maintainability warnings for C ([Kharma
et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib230)). Step-by-step prompting could yield
more efficient code on complex problems ([Niu et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib343)).

##### Reasoning effort and prompt sensitivity.

Reasoning effort is the main knob frontier APIs expose, yet on A.S.E
slow-thinking configurations tended to trail fast-thinking ones ([Lian
et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib255)), and no study we found varies effort
within one model while measuring R/M or EFF. Sensitivity is better
documented: one changed character can flip code from secure to
vulnerable ([Sternfeld et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib494)); benign but less
normative prompts make insecure code likelier, mitigated by
chain-of-thought and self-correction prompts ([Wang et al.,
2026b](#as1_bib.bib527)); two security prompts built on similar
principles differed markedly ([Bruni et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib61)); and
under-specification costs almost no correctness on the richer
LiveCodeBench ([Akli et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib15)).

##### Highlighted techniques.

In
Table [S28](#as1_S18.T28 "Table S28 ‣ Prompting ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
(selection rule in §), landmarks mostly structure reasoning before
coding; recent leaders condition the prompt on a task or model diagnosis
from another LLM or analyzer (ECO, BRACE, CSDD) optimize the prompt
itself (MPCO, SecureForge), or restate the problem before coding
(StoryCoder retells it as a narrative). SecureForge mines benign prompts
whose code a static analyzer flags, broadens them by MCMC rephrasing,
and evolves a system prompt against them with GEPA, reporting weakness
rates up to 48% lower on test-passing outputs with test pass rates
essentially unchanged ([Liu et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib262)).

Caveats. Landmarks’ quality evidence is human-rated and partly
unquantified; Code2API’s ratings judge method names produced from
human-written snippets. Several baselines are weak. ECO is compared with
instruction-only prompting at best of five samples and lowers 3B-model
accuracy from 55.22 to 37.80. StoryCoder’s quality evidence is
structural: its correct CodeForces solutions contain more functions
(1.820 to 2.338 with Gemini-2.5-Flash), which its authors read as
modularity without measuring maintainability. MPCO reports an aggregate
rank, yet on one of its five projects few-shot prompting’s mean
improvement (19.29) exceeds MPCO’s (19.06). BRACE’s Safe Code Rate is a
trained judge classifier’s verdict; its average HumanEval pass@1 barely
changes but drops on Gemma3-4B. CSDD rests on one application built
twice by one developer with the same assistant. MPCO and CSDD omit
correctness, and no row reports an effect on a non-targeted dimension.

##### Effects on correctness and on non-targeted dimensions.

Where correctness is measured, signs conflict. RCI’s security gain cost
about ten pass@1 points (ten samples, one model) ([Bruni et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib61)); the PIE retrieval prompts show the same tension
(§); security-prompting studies more often report a drop or no change
than a gain, and many skip correctness. Effects on non-targeted
dimensions can be adverse (WA-0CoT’s warnings); SCoT’s human study rates
correctness, smells and maintainability (0–2 scale, 200 programs per
method) ([Li et al., 2025b](#as1_bib.bib248)).

##### Compute fairness.

Variants are rarely token-matched. RCI adds at least two calls per
sample, yet [Tony et al. (2025)](#as1_bib.bib518) and [Bruni et al.
(2025)](#as1_bib.bib61) compare it with single-call prompts rather than
a resampled security prompt or an analyzer loop (§). No highlighted
technique adding calls (meta-prompter, risk selector, primer synthesis,
synthetic tests) has a budget-matched baseline either, and A.S.E
compares across model variants.

##### Limitations.

\(i\) _Old or closed models_: the main security studies use GPT-3 to
GPT-4o; GPT-3.5-turbo was hurt by prompts that helped GPT-4o ([Bruni
et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib61)). (ii) _Static analyzers as sole oracle_:
these overestimate security by 7 to 21 times, with 37 to 60% of “secure”
outputs non-functional ([Tessa et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib513)). (iii)
_Small samples_: nine problems in [Apsan et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib35),
no inferential tests in [Bruni et al. (2025)](#as1_bib.bib61). (iv)
_Inconsistency_: SCoT gives both 15.90% and 16.17% as its
maintainability gain ([Li et al., 2025b](#as1_bib.bib248)). (v)
_Uncontrolled baselines_: the ISO study’s baseline came from an earlier
batch ([Pereira and Garcia, 2026](#as1_bib.bib413)). (vi) _Prompt
fragility_: one wording per condition, the norm, confounds technique and
phrasing.

### S17.2. Tool-feedback loops

##### Security-scanner loops.

FDSP ([Alrashedy et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib20)) returns the Bandit
report, requests several candidate fixes, and iterates each until Bandit
is clean; LLM-verbalized reports add only 1% to 2%. With CodeQL, raw
diagnostics help every model, while a stronger model’s explanations help
mainly strong instruction followers and not consistently more than raw
feedback on real-world tasks ([Yan et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib567)).
Codexity ([Kim et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib234)) returns Infer and
CppCheck findings for C; [Dolcetti et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib118)
return one Infer finding at a time, including known false positives,
which models also “fixed”. SecureFixAgent ([Gajjar et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib133)) re-runs Bandit after each patch from small
LoRA-tuned models; FRANC ([Siddiq et al., 2024a](#as1_bib.bib477)) turns
Bandit messages into repair prompts; PromSec ([Nazzal et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib339)) rewrites the prompt, not the code; [Sriram
et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib488) append GCC, CodeQL and KLEE diagnostics
plus retrieved repairs. Filtering returns nothing: a fine-tuned
vulnerability detector discards flagged completions ([Chan et al.,
2023](#as1_bib.bib66)). LLMSecGuard ([Kavian et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib229)) proposes a Semgrep/Weggli loop without results.
AutoSafeCoder’s ([Nunez et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib345)) “Static Analyzer
Agent” is an LLM (Bandit only evaluates), so its signal source is
other-LLM.

##### Maintainability and multi-dimension loops.

[Blyth et al. (2025)](#as1_bib.bib58) is the closest quality-loop
template: Bandit and Pylint issues are tagged inline, security issues
ordered by severity weights, and a candidate kept only if its fitness
($`-\infty`$ on any test failure) does not worsen. CORE ([Wadhwa et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib522)) filters: a proposer samples revisions from the
CodeQL or SonarQube check description and vendor fix advice, the
analyzer discards failures, and a ranker LLM scores the rest against a
reviewer rubric. CodeCureAgent ([Joos et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib227))
repairs SonarQube warnings agentically; its change approver requires a
build, the warning removed without new ones, and passing tests. [Abtahi
and Azim (2025)](#as1_bib.bib1) send SonarQube issue tables to GPT-3.5
Turbo, then leftovers to GPT-4o; [Islam et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib215)
feed 14 metrics from Pylint, Radon, JSCPD, Bandit and others to several
LLMs; LLMLOOP ([Ravi et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib444)) chains compiler,
test, PMD and mutation loops for Java but reports no PMD violation
counts.

##### Compiler and linter guardrails.

Compiler loops target COR: ProCoder ([Bi et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib57))
turns project-context compiler errors into retrieval queries until the
code compiles. SWE-agent ([Yang et al., 2024b](#as1_bib.bib570)) reverts
edits that a restricted flake8 check flags for syntax or undefined
names, raising resolved SWE-bench Lite issues from 15.0 to 18.0.

##### Profiler and performance loops.

EffiLearner ([Huang et al., 2024a](#as1_bib.bib181)) returns per-line
line_profiler and memory_profiler output; format matters, as aggregate
time and memory alone _increased_ CodeLlama-70B’s execution time by
51.9% while the profile cut it by 9.6%. SysLLMatic ([Peng et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib408)) adds async-profiler or perf flame-graph
hotspots and an optimization-pattern catalog; Optimo ([Peng et al.,
2026b](#as1_bib.bib412)) finds bottlenecks by differential profiling;
PerfAgent ([Deng et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib116)) gives a
repository-level agent a py-spy hotspot summary; PerfCodeGen ([Peng
et al., 2025b](#as1_bib.bib410)) returns only the slowest unit test.

##### Evolutionary search.

AlphaEvolve “orchestrates an autonomous pipeline of LLMs, whose task is
to improve an algorithm by making direct changes to the code” and keeps
the variants one or more evaluators score best; at Google it yielded a
more efficient data-centre scheduling heuristic and multiplied two
$`4\times 4`$ complex-valued matrices with 48 scalar multiplications
([Novikov et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib344)). Open successors aim the
search at program efficiency: CodeEvolve selects targets from Java
Flight Recorder profiles ([Borra et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib60)) and
ContextEvolve compresses the search context into agents’ summaries ([Su
et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib496)); SBLLM applies genetic-operator-style
prompts to a population of optimized programs ([Gao et al.,
2025b](#as1_bib.bib136)). All inherit the evaluator’s weaknesses: a
timing evaluator rewards noise (§), and none of the studies we found
scores evolved code for R/M.

##### Highlighted techniques.

Table [S31](#as1_S18.T31 "Table S31 ‣ Tool-feedback loops ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
lists the highlighted techniques (selection rule in §). [Blyth et al.
(2025)](#as1_bib.bib58) tag a few Bandit and Pylint issues, chosen by
severity weight, inline in GPT-4o’s code each round and keep a revision
only if its test-gated fitness does not fall; over ten rounds
Bandit-flagged snippets fell from 45.05% to 13.41% while the pass rate
rose from 36.7% to 46.59%.

##### Caveats.

Several headline gains rest on weak comparisons. PerfCodeGen is compared
only with the base model, not other refinement methods. CodeEvolve’s
baseline is a single LLM call evaluated with a different model (Claude 4
Sonnet), and one function at 90.34$`\times`$ drives its average speedup.
Optimo uses only GPT-4o and consumes more tokens and API calls than its
baselines. Security results are tool-scored and small: Dolcetti et al.’s
best model fixed 39 out of 44 findings. FRANC reports no pre-repair
value; PromSec shows CWE counts only in plots, and the unit-test
re-evaluation of [Dai et al. (2026a)](#as1_bib.bib97) contradicts its
COR gain. Filtering also shrinks output: for text-davinci-003, scenarios
with a valid completion fell from 27 to 24. Correctness is unreported
for the filtering and FRANC results and unchecked after the Infer
repairs.

##### Effects on correctness and non-targeted dimensions.

Correctness held or rose mainly behind a test or fitness gate. Blyth et
al. raise pass@1, LLMLOOP’s PMD stage leaves it essentially unchanged
(79.51% to 79.57%), and the profiler loops keep only test-passing
candidates, though EffiLearner, checking only open tests, still loses a
little pass@1 for most models. Ungated, correctness is mostly unmeasured
(FDSP, Codexity, SecureFixAgent, [Yan et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib567),
[Islam et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib215)) or falls: AutoSafeCoder’s
abstract claims “no compromise in functionality” while its table shows
pass@1 dropping, and PromSec, validated mainly by code-graph similarity,
lost Pass@1 under the unit tests of [Dai et al.
(2026a)](#as1_bib.bib97). Exceptions run both ways: a gate is a
safeguard, not a guarantee.

Goodhart’s law also recurs. Reviewers rejected 55.11% of CORE’s
CodeQL-passing revisions, and without its change approver CodeCureAgent
would have admitted 249 incorrect fixes. [Islam et al.
(2026)](#as1_bib.bib215) discarded later iterations in which local
models removed the code, since empty output scored a perfect
Maintainability Index and no code smells; [Dai et al.
(2026a)](#as1_bib.bib97) find secure-generation techniques often delete
vulnerable lines or emit “garbage code”; PerfAgent’s authors saw agents
cache results inside benchmark timing loops. Ruff appears only as an RL
reward (§), where alone it pushed models toward shorter completions
without improving correctness ([Skopin and Kotelnikov,
2026](#as1_bib.bib482)). Scanner gates miss structural regressions:
Semgrep gating raised latent security degradation from 12.5% to 20.8%
because removed defensive logic triggers no rule ([Chen et al.,
2026e](#as1_bib.bib76)), and runtime exploits were confirmed for 14.53%
of Bandit-Semgrep-clean samples ([Pourleyli et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib420)). Yet most security loops are scored by their
driving tool; when FDSP adds CodeQL, GPT-4’s gain shrinks from 32.7
points (Bandit) to 10.2 (CodeQL).

Loops also introduce issues: 5% of Blyth et al.’s iterations introduced
new security vulnerabilities, convention issues most often;
Checkov-driven Terraform repair regressed security in 3.3% (strict) to
13.8% (inclusive) of scenarios ([Agyekum and Santos,
2026](#as1_bib.bib5)). Among efficiency loops, only SysLLMatic reports a
non-targeted dimension (cyclomatic complexity -0.95% to +21.05%). Few
security-only loops report readability or efficiency, and no
maintainability-only loop we found reports runtime.

##### Compute fairness.

Every loop spends extra calls, but few face an equal-budget baseline.
Blyth et al. allow up to 10 repair calls plus one to infer function
names, against one generation. FDSP’s ablation credits most of its gain
to sampling $`J`$ candidate fixes (10.0% vulnerable with a single
solution, 7.4% with full FDSP), confounding its comparison with
single-response Bandit feedback. CORE draws 10 proposals plus ranker
calls; SecureFixAgent averages 3 to 4 iterations and AutoSafeCoder adds
150 fuzzing iterations, both against a single pass. Codexity needs 1.8
repair iterations and 98.6 seconds per generation with a found
vulnerability; CodeCureAgent reports 139K tokens and about 2.9 cents per
warning; PerfAgent, in a rare budget-aware comparison, beats an oracle
best-of-five baseline at lower cost. Counting repair cost, self-repair
gains are often modest ([Olausson et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib368)).

##### Limitations.

Several loops use one model (Blyth et al., AutoSafeCoder, LLMLOOP,
CodeCureAgent); the multi-model static-analysis loops (FDSP, [Yan et al.
(2026)](#as1_bib.bib567), [Islam et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib215)) lack a
test gate. Benchmarks are small or narrow (SecurityEval has 121 prompts;
Abtahi and Azim study one project), and some preprints report
carelessly: [Sriram et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib488) misattribute
Self-Debug. CORE’s human review used one label per revision.

### S17.3. Self-refinement

##### Intrinsic self-feedback.

Self-Refine alternates feedback and refine prompts on one model ([Madaan
et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib276)); it is the only canonical method
evaluated on readability, but that task rewrites existing CodeNet
programs, scores the fraction of variables GPT-4 judges appropriately
named, and checks no behavior. Outside code, LLMs struggle to correct
their reasoning without external feedback, sometimes getting worse
([Huang et al., 2024c](#as1_bib.bib185)); a TACL survey finds
self-correction works mainly with reliable external feedback and many
positive reports rest on unfair evaluations ([Kamoi et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib228)). On EffiBench, an unsupervised Self-Refine
prompt _increased_ CodeLlama-70B execution time ([Huang et al.,
2024a](#as1_bib.bib181)).

##### Execution-grounded self-repair.

Self-Debug adds unit-test results and model-written code explanations
([Chen et al., 2024b](#as1_bib.bib74)); Self-Edit passes the
example-test result as a comment to a fault-aware editor ([Zhang et al.,
2023a](#as1_bib.bib595)); Reflexion keeps verbal reflections in an
episodic memory ([Shinn et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib473)); LDB exposes
intermediate variable values per basic block ([Zhong et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib608)); CRITIC critiques with tools, but its
program-synthesis tasks are mathematical ([Gou et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib159)). All five are correctness-only, and the oracle
is their weak point: Reflexion’s self-generated MBPP Python tests have a
16.3% false-positive rate ([Shinn et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib473)), and
self-generated tests bias self-debugging toward misleading feedback
([Chen et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib73)).

##### Self-refinement toward a quality target.

Quality-targeted variants replace the test oracle with a non-functional
signal
(Table [S32](#as1_S18.T32 "Table S32 ‣ Self-refinement ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
EffiLearner, on the border with §, feeds execution-time and memory
profiles back to the model ([Huang et al., 2024a](#as1_bib.bib181)).
Controlled Self-Evolution adds diversified initial plans,
feedback-guided mutation and a cross-task memory on EffiBench-X ([Hu
et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib177)). A three-round Reflexion protocol
returning the CWEs flagged by the Insecure Code Detector (ICD) raised
the secure rate of five open code models ([Datta et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib100)).

##### Open-ended “improve this code” loops.

Untargeted iteration can degrade security. Over 40 rounds of GPT-4o
“improvements” to 10 secure C and Java programs, critical
vulnerabilities rose by 37.6% after five iterations, and code complexity
correlated with vulnerability counts ([Shukla et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib474)). In a 2026 study of three models, 43.7 % of
GPT-4o chains had more vulnerabilities than the baseline after ten
rounds, and a static-analysis gate raised the latent degradation rate
from 12.5% to 20.8 %, as rules miss removed defensive logic ([Chen
et al., 2026e](#as1_bib.bib76)).

##### Reasoning models as built-in refinement.

Large reasoning models critique and revise inside a single call. Their
traces contain flaw-detection and style-check actions, analyzed only
against correctness ([Halim et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib167)). The cost is
“overthinking”, verbose and redundant reasoning ([Sui et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib497)), and a 2026 audit finds more capable models
generate more bloated and coupled code ([Zhu et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib611)). No study we found compares explicit refinement
with internal revision at matched tokens on any quality dimension.

##### Highlighted techniques.

Table [S33](#as1_S18.T33 "Table S33 ‣ Self-refinement ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
lists all 6 eligible general-purpose techniques (selection rule in §).
Besides Self-Refine, they ground revision in structure (CodeChain,
GRASP), in memory of past repairs (RefleXGen and Safety Sidecar, which
share a first author) or in CodeQL findings (SecCode, partly a tool
loop, §).

Caveats. Loop and instrument overlap: SecCode feeds CodeQL findings into
the loop, and Safety Sidecar uses CodeQL in both pipeline and
evaluation, computing rates only over compilable samples. RefleXGen and
Safety Sidecar report a digit-for-digit identical base row under
different model names (CodeQwen, qwen3-coder-plus). Correctness can
suffer: RefleXGen lowers CodeQwen’s pass rate from 86.7 to 69.8, and
GRASP reports an occasional trade-off at $`k=1`$ and compares with
baselines only in Python. CodeChain’s headline result is correctness
(relative pass@1 gain of 35% on APPS); its modularity gain is a GPT-4
Likert judgement shown only as a figure. No row reports an effect on a
non-targeted dimension.

##### Effects on correctness and non-targeted dimensions.

EffiLearner optimizes only code that already passes the public tests;
its pass@1 on hidden tests fell by 0% to 0.5%. The security loops in
Table [S32](#as1_S18.T32 "Table S32 ‣ Self-refinement ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
run a detector but no functional tests. Few studies measure a
non-targeted dimension, one being the complexity analysis of [Shukla
et al. (2025)](#as1_bib.bib474), so a loop may degrade one dimension
while optimizing another, unnoticed.

##### Compute fairness.

[Olausson et al. (2024)](#as1_bib.bib368) set the standard: against
i.i.d. sampling at an equal number of programs, self-repair gains on
HumanEval and APPS are often modest and sometimes absent, and feedback
quality is the bottleneck. Self-Debug reports matching baselines that
draw over ten times as many candidates ([Chen et al.,
2024b](#as1_bib.bib74)); a 2026 study finds self-repair more
token-efficient than resampling, but repair decodes greedily and
resampling at temperature 0.8 ([Arimbur, 2026](#as1_bib.bib40)). No
quality-targeted study we found, the highlighted ones included, is
budget-matched; they compare the final iteration with the initial
output, and Self-Refine’s no-refinement baseline makes fewer calls.

##### Limitations.

Among canonical methods, the R/M evidence is one LLM-judged naming
metric. In the Reflexion-plus-ICD study the detector that writes the
feedback also scores the result, so part of the gain may reflect fitting
its rules rather than more secure code. The degradation studies use few
models and seed programs. Most correctness-only methods were evaluated
on near-saturated HumanEval and MBPP.

### S17.4. Multi-agent pipelines

##### Process-mimicking role pipelines.

ChatDev chains design, coding and testing through role-agent chats
([Qian et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib421)), MetaGPT encodes standardized
operating procedures in role prompts ([Hong et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib174)), and Self-collaboration uses analyst, coder and
tester roles ([Dong et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib119)). Quality is
prompted, not evaluated: Self-collaboration’s tester reports on
“functionality, readability, and maintainability” but results are
pass@1, and ChatDev’s “Quality” multiplies completeness, executability
and requirement consistency. Among highlighted role pipelines
(Table [S34](#as1_S18.T34 "Table S34 ‣ Multi-agent pipelines ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")),
removing FlowGen’s testing raised error-smell density by 702.2% on
average ([Lin et al., 2025b](#as1_bib.bib261)), and C3’s role
competition cut “collaboration degeneration” from 32.4% to 12.8% ([Gu
et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib161)).

##### Coder–tester and coder–reviewer loops.

AgentCoder (programmer, test designer, test executor) ([Huang et al.,
2023](#as1_bib.bib180)) and MapCoder (similar-problem retrieval,
planning, coding, debugging on sample I/O) ([Islam et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib214)) are correctness-only. The simplest
quality-oriented design, coder plus reviewer, is re-evaluated in §.
CudaForge, typical of the efficiency group, grounds its Judge reviewer
in Nsight Compute hardware metrics; with OpenAI-o3 it reaches a
1.68$`\times`$ average speedup over PyTorch on KernelBench at 97.6%
correctness ([Zhang et al., 2025c](#as1_bib.bib601)).

##### Security-specialist agents.

AutoSafeCoder adds a “Static Analyzer Agent” and a fuzzing agent to a
coder ([Nunez et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib345)), but the analyzer is an
LLM prompted to find CWEs, with Bandit only scoring the result, so
static-analysis feedback goes untested. MACGen passes structured
artifacts, not a shared dialogue, between planner, security advisor,
coder and reviewer ([Yu et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib576)).
Multi-LLMSecCodeEval (preprint) compares ten single-model, ensemble,
collaborative and hybrid pipelines ([Sabir et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib450)): on SecLLMEval, ensembles with static analysis
beat a single LLM at secure generation by up to 47.3%, LLM-only
collaboration by 8.9% to 22.3%. Likewise, feeding CodeQL and Bandit
findings to the generator in [Surikov (2026)](#as1_bib.bib499) deepened
the pooled drop in analyzer findings from 42% to 57%.

##### Repository-level agents.

SWE-agent’s agent-computer interface ([Yang et al.,
2024b](#as1_bib.bib570)), the OpenHands platform ([Wang et al.,
2025b](#as1_bib.bib532)) and Agentless’s fixed localization, repair and
validation phases (32.00% on SWE-bench Lite at \$0.70 per issue ([Xia
et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib554))) are all scored by resolved issues, yet
SWE-agent’s case study notes a test-passing patch that ignores an
existing utility function, “which could lead to less maintainable or
portable code”.

##### Quality of agent-produced code.

Controlled studies point to complexity growth: six
analyst–coder–tester–debugger configurations (GPT-4o family, HumanEval)
form two complexity clusters 50-130% apart, the heavier with no pass@1
advantage ([Ashrafi, 2026](#as1_bib.bib42)). On SlopCodeBench, where 15
agents repeatedly extend their own solutions, structural erosion rose in
77% of trajectories and agent code was 2.3x more verbose than code in
473 open-source Python repositories; quality guidance lowered initial
verbosity and erosion, not the degradation rate ([Orlanski et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib401)). A technical-debt audit finds code volume tracks
structural degradation ([Zhu et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib611)). Field
evidence comes mostly from AIDev’s 932,791 agent-authored pull requests
(PRs) ([Li et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib247)). In another sample, 83.8% of
567 Claude Code PRs were merged ([Watanabe et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib536)); rejected agent PRs are larger and often fail CI
([Ehsani et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib125)); in merged bug-fix PRs
SonarQube finds mostly code smells, with per-agent differences largely
vanishing after churn normalization ([Cynthia et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib96)). On security, an LLM judge flags at least one
security smell in 38.9% of PRs from five agents ([Sakib et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib452)), but a matched comparison finds agent code
_less_ likely than human code to have one (odds ratio 0.63), with revert
rates varying by vendor ([Kraishan, 2026](#as1_bib.bib235)).

##### Highlighted techniques.

Table [S34](#as1_S18.T34 "Table S34 ‣ Multi-agent pipelines ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
lists the highlighted techniques (selection rule in §). They differ less
in agent count than in what agents exchange: development roles, security
critiques or, for EFF, several agents’ candidates and, recently, shared
search memory such as LessonL’s banked lessons. ACCLAIM lets a guiding
agent interleave LLVM compiler passes with LLM rewriting agents at
source, IR and assembly level under one call budget, reaching a
1.25$`\times`$ geometric-mean speedup over clang -O3 on C programs
against 1.18$`\times`$ for a source-only agent at equal budget ([Mikek
et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib301)). MaintainCoder has
requirements-analysis, design-pattern and framework agents agree on an
architectural blueprint before a coding agent and an execution-driven
optimizer write the code, raising post-modification Pass@5 on APPS-Dyn,
a test of how well code absorbs new requirements, from 59.5 for plain
DeepSeek-V3 to 62.5 ([Wang et al., 2025c](#as1_bib.bib534)).

Caveats. Headline numbers often overstate typical gains. ContextEvolve’s
33.3% comes from one task; its average margin over the top baseline is
6.5%, using over three times OpenEvolve’s API calls (but fewer tokens).
On LessonL’s benchmark, OpenAI o3 alone reaches 2.21, above LessonL, and
incorrect or slower code counts as speedup 1. MARCO matched or beat its
baseline on 44 of 75 problems. INDICT’s strongest baseline, Reflexion+,
reaches 86.9, and its safety score comes from a rule-based detector on a
20% validation split. SecAwareCoder is evaluated on its own benchmark,
CodeSecEval. [Surikov (2026)](#as1_bib.bib499) use 26 prompts, score
their second configuration with the analyzers supplying its feedback,
and their remediation introduced new vulnerabilities in 15-22% of cases.
C3’s maintainability gain is a human rating on which it ties two other
variants; four of the ten techniques report no correctness result.

##### Effects on correctness and non-targeted dimensions.

AutoSafeCoder shows the trade-off this survey seeks: with GPT-4o it cut
Bandit-flagged vulnerable SecurityEval samples from 59/121 (49%) to
44/121 (36%) but lowered HumanEval pass@1 from 0.9085 to 0.8780, though
its abstract reports “no compromise in functionality” ([Nunez et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib345)). Multi-LLMSecCodeEval does not evaluate
correctness ([Sabir et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib450)); MACGen uses the
stronger joint functional-and-secure metric, raising BaxBench F&S@1 from
21.17% (direct prompting, GPT-4o) to 31.12% ([Yu et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib576)). Few security or efficiency pipelines also
report R/M, and in the field merge success does not reflect post-merge
quality ([Cynthia et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib96)).

##### Compute fairness.

Few pipelines are compared with a single agent at equal cost. MapCoder
averages 16.7 API calls and 21.25 thousand tokens per problem against 1
call and 0.64 thousand for direct prompting, a limitation it
acknowledges ([Islam et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib214)). AgentCoder’s 56.9K
HumanEval tokens (vs. 138.2K for MetaGPT) are compared only with
multi-agent frameworks, and its abstract pairs MetaGPT’s token count
with another baseline’s pass@1 ([Huang et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib180)).
Neither MACGen’s 16% of INDICT’s tokens ([Yu et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib576)) nor CudaForge’s roughly \$0.3 per kernel
(compared with another agentic system) ([Zhang et al.,
2025c](#as1_bib.bib601)) is matched to a single agent. In ChatDev with a
reasoning model, code review, where quality checks would sit, took 59.4%
of tokens ([Salim et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib453)). The multi-agent
benefit shrinks as base models improve ([Gao et al.,
2025a](#as1_bib.bib135)), and a failure taxonomy of 1600+ traces notes
often minimal multi-agent gains on popular benchmarks ([Cemri et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib63)).

##### Limitations.

The security pipelines use one or two benchmarks, often one model, and
AutoSafeCoder is a preprint. Most field studies share one AIDev
snapshot, use different instruments (SonarQube, LLM judges, rule-based
smell detectors) and cannot fully separate agent output from human
edits; one finds humans introduced most leaked secrets in agent-assisted
PRs ([Sakib et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib452)).

### S17.5. Retrieval

##### Security knowledge.

Designs differ in the retrieved unit
(Tables [S35](#as1_S18.T35 "Table S35 ‣ Retrieval ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
and [S36](#as1_S18.T36 "Table S36 ‣ Retrieval ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
RESCUE finds SecCoder’s raw demonstrations ([Zhang et al.,
2024a](#as1_bib.bib593)) do not significantly improve SecurePass@1,
suggesting underused security knowledge, and instead hierarchically
retrieves distilled guidelines and sliced examples ([Shi and Zhang,
2026](#as1_bib.bib471)). SEEK scopes CWE-graph retrieval with planner
and selector agents ([Gadey et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib132)). CodeGuarder
(20.12% relative gain in security rate) and MA-CoT (security principles
plus a language-specific checklist) retrieve before generation ([Lin
et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib258); [Kharma et al.,
2026b](#as1_bib.bib231)); AutoPatch retrieves after it ([Seo et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib466)), SOSecure after a first draft, a post-generation
loop ([Mukherjee and Hellendoorn, 2026](#as1_bib.bib337)).

##### Efficiency exemplars.

Stand-alone EFF retrieval is rarer and mostly optimizes existing
programs; hybrids with profiling or search loops are more common (§).
PIE retrieves slow–fast pairs as few-shot examples (1.34$`\times`$
speedup at Best@1) ([Shypula et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib475)); RAPGen
retrieves an instruction mined from past fixes ([Garg et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib137)). RAS builds on PIE; SemOpt and PEACE use RAPGen
as a baseline ([Anupam et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib34); [Zhao et al.,
2026b](#as1_bib.bib603); [Ren et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib449)). An
unrelated AutoPatch adds control-flow-graph analysis to historical
examples ([Acharya et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib2)). A few retrieve similar
solved problems for generation from a specification.

##### Reuse versus reimplementation.

Without repository retrieval, GPT-3.5 in A3-CodGen reuses no local
functions and writes redundant new ones ([Liao et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib257)). Conversely, in CodeRAG-Bench models copy
context functions, sometimes overwriting the queried one, and
over-complicate programs ([Wang et al., 2025d](#as1_bib.bib535)).
Agent-authored pull requests miss reuse opportunities and are more
redundant than human ones ([Huang et al., 2026c](#as1_bib.bib184)).
Otherwise, R/M of RAG output is rarely measured (except by KPC and
LAIL), and few methods retrieve style guides or project conventions.

##### Risks of retrieved content.

One poisoned knowledge-base example can compromise up to 48% of
generated code ([Lin et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib259)), and a backdoored
retriever makes GPT-4o generate vulnerable code in over 40% of targeted
scenarios ([Li et al., 2025e](#as1_bib.bib251)). Staleness is the
non-adversarial analogue: obsolete repository snapshots induced stale
helper references in 15/17 Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct samples ([Weng
et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib539)). Few methods besides CodeGuarder are
evaluated under poisoning ([Lin et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib258)).

##### Highlighted techniques.

Table [S36](#as1_S18.T36 "Table S36 ‣ Retrieval ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
lists the highlighted techniques (selection rule in §).

Caveats. RAPGen and SemOpt score agreement with developer fixes (expert
and author judgment), not measured speed. PEACE’s opt rate is relative
to GPT-4o prompting, not the original code. RAS normalizes LLM calls
across baselines. PIE’s authors note that speedup “may, however, come
with some cost of correctness”. KPC’s rate comes from the authors’
manual review. LAIL is evaluated mainly by Pass@1, with quality a
secondary human rating. AutoPatch uses its authors’ dataset, and its
abstract gives 95.0 percent accuracy versus 94.12% in its results table.
MA-CoT only compiles or syntax-checks outputs, draws one sample per
configuration on its own dataset and gains over a plain prompt; its
authors report that generic CoT and zero-shot security prompts may
themselves increase vulnerabilities.

##### Effects on correctness, compute fairness and limitations.

Security RAG methods that measure correctness mostly report it preserved
or improved, unlike security prompting (§), though a minority of
extracted studies report a drop; efficiency retrieval, as in PIE, may
cost correctness. Budgets are rarely matched: RESCUE’s distillation and
SEEK’s agents face single-call baselines, and only RESCUE (input tokens)
and SEEK (latency) report cost in
Table [S35](#as1_S18.T35 "Table S35 ‣ Retrieval ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code").
Limitations: SecCoder uses models up to 6.7B parameters; SEEK is a
recent preprint; security metrics rest on CodeQL and benchmark-specific
checks, which can overestimate security (§); A3-CodGen counts calls to
existing functions, not whether code is better.

### S17.6. Decoding

##### Constrained decoding and steering.

Synchromesh enforces syntax, scope and typing on partial programs in
three domain-specific languages ([Poesia et al.,
2022](#as1_bib.bib416)); type-constrained decoding extends this
well-formedness target to TypeScript, more than halving compilation
errors ([Mündler et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib338)). For R/M, PG-TD swaps
its test reward for a length or comment reward ([Zhang et al.,
2023b](#as1_bib.bib599)) and RPG penalizes structural repetition ([Dong
et al., 2025b](#as1_bib.bib121)). For SEC, constrained beam sampling
writes constraints for each of the 91 CodeGuard+ prompts from the CWE it
might trigger ([Fu et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib129)); co-decoding replaces
the rules with a small security model ([Hu et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib176)); and 2026 steering methods (SCS-Code, DuoSteer)
use the target’s own activations. MRepE, the only R/M steering method we
found, combines comment-density, naming and cyclomatic-complexity
vectors while bounding correctness loss ([Gao et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib134), preprint). [Sandoval et al.
(2026)](#as1_bib.bib454) trace insecure generation to one late layer;
per-vulnerability steering vectors “reduce insecure generation by up to
74%” across five models.

##### Sample-and-select.

MBR-exec keeps the candidate whose execution results agree most with the
others ([Shi et al., 2022](#as1_bib.bib470)); CodeT adds model-generated
tests ([Chen et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib67)); Coder-Reviewer rescores by
instruction likelihood because likelihood-only reranking is “prone to
preferring degenerate solutions” ([Zhang et al.,
2023c](#as1_bib.bib600)); LEVER learns a verifier over program and
execution result ([Ni et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib340)). Without execution
feedback, a code process reward model is no better than a random reward
in best-of-$`N`$ ([Li et al., 2025d](#as1_bib.bib250)); FunPRM
meta-learns step-reward corrections from unit-test outcomes ([Zhang
et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib598)). Quality-aware selection needs a quality
preference model: CodeFavor learns pairwise preferences from commits and
critiques, improving preference accuracy for correctness, efficiency and
security “by up to 28.8%” ([Liu et al., 2024a](#as1_bib.bib264));
Priority Sampling, a deterministic confidence-ordered search over unique
samples, raises a compiler model’s code-size gain over -Oz “from 2.87%
to 5%” ([Grubisic et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib160)). Test-time scaling
adds sequential revision to execution-grounded selection ([Li et al.,
2025a](#as1_bib.bib245)); CodeMonkeys selects among repository edits
with model-generated tests ([Ehrlich et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib124)).
_The quality-verifier gap is now partly closed:_ SecCodePRM (ICML 2026),
a step-level security reward model trained on analyzer labels, outranks
probability ranking for best-of-$`N`$ on CWEval ([Yu et al.,
2026b](#as1_bib.bib578)). For EFF, surprisal-guided selection is a
preprint ([Barnes, 2026](#as1_bib.bib52), preprint) and PIE’s Best@$`k`$
(fastest program passing all tests in a simulator) an oracle bound
([Shypula et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib475)). We found no peer-reviewed R/M
or EFF selector, and none reranking by static maintainability scores or
profiled instruction counts.

##### Highlighted techniques.

Table [S38](#as1_S18.T38 "Table S38 ‣ Decoding ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
lists the highlighted techniques (selection rule in §). MoC trains
per-CWE linear probes on a code model’s hidden states and, only when a
probe flags a vulnerable state, adds a decaying mix of correction
vectors, raising Qwen2.5-Coder-7B’s CodeQL security ratio on the SVEN
test set from 76.8 to 85.7 with HumanEval pass@1 79.9 $`\to`$ 81.2 ([Yu
et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib577)). RobGen uses a small classifier to
predict whether the next line should open an if guard and, when if is
among the three most likely tokens, raises its logit, cutting the share
of DeepSeekCoder-1.3B’s CoderEval Java outputs that GPT-4o judges less
robust than the reference from 42.2% to 28.7% with Pass@1 slightly
higher ([Li et al., 2025h](#as1_bib.bib254)).

##### Caveats.

Correctness effects are mixed. PG-TD’s length penalty slightly lowers
the public-test pass rate (23.14 to 22.82); constrained beam sampling
lowers Llama3-8B pass@1 from 82.20 to 72.21, and an independent study
found, and repaired by script before testing, indentation issues in most
CodeGuard+ outputs for CodeLlama and Mistral ([Dai et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib97)); SCS-Code lowers CodeLlama pass@1 from 68.1 to
65.7, whereas DuoSteer reports an average correctness change of +7.5%.
RPG improves on repetition penalty, which also cuts repetition but
lowers HumanEval pass@1 to 0.092 (greedy: 0.301; RPG: 0.325). Evidence
is thin for several recent rows: surprisal selection rests on 10
task–seed pairs (sign test $`p=0.125`$); FunPRM targets correctness, and
its readability gain comes from three raters on 100 pairs, read off a
figure; DuoSteer reports both a test-swept and a held-out configuration
protocol.

##### Effects on correctness and non-targeted dimensions.

Correctness selectors measure no other dimension. With the QC3-30B
generator, SecCodePRM raises func@1 by 11.09 points alongside security
([Yu et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib578)). The ICSE 2026 re-evaluation finds
CodeGuard+’s security gains limited or negative on Mistral and notes the
original never measured the indentation defect above ([Dai et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib97)); its implementation also returns no code without
its constraints ([Wendlinger et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib538)). No
steering study we found measures SEC after R/M steering or the reverse.

##### Compute fairness.

Selectors compared at equal $`N`$ are budget-matched; comparisons with
one greedy sample are not. CodeT samples 100 test generations per
HumanEval problem ([Chen et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib67)); CodeMonkeys
spends approximately 2300 USD and resolves 57.4% of issues from a pool
whose oracle coverage is 69.8% ([Ehrlich et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib124)); type constraints add 39.1% average HumanEval
runtime ([Mündler et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib338)). Surprisal selection
is free only because every compared strategy already tests all samples
([Barnes, 2026](#as1_bib.bib52)). Best-of-$`n`$ at equal verifier and
call budget is thus the baseline for iterative methods (§–§), as in §.

##### Limitations.

Logit- and activation-level methods need white-box access (surprisal
selection needs sequence log-probabilities); of the highlighted
techniques only FunPRM does not. The ICSE 2026 study could not run three
of four security techniques on commercial models ([Dai et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib97)), and none applies to the frontier APIs of §.
Per-prompt CWE constraints do not transfer to unseen tasks, and CodeQL
labels miss vulnerabilities ([Dai et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib97)).

### S17.7. Training

##### Data curation and supervised fine-tuning.

phi-1 filtered web code with a classifier trained on GPT-4 “educational
value” ratings of about 100k files, added GPT-3.5-generated textbooks,
and reached 50.6% HumanEval pass@1 at 1.3B ([Gunasekar et al.,
2023](#as1_bib.bib162)). Open pipelines followed: The Stack v2 removes
low-quality files heuristically ([Lozhkov et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib273)); OpenCoder applies over 130 language-specific
rules and reports that filtering by GitHub stars reduced diversity and
worsened the model ([Huang et al., 2025b](#as1_bib.bib186)); Seed-Coder
distills an LLM oracle’s readability, modularity, clarity and
reusability scores into a 1.3B regression scorer ([Seed et al.,
2025b](#as1_bib.bib465)); and SwallowCode combines pylint-based
filtering with LLM rewriting that “enforces style conformity” ([Fujii
et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib131)). Some studies clean the code itself:
[Jain et al. (2024)](#as1_bib.bib216) rename variables and modularize
solutions with an LLM, gaining up to 30% correctness. Few curation
studies measure R/M of generated code: beyond the SmellCC row of
Table [S40](#as1_S18.T40 "Table S40 ‣ Training ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"),
[Xue et al. (2026b)](#as1_bib.bib565) report 79.6% and 83.1% fewer
smells for DeepSeek-V2 and Qwen-Coder (their refactoring tool kept only
91.3% correctness in its own test verification), and [Kuang et al.
(2026)](#as1_bib.bib236) find that data refactoring, selection and
cleaning raise the Maintainability Index of generated code while
synthesis and augmentation lower it. Large pretraining pipelines filter
for readability-like properties but report only functional benchmarks.

##### Preference optimization with quality signals.

Preference optimization learns from pairs of better and worse programs.
CodeUltraFeedback draws responses from 14 LLMs and brought
CodeLlama-7B-Instruct to a CUF-Bench judge score of 7.08 (GPT-3.5-Turbo:
7.18) and pass@1 from 37.9 to 43.1, though DPO variants scored slightly
below SFT alone ([Weyssow et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib540)). CodeDPO
reaches a 1.45x speedup on HumanEval+ with MagiCoder-S-DS-6.7B at 83.5%
correctness ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib596)). PLUM ([Zhang
et al., 2024b](#as1_bib.bib594)) and AceCoder ([Zeng et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib591)) (unrelated to ACECode below) use synthesized
tests for correctness only. For efficiency, Mercury found DPO stronger
than SFT ([Du et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib122)), while Afterburner found
both “rapidly saturate” ([Du et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib123)).

Several security results share a mechanism: secure and insecure programs
often differ in a few tokens (a sanitizer call, a parameterized query),
which a sequence-level loss dilutes. Hence SVEN and SafeCoder mask their
losses to the changed regions ([He and Vechev, 2023](#as1_bib.bib170);
[He et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib171)), Localized Preference Optimization
(LPO) masks security-relevant tokens after finding SimPO ineffective
([Hasan et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib168)), and SRCode assigns token-level
RL rewards ([Quan et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib424)).

##### Security-targeted training.

Security training has moved from curated fixes (SVEN, SafeCoder) to
synthesized data and then RL. HexaCoder synthesizes vulnerable and
repaired pairs with a CodeQL oracle ([Hajipour et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib166)); ProSec synthesizes vulnerability-inducing
instructions from CWEs and trains on preference pairs ([Xu et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib561)); LPO refines its distilled pairs with CodeQL and
Bandit feedback, reporting 31% and 64% fewer insecure files on Phi-2 and
StarCoder2-7B ([Hasan et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib168)). RL methods
include PurpCode (rule-referencing SFT plus multi-objective RL) ([Liu
et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib266)), SecCoderX (a learned vulnerability
reward model in place of the analyzer) ([Wu et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib541)), SRCode ([Quan et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib424)),
and pilots such as SecureCodeRL, whose evaluation had no Bandit findings
at all ([Sijwali and Saha, 2026](#as1_bib.bib479)). Training has also
reached coding agents: SecureVibe applies SFT and execution-feedback RL
to the agent’s security planning and testing, raising security pass@1 by
6.9 points on BaxBench and 11.5 on SusVibes, and functionality pass@1 by
4.1 on SWE-bench Verified ([Wang et al., 2026c](#as1_bib.bib528)).

##### Efficiency-targeted training.

Efficiency work uses profilers or simulators as the signal. PIE
fine-tunes on 77,967 human performance-improving C++ edit pairs timed in
the gem5 simulator, adding performance-conditioned generation and
self-play data ([Shypula et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib475)); EffiCoder
fine-tunes on the fastest correct candidate from several LLMs ([Huang
et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib183)). ACECode trains with proximal policy
optimization (PPO) on a combined correctness-runtime reward ([Yang
et al., 2024a](#as1_bib.bib569)); Afterburner runs Group Relative Policy
Optimization (GRPO) in an iterative refinement loop ([Du et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib123)); SuperCoder rewards assembly speedup over gcc
-O3 ([Wei et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib537)); [Nichols et al.
(2026)](#as1_bib.bib341) align models to serial and OpenMP code
performance; and RLPF ranks failed programs by execution progress and
correct ones by improvement toward an expert reference ([Jing et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib225)). Making execution time a usable reward is itself
studied: [Chambon et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib65) report that “once
timing drives the reward, small problems in measurement noise, reward
sparsity, or GRPO instability overwhelm the signal and make RL fail”;
with a calibrated sandbox and adapted GRPO they raise strict top-50%
pass@1 on their optimization tests from 18.0% to 31.3% on Qwen 2.5 7B
and from 30.7% to 50.4% on CWM 32B “while preserving pure-correctness
scores”. The largest RL efficiency gains are on GPU kernels: Kevin’s
multi-turn RL raises its base model’s kernel correctness from 56% to 82%
and mean speedup over PyTorch Eager from 0.53x to 1.10x, finding serial
refinement more useful than parallel sampling ([Baronio et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib53)); CUDA-L1 reports an average speedup of x3.12
(median x1.42) over default KernelBench baselines ([Li et al.,
2025f](#as1_bib.bib252)); and CUDA Agent reports 100%, 100% and 92%
faster rates over torch.compile on the three KernelBench levels ([Dai
et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib98)). Kernels fall outside the
general-purpose scope of the highlighted techniques (§) but show what a
precise, cheap-to-measure efficiency reward can do.

##### Reinforcement learning with program-analysis rewards.

REAL is the clearest attempt to train for SEC and R/M jointly with COR
(its maintainability detector is MyPy type checking) ([Yao et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib573)). Its motivating negative result is that
“optimizing for code quality alone leads to reward hacking”, with the
model emitting empty code or comments that maximize quality scores; its
ablation confirms that a quality-only reward yields safer but less
functional code. In 2026, [Jolfaei et al. (2026)](#as1_bib.bib226) map
Ruff violations to the tokens causing them, and [Skopin and Kotelnikov
(2026)](#as1_bib.bib482) find that static-analysis penalties alone bias
small models toward shorter completions. Themis trains code reward
models with readability and maintainability criteria, citing “the
limited proficiency of current RMs beyond scoring for functional
correctness” ([Paul et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib406)); we found no
well-documented study using such a model as an RL reward and measuring
R/M with independent instruments.

##### Side effects of reward optimization.

The first side effect is _length_. In RL from human feedback, “a purely
length-based reward reproduces most downstream RLHF improvements”
([Singhal et al., 2023](#as1_bib.bib481)); DPO also exploits verbosity
([Park et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib402)); ODIN counters it by discarding a
dedicated length head of the reward model ([Chen et al.,
2024a](#as1_bib.bib70)); and in RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR), GRPO
has an optimization bias that “artificially increases response length
(especially for incorrect outputs)” ([Liu et al.,
2025d](#as1_bib.bib272)). Since length moves with lines of code, comment
density and complexity metrics, judge-based R/M rewards face the same
confound, which no code study we found controls for. Analyzer-only
rewards pull the other way, toward short or empty code ([Skopin and
Kotelnikov, 2026](#as1_bib.bib482); [Yao et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib573)); PurpCode reports that with binary rewards
“models learn that generating no code is always ‘secure’ ” ([Liu et al.,
2025a](#as1_bib.bib266)).

The second is _exploitation of the test oracle_ behind every correctness
term. In a frontier RL run, an agent planned to “circumvent the tests by
making verify always return true” ([Baker et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib51)); on ImpossibleBench, whose tests contradict the
task, GPT-5 cheats on 76% of Oneoff-SWEbench tasks ([Zhong et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib610)); 28.5% of a SWE-bench Verified sample have tests
accepting an incorrect patch ([Rajan, 2026](#as1_bib.bib443)); in CATCH,
a chain-of-thought monitor’s protection erodes as the policy learns to
mislead it with code comments ([Wang et al., 2026f](#as1_bib.bib531));
and hacking learned in production coding environments generalizes to
broader misalignment ([MacDiarmid et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib275)). A
correctness term thus does not prevent degenerate code: a special-cased
solution is “correct” yet unmaintainable.

##### Highlighted techniques.

Table [S40](#as1_S18.T40 "Table S40 ‣ Training ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
lists the highlighted techniques (selection rule in §). Landmarks curate
or mask _data_; recent leaders shape the _objective_, mostly through
reinforcement-learning rewards. MPCoder learns Checkstyle style
attributes, per-user style vectors and a shared, contrastively trained
style adapter so that one CodeLlama-7B model writes Java in each user’s
own style, raising its Coding Style Score on PCISparse from 46.29 to
66.18, while HumanEval-X Java correctness falls from 30.49% to 26.18% on
that dataset ([Dai et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib99)).

Caveats. Several gains are measured with the training instrument:
CodeUltraFeedback’s GPT-3.5 judge also labelled the training data (with
a GPT-4-Turbo judge the authors report “more mitigated effects”), and
REAL evaluates with its reward’s program-analysis detectors. SafeCoder
“does not achieve strong generalization across different CWEs”. CodeDPO
times only problems solved both before and after training. PurpCode’s
baseline is its own untrained base model, SecCoderX’s the unaligned
model, and Afterburner is evaluated on the same authors’ Venus
benchmark. Correctness costs are uneven
(§[S17.7](#as1_S17.SS7.SSS0.Px8 "Effects on correctness and non-targeted dimensions. ‣ S17.7. Training ‣ S17. Per-family detail: studies, highlighted techniques, effects, compute fairness and limitations ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")).
No highlighted technique reports an effect on an untargeted dimension.

##### Effects on correctness and non-targeted dimensions.

Correctness. The security literature reports small correctness costs,
which the evidence partly supports: SVEN “closely matches the original
LMs in functional correctness” ([He and Vechev, 2023](#as1_bib.bib170)),
although its CodeGen-2.7B pass@1 falls from 14.0 to 11.7, and ProSec and
PurpCode report no or minimal utility loss ([Xu et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib561); [Liu et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib266)). SafeCoder
leaves StarCoder-1B’s correctness unchanged, but on Phi-2, against
standard instruction tuning, raises security from 69.9 to 90.9 while
lowering HumanEval pass@1 from 48.3 to 46.1 ([He et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib171)). LPO lowers Mistral-7B’s HumanEvalX pass@1 from
37.1 (SFT) to 28.7, and without its regularizer gains security “at a
steep cost of decreased general coding ability” ([Hasan et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib168)). On SecCodePLT+ the SFT baseline’s function
score (0.8659) exceeds REAL’s (0.7561) ([Yao et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib573)). SecCoderX, whose metric weights safety rate by
functional correctness, reports that prior methods “often degrade ESR by
14-54%” ([Wu et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib541)). Efficiency tuning shows
the same tension: ACECode describes PIE as “improving efficiency but
compromising correctness” ([Yang et al., 2024a](#as1_bib.bib569)), ECCO
finds that “no existing methods can improve time/space efficiency
without sacrificing functional correctness” ([Waghjale et al.,
2024](#as1_bib.bib523)), and a stricter test-coverage reward on hard
problems “reduces optimization failures but increases correctness
failures” ([Zheng et al., 2026a](#as1_bib.bib605)). Conversely,
correctness-only RLVR neglects efficiency: 36.6% of the RLVR baseline’s
correct programs were slow, versus 15.0% for RLPF ([Jing et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib225)). The correctness gains of EffiCoder, ACECode,
Afterburner and SuperCoder cannot be separated from ordinary training on
verified solutions.

Non-targeted dimensions are rarely measured (only 15 of 124 studies): no
security study in
Tables [S39](#as1_S18.T39 "Table S39 ‣ Training ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
and [S40](#as1_S18.T40 "Table S40 ‣ Training ‣ S18. Per-family result tables and highlighted techniques ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
reports readability or runtime, nor any efficiency study security or
readability. LPO’s data pipeline hints at the risk: repeated security
refinement produced “overengineered and low quality code, training on
which reduced models’ code utility” ([Hasan et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib168)). Terminology blurs the picture: LPO’s “code
quality” means pass@$`k`$, and REAL measures security and
maintainability in separate scenarios, not on the same outputs.

##### Compute fairness.

Training-time methods trade a one-off training cost for no extra
inference calls, so per-query comparison with the loops of § is not
meaningful; most studies report training cost in no form permitting
amortization (phi-1’s 8 A100s for 4 days excepted). Some headline
numbers include inference-time search (PIE’s 6.86 speedup is the best of
eight generations; Afterburner iterates with sandbox execution), and
comparisons with inference-time baselines, such as REAL against
constrained decoding and prompt optimization, are not budget-matched.

##### Limitations.

_Base-model dependence._ Most studies train models of at most 7B, REAL
notes that “reinforcement learning often requires a reasonably strong
base model” ([Yao et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib573)), and transfer to
frontier models is untested. _Oracle circularity._ Training signal and
evaluation often share an analyzer family or judge (§), and analyzers
disagree: REAL found CodeQL “unexpectedly ineffective” on SecCodePLT+,
and PurpCode found CodeGuru detects more vulnerabilities than CodeQL.
_Contamination._ Synthetic data from GPT-3.5, GPT-4 or frontier LLMs may
overlap with public benchmarks; phi-1 studied contamination and PurpCode
excluded benchmark sources, but many studies report neither.
_Reproducibility._ Data are often partly closed (phi-1 omits
synthetic-data details “for proprietary reasons”), and RL results depend
on checkpoint selection, as RLPF notes.

### S17.8. Hybrid and other techniques

The 191 studies of the hybrid and other group (§) are grouped here by
the mechanisms their signal sources map to: retrieval (retrieved
knowledge), self-refinement (the model’s own critique), another LLM (a
critic, reviewer or second agent), tool feedback (static analyzer,
compiler, test execution or profiler), a learned verifier, training
(training-time stage or a reward model) and decoding (in-decoding
stage). Human input, used by 17 studies, is not counted as a mechanism.
For each combination, the number of studies and up to four
representative studies are listed; studies without a bibliography entry
are named by their technique and record identifier
(§[S4](#as1_S4 "S4. ##### Domains.

By keywords in their languages, benchmarks and titles, 111 of the
studies work on specialized code: GPU or accelerator kernels (66),
hardware design in Verilog, VHDL, Chisel or high-level synthesis (24),
C-to-Rust migration (20), parallel code with OpenMP, MPI or OpenACC (9),
smart contracts (3) and PLC programs (2); a study can fall under
several. 90 evaluate on Python. The keyword match is approximate; the
head-to-head excludes domain-specific techniques by the pass-2 rule of
§, not by these keywords.

##### Targets and effects.

By technique row, the target improves in 112 of 122 efficiency rows, 39
of 46 security rows and 33 of 35 readability/maintainability rows;
correctness is unreported in 31, 9 and 3 of them. Efficiency rows thus
carry most of the unreported correctness, as in the review overall.

## S19. The model landscape: sampling, reasoning, cutoffs and vendor reports

### S19.1. Overview of the 2025–2026 models

Most techniques in §§– of the main article were evaluated on
now-superseded models.
Table [S9](#as1_S7.T9 "Table S9 ‣ S7.3. Model landscape ‣ S7. Additional Tables ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
(§[S7.3](#as1_S7.SS3 "S7.3. Model landscape ‣ S7. Additional Tables ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
lists frontier closed and major open-weight and code-specialized models
released January 2025 to October 2026, under vendor names, with
vendor-reported coding scores, architecture and training cutoffs; the
Supplementary Material
(§[S5](#as1_S5 "S5. Model releases, January 2025 to October 2026 ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code"))
lists every release with its month and source. The experiments (§) use a
fixed subset.

#### S19.1.1. Frontier and open-weight models

##### Frontier closed models.

Frontier vendors now ship tiered flagships every few months. Anthropic’s
fifth generation adds a top tier, Claude Fable, alongside Claude Mythos
variants whose most sensitive capabilities go to vetted users via a
trusted access program ([Anthropic, 2026h](#as1_bib.bib32)); current
models are Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5
([Anthropic, 2026f](#as1_bib.bib30)). OpenAI moved to three tiers per
generation: GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra and Luna ([OpenAI,
2026g](#as1_bib.bib393)), then GPT-6 Astra, Sol and Luna ([OpenAI,
2026i](#as1_bib.bib395)). Google’s Gemini 2.5 and Gemini 4 Argon are
sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models ([Comanici et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib91); [Google DeepMind, 2026d](#as1_bib.bib157)), and
xAI’s recent cards name the vendor SpaceXAI, “a doing-business-as (DBA)
name of XAI LLC” ([SpaceXAI, 2026b](#as1_bib.bib486)).

##### Open-weight and code models.

The largest open-weight models are MoEs from DeepSeek, Qwen, Z.ai,
Moonshot, MiniMax and Xiaomi, up to 2.4T total and 95B active parameters
for Qwen3.8 ([Qwen Team, 2026e](#as1_bib.bib439)). Western releases are
mostly smaller (gpt-oss, Gemma, Llama 4, Olmo, Muse Glimmer), except
NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Ultra and Mistral Large 4 (weights announced, not
yet released). Technical reports describe DeepSeek-R1 ([DeepSeek-AI
et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib113)), Kimi k1.5, K2 and K2.5 ([Team et al.,
2025c](#as1_bib.bib503); [Team et al., 2025b](#as1_bib.bib502); [Team
et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib505)), MiniMax-M1 ([MiniMax et al.,
2025a](#as1_bib.bib311)), Magistral ([Mistral-AI et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib328)), OLMo 2 ([OLMo et al., 2024](#as1_bib.bib369)),
Llama-Nemotron ([Bercovich et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib55)), and Gemma 3
and Gemma 4 ([Team et al., 2025a](#as1_bib.bib500); [Team et al.,
2026a](#as1_bib.bib501)), the latter pairing dense and MoE variants;
Ai2’s Olmo 3 also releases its training data ([Olmo et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib370)). Code-specialized releases include Meta’s CWM
([FAIR CodeGen team et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib128)), Qwen3-Coder and
Qwen3-Coder-Next ([Qwen Team, 2025d](#as1_bib.bib428); [Cao et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib62)), Mistral’s Devstral ([Mistral AI,
2025c](#as1_bib.bib315)) and Ai2’s SERA coding agents ([Shen et al.,
2026b](#as1_bib.bib468)).

##### Benchmarks.

Vendor benchmarks changed as fast as the models. By September 2026 the
top SWE-bench Verified entry on the vals.ai leaderboard (grey
literature) reached 97.00% ([Vals AI, 2026](#as1_bib.bib520)), and
OpenAI “stopped reporting SWE-bench Verified scores” in February 2026
([OpenAI, 2026m](#as1_bib.bib399)). Recent cards report SWE-bench Pro (a
public set plus held-out and proprietary commercial repository sets)
([Deng et al., 2026b](#as1_bib.bib117)), Terminal-Bench 2.0 to 4.0
([Merrill et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib284)) and DeepSWE. On Terminal-Bench
2.1, open models report 90.6% (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, above Claude Opus 5
at 89.1%) ([DeepSeek-AI, 2026d](#as1_bib.bib112)), 88.3 (Kimi K3)
([Moonshot AI, 2026c](#as1_bib.bib334)) and 88.2 (GLM-5.3) ([Z.ai,
2026g](#as1_bib.bib588)), against 88.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol ([OpenAI,
2026g](#as1_bib.bib393)). Harnesses differ, so the numbers are not
comparable, but open weights, required for decoding- and training-time
techniques (§, §), no longer trail far on correctness.

How vendors moved away from user-controlled sampling, what reasoning
models change for code quality, the training cutoffs that define our
contamination windows, and what vendors themselves report about code
quality are detailed in the following subsections.

### S19.2. The Retreat From Sampling Control

From Claude Opus 4.7 onward, non-default temperature, top_p or top_k
values on Anthropic’s models “return a 400 error on every request,
regardless of whether thinking is used”; older models restrict them only
with thinking on ([Anthropic, 2026i](#as1_bib.bib33)). OpenAI’s GPT-6
guide says to drop temperature and top_p unless reasoning effort is none
([OpenAI, 2026l](#as1_bib.bib398)). Google recommended Gemini 3’s
default temperature of 1.0 ([Google, 2026a](#as1_bib.bib146)), and for
Gemini 4 Argon sampling parameters “are ignored” ([Google,
2026f](#as1_bib.bib151)). xAI’s reasoning models cannot turn reasoning
off and reject penalty and stop parameters ([SpaceXAI,
2026c](#as1_bib.bib487)). Only an effort level remains. Greedy decoding
and temperature sweeps, the usual pass@$`k`$ setting in the surveyed
papers, are not reproducible on these APIs; variance must come from
repeated samples at a recorded effort, and logit-level techniques (§)
need open weights.

### S19.3. Reasoning Models and Code Quality

Most flagships since mid-2025 are reasoning models with adjustable
effort. Vendors report effort’s effect on correctness and cost, not
quality; independent evidence covers only security. On CWEval, o4-mini
produced secure code more often than the non-reasoning Claude 3.7
Sonnet, yet a non-reasoning model in an agentic workflow matched it
([Saul et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib456)). SecPI reports that “even
state-of-the-art RLMs frequently introduce critical security
vulnerabilities” and that generic security reminders “consistently
degrade functional correctness” ([Wang et al., 2026d](#as1_bib.bib529)).
We found no study of reasoning effort’s effect on readability,
maintainability or efficiency. Hidden reasoning also complicates compute
fairness: an added critique step competes with the model’s own
deliberation (§).

### S19.4. Training Cutoffs and Contamination Windows

Stated cutoffs range from June 2024 for gpt-oss ([OpenAI et al.,
2025](#as1_bib.bib400)) and GPT-4.1 ([OpenAI, 2025h](#as1_bib.bib378)),
and August 2024 for Llama 4 and Gemma 3 ([Meta, 2025](#as1_bib.bib285);
[Google DeepMind, 2025a](#as1_bib.bib152)), to Jun 2026 for Anthropic’s
current models ([Anthropic, 2026f](#as1_bib.bib30)) and June 2026
pretraining for Grok 4.7 ([SpaceXAI, 2026a](#as1_bib.bib485)). Two
details widen these windows. Some vendors date data separately: Nemotron
3 Ultra’s pre-training data runs to September 2025 and its post-training
data to May 2026 ([NVIDIA, 2026f](#as1_bib.bib367)), and Grok 4.6 used
“data generated as late as June 2026 in its supplemental training”
([SpaceXAI, 2026b](#as1_bib.bib486)). And DeepSeek, Qwen, Z.ai and
Moonshot state no cutoff in the sources we examined, so date splits for
them must first probe the cutoff; open training data, as in Olmo 3
([Olmo et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib370)), permits a direct audit.
Memorization of older benchmarks is documented: from issue text alone,
models find the buggy file of a SWE-bench Verified issue with “up to 76%
accuracy”, against “up to 53%” on other repositories ([Liang et al.,
2026](#as1_bib.bib256)), and agents degrade without familiar repository
cues ([Chen et al., 2026d](#as1_bib.bib72)). Date-tagged benchmarks
allow evaluation “only on time-windows after the model’s cutoff date”
([Jain et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib217)), but with frontier cutoffs in
mid-2026 such windows hold only months of tasks. See § for benchmark
choice under this constraint; § reports contaminated and post-cutoff
splits separately.

### S19.5. What Vendors Report About Code Quality

The NF column of
Table [S9](#as1_S7.T9 "Table S9 ‣ S7.3. Model landscape ‣ S7. Additional Tables ‣ Supplementary Material for “Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code” ‣ Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code")
is mostly nr. On security, Qwen reports SecCodeBench and CWEval ([Cao
et al., 2026](#as1_bib.bib62); [Qwen Team, 2026b](#as1_bib.bib436)),
Meta CyberSecEval insecure-code tests ([Meta, 2026f](#as1_bib.bib291)),
and xAI an internal eval, SecureCodeReview ([SpaceXAI,
2026b](#as1_bib.bib486)). On efficiency, MiniMax reports SWE-Perf,
SWE-fficiency and KernelBench Hard ([MiniMax, 2025b](#as1_bib.bib303);
[MiniMax, 2026a](#as1_bib.bib305)). Closest to maintainability is
FrontierCode, which “measures whether AI-generated pull requests would
be mergeable by open-source maintainers, measuring behavioral
correctness, regression safety, scope discipline, style, and adherence
to codebase conventions” ([SpaceXAI, 2026b](#as1_bib.bib486)); Google,
OpenAI and Anthropic also report it ([Google DeepMind,
2026b](#as1_bib.bib155); [OpenAI, 2026i](#as1_bib.bib395); [Anthropic,
2026d](#as1_bib.bib28)), but since it includes correctness it does not
isolate R/M. Mistral adds a blind human rating of “coding quality”
([Mistral AI, 2026b](#as1_bib.bib326)), and OpenAI an extraneous-edit
rate ([OpenAI, 2025h](#as1_bib.bib378)). No vendor reports complexity,
code smells or lint violations, and system-card cyber-security sections
measure offensive capability, not ordinary generated code’s security.
Independently, a SonarQube analysis of 4,442 Java assignments found “no
direct correlation” between pass@1 and “the overall quality and
security” of the generated code ([Sabra et al., 2025](#as1_bib.bib451)).
